paragraphs.text: Treatise of our most pious emperor Justinian, sent to Menas, the most holy and most blessed archbishop and patriarch of the fortunate city, against the impious Origen and his [?]. It has always been, and still is, our earnest concern that the orthodox and blameless faith of Christians, and the good order

of the most holy catholic [?] and apostolic church of God, be kept undisturbed in every respect, and we place this care first among all others. Through it we believe that the kingdom in this present world has been handed down to us by God and is preserved, and that the enemies of our state are made subject to us; through it, too, we hope to find mercy before his goodness in the age to come. For even though the enemy of the human race keeps devising all sorts of pretexts by which he strives to lay snares for human souls, God's love for humankind nevertheless brings his wickedness to nothing, exposes his adversaries, and does not allow his own flock to be harmed or scattered. We say this because it has come to our attention that certain people, who do not keep the fear of God in mind and do not understand how to discern sound doctrine (the discernment through which everyone who [?] the truth is saved), have abandoned the divine Scriptures and the holy fathers, whom the catholic church of God holds as its teachers and by whom every heresy everywhere has been driven out and the orthodox faith made clear, and instead lay claim to Origen and to his pagan, Arian and Manichaean doctrines, through which he fell into the pit. How can such people be counted among Christians, when they champion the cause of a man who strove to hand down the teachings of the pagans, the Manichaeans, the Arians and the other heretics? Above all, he blasphemed against the holy and consubstantial Trinity itself and dared to say that the Father is greater than the Son, the Son greater than the Holy Spirit, and the Holy Spirit greater than the other spirits. To his impiety he added this as well, saying that the Son cannot see the Father, nor the Holy Spirit the Son; that the Son and the Holy Spirit are creatures; and that what we are in relation to the Son, the Son is in relation to the Father. He also adds this to his blasphemies, in the first book of his work On First Principles, saying in these very words: "In the beginning that we conceive of, God by his will brought into being as great a number of intellectual substances as he was able to sustain. For we must say that God's power too is finite, and we must not remove its limits on the pretext of reverent speech. For if the divine power is infinite, it necessarily cannot even understand itself, since by nature the infinite cannot be grasped. He has therefore made as many things as he could take hold of, keep in hand, and hold together under his providence, just as he also prepared as much matter as he was able to set in order." What greater blasphemy against God could Origen have uttered? He devised grades within the holy Trinity, wanting even by this means to introduce polytheism, and he talked fantastic nonsense about the very power of God being limited. Also full of every impiety is this part of his mythology: the claim that all genera and species are co-eternal with God, and that of the — The holy and ecumenical fifth council took place [?] of the emperor Justinian, and it anathematized Origen and his impious writings and [?] doctrines, as well as those of Evagrius and of Didymus, who held Origen's opinions; from the book of the acts of the [?] —

rational beings, those that sinned, and so fell from the state in which they had been, were cast into bodies as punishment, in proportion to their own sins; once purified, they are brought back again to the state in which they were before, putting off evil and their bodies entirely; and then a second, a third and many more times they are cast into different bodies for punishment. He also supposes that various worlds have come into being and are coming into being, some already past and others still to come. Who is so foolish that he does not shudder in his mind on hearing such things, because of the sheer excess of impiety? Who would not loathe the madman Origen, who invented such blasphemies against God and set them out in writing? Since these are forbidden to all Christians and plainly expose their own impiety, we thought it superfluous to grant them a refutation. If, then, all heretics have been cast out of the most holy church for perverting perhaps one or two doctrines, and have been placed under anathema together with their own teachings, what Christian at all will tolerate championing Origen himself and his wicked writings? He uttered so many blasphemies, supplied almost all heretics with so much material for perdition and blasphemy, and for that reason was long ago placed under anathema by the holy fathers together with his abominable doctrines. Even if one grants that Origen, that fighter against God, mixed some orthodox doctrines into his wicked writings, as is also found among the other heretics, these do not belong to him but to the holy church of God. And he contrived this very thing maliciously, in order to deceive the simpler sort. Nourished on the myths of the pagans and wanting to spread them further, he made a show of interpreting the divine Scriptures, so that by mixing his abominable doctrines into his commentaries on the divine Scriptures he might maliciously introduce his pagan and Manichaean error and his Arian madness, and be able to ensnare those who are not well versed in the divine Scripture. For what else did Origen [?] than what was said by Plato, who spread the madness of the pagans far and wide? And from whom else did Arius take the disease he wrote up as his own, if not from the man who, to the ruin of his own soul, devised grades within the holy and consubstantial Trinity? In what does he fall short of the Manichaean, when he says that human souls were cast into bodies for punishment because of sin? He holds that they were first minds and holy powers, then grew sated with divine contemplation and turned to the worse, and so grew cold toward the love of God, were therefore called souls, and were cast into bodies as punishment. This alone would have been enough for his complete condemnation, since it belongs to pagan impiety. For when God said, "Let us make man in our image and likeness," it turns out, according to that man's empty arguments, that a body alone, without a soul, came to be in the image and likeness of God, if the soul existed beforehand at all and was cast or enclosed into the body after the body had come to be. And one would be absolutely bound to say that God himself, the Creator of man, is a body, since he made the body in his own image and likeness. But how can

a body be the image of the bodiless? So may it never happen that Christians assent to these things. If, according to Origen's blasphemy, souls existed beforehand and were sent down into bodies as punishment because they had sinned, so that they might be disciplined and come to their senses, then they ought to sin no longer. For if the body was given to the soul as punishment for sin, so that by suffering it might be trained to honour God, how is it that the body works and strives together with it in sinning, which does not happen to those being punished? Bonds, prisons, fetters and, in short, all such things serve to restrain the punished from doing wrong and from sinning. A chain is not given to someone who has sinned as a helper in sin so that he may sin more, but so that, tormented by his chains, he may stop sinning. It is therefore perfectly clear that souls were not cast into bodies to correct earlier sins, as their nonsense has it. Rather, God created the body and the soul at the same time, that is, the complete human being. That is why we await recompense for the deeds done through the body, whether good or bad. This is what the divine apostle Paul teaches us when he says: "For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive what is due for the things done through the body, whether good or bad." We must therefore pay attention to the Apostle's words: he did not say that the one being judged must receive what is due for what he did before the body. If a human being is punished by the Judge of the earth, or found worthy of due honour, only for what he did through the body, and there is no mention whatever of earlier sins, it is clear that souls do not exist before bodies. For if they had existed beforehand, the Apostle would have said "the things done before the body" as well as "the things done through the body." That human souls are intellectual and rational is agreed by all, and we do not think that even those who champion Origen deny it. Let those who hold Origen's views tell us, then: if, as they say, their souls existed before their bodies, in what rank were they before they entered the bodies, and what were they doing? For if they existed beforehand, they ought to know where they were and how they came to be here. If they cannot possibly say this, because it is not the truth, then clearly their teachings are myths. Perhaps they will say that only after entering the bodies are souls able to discern and know what they do. But if they say this, then by their empty arguments the body turns out to be more precious than the soul, since it bestows on the soul the gift of becoming intellectual and rational. To say this is full of utter folly and absurdity. And why at all, if the soul existed beforehand as they claim, would it need any learning or teaching once it is in the body, being introduced little by little and advancing to greater and more perfect things? For if it existed beforehand, it would know what is beneficial and need no learning, and since it possessed knowledge it would correct itself by its own diligence. If it knew its fault, it would not be taught, since it would already understand. But if it is taught because it is ignorant, it did not know beforehand; and if it did not know beforehand, it did not exist beforehand. So it is clear that it did not exist beforehand. For God alone is the cause of our coming into being: just as he made us when we did not

exist, so too, once we have come to be, he saves us by his own grace, if we prove worthy and fit. For when God said, "Let us make man in our image and likeness," he created both at the same time: he formed the body and created the intellectual and rational soul. God formed the body and at once created the soul, making the human being complete. For a body without a soul is not a human being, nor is a soul without a body. If the soul existed beforehand, as Origen babbles, why did the most holy prophet Zechariah say, "who forms the spirit of man within him"? If it had existed beforehand, he should rather have said "who encloses" or "who sends down the spirit of man within him." But by saying "forms," the prophet shows that God made the soul, just like the body, by his own power and goodness, without its existing beforehand. So when it is said that man came to be in the image and likeness of God and was granted the divine breath, this shows that the soul was created not only intellectual and rational but also immortal, so as to rule over all the works on earth. This is also what the theologian Gregory said of the soul: that it is from God and divine and shares in the nobility from above. This is not meant in the sense that some, who indulge their imaginations, claim, that the soul is of the divine substance. It means that the soul came into being through God's breath and received from him the gift of being intellectual, rational and immortal, so that it does not die together with the body as the irrational animals do, but by grace shares in the nobility from above, that is, in immortality. John, patriarch of Constantinople, among the saints, bears witness to this in his eleventh discourse on creation, where he says: "'And he breathed,' it says, 'into his face the breath of life, and the man became a living soul.' Here some senseless people, moved by their own reasonings and thinking nothing worthy of God, without taking into account that the words are an accommodation to us, attempt to say that the soul is from the substance of God. What madness! What folly!" That is what the father says on the matter. Notice that of all the other works on earth God said, "Let it come to be" and "Let the earth bring forth," and it was so. But of man he says, "Let us make man," and not only "Let us make," but "in our image and likeness"; and taking dust from the earth he formed man with his own hands, "and breathed into his face the breath of life, and the man became a living soul." From this, then, one can see how God made man more honourable than all the other creatures on earth. All the others he spoke into being by a word, and they came to be; but man, as has been said, he created himself with his own hands, according to the divine Scripture. And he subjected everything he had made on earth to the man who came into being on the sixth day, so that the man might be master of all the creatures on earth, which had already come into being and been prepared for him, while he himself was mastered by his Maker. The theologian Gregory, among the saints, also teaches us this in his oration on New Sunday, saying: "Thus a first is counted among the days, and a second, and a third, and so on up to the seventh, the day of rest from works. Among these days the things that came to be are distributed, set in order by ineffable principles, and not

brought forth all at once by the all-powerful Word, for whom merely to think or to speak is a deed accomplished. If man was revealed last, and honoured with God's hand and image, there is nothing surprising in that. For, as for a king, the palace had to be prepared first, and then the king brought in, already escorted by all things." If, then, according to the teaching of the theologian Gregory, man was revealed last and honoured with God's hand and image, if everything was prepared for him beforehand by God, and if, as for a king, the palace was set up first and he was then brought in by God as king, already escorted by all things, how can those who rave after Origen say that souls existed beforehand and are sent down into bodies because of sin, bound to pay the penalty for sins committed earlier? Gregory, among the saints, says the very opposite: that man came into being after all things, was honoured by God, and reigns over everything on earth. This is no sign of punishment; on the contrary, it shows every kind of providence and kindness. In agreement with the theologian Gregory, John, patriarch of Constantinople, among the saints, teaches us in his eleventh discourse on creation, saying: "But perhaps someone might say: Why, if the soul is more precious than the body, is the lesser created first, and then the greater and superior? Do you not see, beloved, that the same thing happened in creation as a whole? Just as heaven and earth, the sun and the moon and all other things were created, and after all of them came man, who was to be entrusted with rule over them all, so in the forming of man the body is formed first, and then the more precious soul. For just as the irrational creatures, which were to be useful for service, are created before man, so that he who was to enjoy their use might find their service ready, so too the body is created before the soul, so that when the soul is brought forth according to God's ineffable wisdom, it may be able to display its own activities through the movement of the body." We say this to show our hearers that we speak the same things as the holy fathers, who everywhere reject the pre-existence of souls. Again, the holy Scripture says of Adam and Eve: "God blessed them and said, 'Increase and multiply, fill the earth and subdue it.'" How, then, if souls existed before bodies, were these pre-existing souls of their myths to increase by God's command? And how could God bless souls that had already fallen into sin, so that they might increase and multiply? Souls that had sinned would have deserved a curse rather than a blessing. And if, according to Origen's myths, souls existed beforehand in some other rank, why did God form Adam alone? Was the soul of Adam the only one that had sinned at that time, and was that why God formed only one body? For if there were other souls before him, other bodies would have had to be formed at the same time to receive them. And how, by their own arguments, could a soul that had sinned and had been cast into a body as punishment be placed by the Lord in the paradise of delight? If it had been cast into a body for punishment, it would have been set not in a paradise of delight but in a place

of punishment. But God loved man, whom he formed after all his other works, so much that even after man had transgressed the commandment God gave him and had for that reason been cast out of paradise, and even as the human race grew and sin multiplied because people's minds were bent diligently on what is worse, God in his goodness did not neglect his own creature. Instead he admonished it in various ways, which the holy Scripture makes known. And since our more grievous illnesses needed a greater cure, the only-begotten Word of God himself, one of the Trinity, that is, one person of the holy Trinity, became man out of his love for humankind while remaining God. He neither changed his divine substance into the human, nor turned his human substance into the divine. He is one and the same, recognized in both natures without confusion and without division. For remaining what he was, he became what he was not. Taking on himself, in his own flesh, the death we owed under the condemnation that followed the transgression, he freed us from eternal death. He became the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, and rising as the firstborn from the dead he raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places, as the apostolic tradition teaches us. For although at the beginning human nature was deprived of paradise through disobedience, nevertheless, as has been said, the only-begotten Son of God, because of the great love with which he loved us, united our nature to himself inseparably according to hypostasis in the womb of the holy and glorious Theotokos and ever-virgin Mary. He granted us a greater grace, freely giving us the kingdom in heaven. John, patriarch of Constantinople, among the saints, also bears witness to this in his discourse on the Ascension, saying: "We who appeared unworthy of the earth have today been brought up into heaven. We who were not worthy even of rule below have ascended to the kingdom above; we have passed beyond the heavens and laid hold of the royal throne. The very nature on whose account the Cherubim guarded paradise today sits above the Cherubim." It has therefore been shown that souls did not pre-exist in heaven and then, after sinning, get sent down into bodies as punishment, as Origen babbles. On the contrary, the whole of human nature, body and soul, was created on earth and has been found worthy of the kingdom in heaven through the goodness that befits God. So those who keep and fulfil God's commandment are found worthy to share in heaven the life of the angels, whom we have been commanded to imitate on earth through our confession toward God. For God, in his inexpressible love for humankind, wished to be glorified on earth by human beings just as he is glorified in heaven by the holy powers, and so he created man as a second angel on earth, so that all things might be filled with the glory of God. That is why the Lord, when teaching how people ought to pray, says: "Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name, your kingdom come, your will be done, as in heaven so also on earth." In agreement with what we have said, the theologian Gregory, among the saints, also, in his oration on holy Pascha,

…teaches, speaking as follows: "Wishing to show this, the Word, the Craftsman, makes one living being out of both natures, the visible and the invisible: he fashions man. He takes the body from matter that already existed, and he places in it life from himself, which Scripture knows as an intellectual soul and the image of God. So he sets man on the earth as a kind of second world, a great one in a small one; another angel, a worshipper of mixed nature; overseer of the visible creation and initiate of the spiritual; king of the things on earth, ruled from above." Notice, then, that when the father says God made man out of both, he adds that God took the body from matter that already existed. But he did not say that the soul pre-existed, or that it came into being from some pre-existing substance. He said that God placed life in man from himself, which Scripture knows as an intellectual soul and the image of God. And when the father says that God made man king of the things on earth, ruled from above, he refutes the claim that souls were thrown into bodies as a punishment. To rule on earth and to be ruled by God alone is not a penalty but a great gift from God. We also think it necessary to say this to those who teach pre-existence: if it were true that souls existed before bodies, they would know and remember what they did before entering bodies, just as after death they know and recognize what they did in their bodies. We will prove from the very words of the gospel that the soul, after it departs this life, knows what it has done. In the Gospel according to Luke, in the passage about Lazarus and the rich man, our Master and Saviour Christ says this: "There was a rich man who was dressed in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day. And a poor man named Lazarus, covered with sores, was laid at his gate, longing to be fed with the crumbs that fell from the rich man's table; the dogs even came and licked his sores. The poor man died and was carried away by the angels to Abraham's bosom. The rich man also died and was buried. And in Hades, where he was in torment, he lifted up his eyes and saw Abraham far off, and Lazarus in his bosom. He called out and said, 'Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am in agony in this flame.' But Abraham said, 'Child, remember that in your lifetime you received your good things, and Lazarus likewise evil things; but now he is comforted here, and you are in agony. And besides all this, a great chasm has been fixed between us and you, so that those who want to cross from here to you cannot, nor can anyone cross from there to us.' He said, 'Then I beg you, father, to send him to my father's house, for I have five brothers, so that he may warn them, and they too may not come into this place of torment.'" So let those who champion the views of Origen be put to shame by the words of the

holy gospel as well. For if souls existed before bodies, they would also know what they had done before the body, just as after departing this life they remember what they did through the body. This is what we have learned from the words of the holy gospel. That the holy fathers, following the divinely inspired Scriptures, condemned such doctrines, together with Origen, who made up these fables, we have already clearly shown from the words of the holy fathers themselves. We will show it no less through the testimonies of the holy fathers that follow. First we will cite Saint Peter, who was bishop of Alexandria and a martyr, who bears witness for us in these words. Of Saint Peter, bishop of the great city of Alexandria and martyr, from the first discourse, on the fact that the soul did not pre-exist and was not cast into a body because it had sinned: "We think it right to set out what concerns the first man, who was made of dust from the earth, to show that he came into being as one and the same at one and the same time, even if he is sometimes spoken of in part as the inner and the outer man. For even though, according to the Saviour's word, he who made the inside also made the outside, he did so once for all and at one time, that is, on the same day, when God said, 'Let us make man after our image and likeness.' From this it is plain that man did not come into being from a joining together, as though one part existed beforehand and another came together with it from somewhere else. For if it was a joining together, why was what was made also recorded?" And after other things: "So it is not possible that souls sinned in heaven before bodies, or that they existed at all before bodies. For this teaching belongs to Greek philosophy, which is foreign and alien to those who wish to live piously in Christ."

Of the same, from the mystagogy he delivered to the church when he was about to receive the crown of martyrdom: "Therefore I urge you, be watchful, for you are about to enter into tribulation again. You know how many dangers my father and bishop Theonas, who brought me up, endured from those who were mad for idols. I received his throne; would that I had received his way of life too. You know also how the great Dionysius hid from place to place, and was harassed by Sabellius besides. And what shall I say of Heraclas and Demetrius, the blessed bishops, and the trials they suffered from the madman Origen, who sowed schisms in the church that have stirred up disturbances to this day?" How then can anyone of sound mind oppose what was said against Origen by Peter, the holy martyr and bishop of Alexandria? He took up the good contest for Christ, and he not only denounced Origen and his abominable doctrines but also testifies that the holy fathers before him endured many trials from that man's derangement. Athanasius among the saints, who was himself also bishop of Alexandria, said this in his discourse on the life of the blessed Antony: "How [?] can you mock us for saying that Christ has been manifested as man, when you derive the soul from the mind and claim that it went astray and fell from the vault of heaven into a body?" Those who hear this must note

that Athanasius among the saints clearly opposes those who say that the mind pre-exists, and that the soul came from it by sinning and fell from the vault of heaven into a body. Of the same holy Athanasius, from the second discourse against the Arians: "The whole visible creation came into being in six days. On the first day came the light, which he called day. On the second, the firmament. On the third he gathered the waters, revealed the dry land, and brought forth the various fruits in it. On the fourth he made the sun and the moon and the whole choir of stars. On the fifth he created the living things in the sea and the birds in the air. On the sixth he made the four-footed animals on the earth, and finally man, made of a rational soul and a body. 'And his invisible attributes, since the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood through the things he has made.' Light is not like night, nor the sun like the moon, nor the irrational animals like rational man, nor angels like thrones, nor these like powers. All of them are creatures, but each of the things made according to its kind is and remains in its own essence as it was made." See, holy Athanasius also hands down the teaching that God made man after all the other creatures, made of a body and an intellectual and rational soul. He did not say that the body was made after all things, so that a pre-existing soul might enter it. He said that man was made after all the creatures, made of a rational soul and a body, showing that God fashioned both, body and soul, at the same time. Another of Origen's blasphemies is the claim that the Lord's soul pre-existed and that God the Word was united to it before he became flesh from the Virgin. Athanasius among the saints refutes this nonsense himself in his letter to Epictetus, where he says: "[?] All who think that the flesh born of Mary existed before Mary, and that before her God the Word had a human soul and was always in it before his coming, will condemn themselves." If, then, as Athanasius among the saints said, the soul of our Lord Jesus Christ, who was made like us in all things apart from sin, did not exist before his sojourn in the flesh, what madness would it be to say that the souls of other human beings exist before their bodies? Let us also hear Basil among the saints, in his discourse on "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God," where he says: "See that the sameness of the word does not mislead you. For how was the human word in the beginning, when man received the beginning of his existence somewhere far down the line? Before man came the wild beasts; before man, the cattle, the creeping things, all that live on land and in water, the birds of heaven, the stars, the sun, the moon, the plants, the earth, the sea, the heaven." See, the father clearly warns us not to be carried away by Origen's myths about the pre-existence of souls. He does not teach us that the human word, that is, the soul, was in the beginning. He cries out plainly that man came into being after all of God's creatures. If, then, all the creatures came before man, how did souls exist beforehand? For the father says that all things came into being not before the body but before

man, who is soul and body together. This shows that both were fashioned at the same time. Gregory of Nyssa among the saints also says, in his treatise on man: "Perhaps it is not outside our present subject to discuss the question disputed in the churches about soul and body. Some of those before us, who wrote the treatise On First Principles, thought fit to say that souls exist beforehand like a people in a city of their own. There too, they say, examples of vice and virtue are set before them. A soul that remains in the good stays free of any union with the body, but if it slips away from its share in the good, it slides down to the life here and so comes to be in a body. Others attend to the order of man's making as Moses gives it and say that the soul comes after the body in time, since God first took dust from the earth and formed man, and then gave him a soul by breathing into him." And a little later: "Those who defend the first view, and teach that the community of souls is older than life in the flesh, do not seem to me to be free of the Greek fables about the transmigration of souls. If one examines it carefully, he will find that their argument is necessarily dragged down to this. They say that one of their wise men claimed that he had been a man, had taken on the body of a woman, had flown with the birds, had grown as a bush, and had been given a life in the water. In my judgment the man who said this about himself was not far from the truth, for doctrines like these, which say that one soul passed through so many forms, are truly worthy of the chatter of frogs or jackdaws, the stupidity of fish, or the senselessness of oaks. The cause of this absurdity is the belief that souls exist beforehand. The starting-point of such a doctrine leads the argument step by step to whatever comes next, and so it proceeds until it reaches this monstrous result. For if the soul is torn away by some vice from the higher community and becomes a man, and if it is agreed that life in the flesh is more subject to passion than the life of eternal and bodiless beings, then a soul entering such a life, where there are more occasions for sin, must necessarily fall into greater wickedness and become more passionate. But passion in a human soul means becoming like the irrational animals. Once it has grown akin to them, it changes into the nature of a beast. And once it has set out on the road of vice, it will never stop advancing toward evil, not even when it has become irrational. For the halting of evil is the beginning of the impulse toward virtue, and there is no virtue in irrational creatures. So it will necessarily always change for the worse, always going on to what is worse and more dishonourable, always finding the worst state of whatever nature it is in. And as the merely sentient lies below the rational, so from the sentient there is a further fall to the insensible. Up to this point their argument, though it strays from the truth, at least draws one absurdity from another by a certain logic. But from here on they make up their doctrine out of things that do not hang together. The logic points to the complete destruction of the soul. For once it has slipped from the higher community, it will be able to stop at no measure

of vice. Through its attachment to the passions it will pass from the rational to the irrational, and from there it will be transferred to the insensibility of plants. The inanimate follows somehow on the insensible, and non-existence follows on the inanimate. So by this logic the soul, on their view, will pass altogether into non-being. Its return to the better will then be impossible. Yet they bring the soul back from a bush to a man. By this they show that life in a bush is to be preferred to the bodiless state. For it has been shown that the soul's progress, since it moves toward the worse, will naturally sink to what is lower still. Below insensible nature lies the inanimate, and to this the starting-point of their doctrine logically leads the soul. But since they do not want this, either they shut the soul up in the insensible, or, if they bring it back from there to human life, they will prove, as has been said, that the life of a tree is better than the first state. For there the fall into vice took place, while from here the return to virtue takes place. So such an argument is shown to be headless and incomplete, which contends that souls live on their own before life in the flesh and are bound to bodies because of vice." Since the father's teaching is plain and repudiates the claim that souls exist before bodies, let us also hear Theophilus among the saints, bishop of Alexandria, from the discourse he wrote to certain monks who held Origen's views. He says this: "So, anathematizing [?] Origen and the other heretics, as we do, and as does Anastasius, bishop of the holy church of the Romans, who for his earlier struggles was appointed the glorious general of a distinguished people, and whom the whole synod of the blessed bishops of the West follows, accepting the verdict of the church of the Alexandrians against the impious man…" Of the same, from the letter to the saints in [?], on account of those who object to the condemnation of Origen's doctrines: "Some have dared to say that Origen is a teacher of the church. Is it right to tolerate such people? If Origen is a teacher of the church, then the Arians, the Eunomians and the pagan Greeks can take pride. The former blaspheme against the Son and the Spirit; the latter are impious just like them and also mock the resurrection of the dead." It is clear, then, from what has been said, that those who hold Origen's views do not follow the holy fathers but follow the error of the Greeks and the madness of the Arians. Cyril among the saints, bishop of Alexandria, in his letter to the monks at Phua, against those who say there is no resurrection of bodies, says this: "They say that some among you deny the resurrection of human bodies. Yet this is part of the confession we make when we come to saving baptism, for when we confess the faith we add that we believe also in the resurrection of the flesh. If we abolish this, and do not believe that Christ has been raised from the dead in order to raise us with himself, our faith is lame. We have left the royal road and are walking

the crooked one. This false belief comes from the derangement of Origen, whom our fathers also renounced and anathematized for perverting the truth. He did not think as a Christian. He went astray by following the nonsense of the Greeks. His disease began here: he says that souls exist before bodies, that they were carried away from holiness into evil desires and fell away from God, and that for this reason God condemned them and put them into bodies, so that they are in the flesh as in a prison." Of the same, from the letter to the monks in [?]: "The church follows the divinely inspired Scriptures. It knows of no soul that exists before bodies, nor of one that sinned before them, for how could something that did not exist sin? We say that the Creator of all things formed the body from earth and gave it life with an intellectual soul. This is how man is made." And after other things: "The all-wise Paul will also confirm that man's soul has not been condemned for earlier sins, as they claim, and sent down into this world. He writes: 'For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive what was done through the body, according to what he has done, whether good or bad.' Why does he say that only what was done through the body will be revealed, and not also what was done before the body, if he knew that the soul had existed and sinned beforehand? If we are judged only for what was done through the body, then clearly we have no sin from before the body. For man's soul did not exist at all before man himself. The meaning of the written law also assures us of this. For if, as the deluded Origen says, the soul received the body as a punishment or penalty for earlier sins, why did the law threaten sinners with death? The righteous ought rather to die, so as to be freed from their bonds and their punishment, and the wicked to live, so that they might go on being punished without being freed from their bonds." From the synodical letter issued by the bishops of Egypt and Alexandria against Origen's doctrines: "This Origen, then, of whom we speak, has become like the abomination of desolation in the midst of the true church. He was ordained presbyter by the canonical and one true [?] hand, but he held the rank of presbyter bare and empty, just as Judas, the thief and traitor, held the rank of apostle. When he began to preach blasphemous homilies, Heraclas, the bishop of blessed memory at that time, a truth-loving ploughman and vinedresser of the church's field, pulled him up from among the good wheat as the evil weed he truly was." And a little later: "Having fallen from heaven to earth like lightning, like his father the devil, and breathing great and terrible fury against the truth, he sailed to the land called Palestine. He settled in Caesarea, the metropolis, and there he stripped the mask entirely from its covering, like the fish that some call the cuttlefish. What was to his liking happened to be

…a dark and black life [?] he vomited out, and there he set it down in writing, and like a Jewish huckster he mixed sweet with bitter under a show of goodness. For what does this evil-scheming madman say? The soul, he says, existed in the heavens before the body; and there, he says, having sinned, it was shut up in prison, that is, sent down into the body, for the purification, he says, and correction of the sins it had committed in the heavens. Here, right from the start, the most impious man spins fables and sets out to fight against the truth. [?] And a little later: “If the soul existed beforehand in the heavens and sinned beforehand there, as Origen, the madman and enemy of God, has said, the most holy prophet ought not to have said, ‘and he forms the spirit of man within him,’ but rather, ‘he shuts up the spirit of man within him,’ or perhaps, ‘he sends it down.’ But since he does not say this, but ‘forms within him,’ he shows this man to be a most grievous wolf, outwardly clothed in fleeces to deceive people to their destruction. For this reprobate, as though he came from heaven and plainly knew what is fashioned there, says not only that the soul existed beforehand but that it sinned beforehand.” It has therefore been shown, from the divine Scripture and from the holy fathers, that the fantasies of the heretics about the pre-existence of souls agree neither with the true faith of Christians nor with right reason. Besides everything else, Origen's folly is shown by this as well: he says that the heaven, the sun, the moon, the stars and the waters above the heavens are ensouled and are certain rational powers. These ideas are clearly rejected also by Basil among the saints in the third homily of his commentary on the Hexaemeron, where he speaks against Origen's doctrines thus: “But we also have something to say to those from the church about the waters that were separated. Under the pretext of anagogy and supposedly loftier ideas, they have taken refuge in allegory, saying that the waters signify figuratively spiritual and incorporeal powers; that the better ones have remained above, upon the firmament, while the wicked ones remained below, in the regions about the earth and in material places. For this reason, they say, the waters above the heavens praise the Lord, that is, the good powers, which through the purity of their ruling faculty are worthy to render fitting praise to the Creator; while the waters under the heavens are the spiritual hosts of wickedness, which fell from their natural height into the depth of evil. Because these are turbulent and rebellious and are tossed by the tumults of the passions, they are called seas, on account of the changeableness and instability of their voluntary motions. But let us dismiss such accounts as the muddle of dreams and old wives' tales, and understand water as water, and accept the division made by the firmament for the reason that has been given. And even if the waters above the heavens are at times called upon to glorify the common Master of all, we do not on that account ascribe a rational nature to them. For the heavens are not ensouled because they declare the glory of God, nor is the firmament a living creature with senses because it proclaims the work of his hands.” Listeners [?] should note that when the father says, “we have something to say to those from the church,” he is speaking of Origen, who had fallen away from the grace of God and from the holy church of God

and of those who think as he does. For he did not say “to those in the church,” but “to those from the church we have something to say.” By saying “we,” he indicated those who belong to the church; by saying “those from the church,” those who have fallen away from it.

The impious Origen had only one aim: to strengthen the error of the Greeks and to sow tares in the souls of the weaker. For this reason we have decided to add also his statement about the resurrection of men from the dead, which deserves laughter but was nonetheless made by him. For he says that at the resurrection the bodies of men are raised spherical. Oh, the folly and ignorance of this deranged man, this expounder of Greek doctrines! Blind in his understanding, and eager to mix fables into the faith of Christians, he set out to insult the very hope and salvation of Christians, that is, the resurrection promised to us, without respect even for the resurrection of the Lord. For the Lord, having risen from the dead and become the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, appeared to the disciples and showed them the piercings of his hands and feet and the wound in his side. And he ate after the resurrection, not because he needed food, but to confirm in this way the nature of the risen body. Indeed, when the Lord was taken up, the angel said to the disciples: “This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven.” But if, as Origen raves, the Lord's body was spherical, how could he have shown the piercings of his hands and feet, or the wound in his side? How could he have eaten, or been recognized at all by the disciples? And how could the bodies of the saints, which were raised after the Lord's resurrection and seen in the holy city, have been recognized by others, if they had a shape other than the one they had in life? So the impious Origen was not established on the rock of the faith. Instead he set forth such blasphemies, and many far worse than these, and it was fitting that at the time of martyrdom he denied Christ and worshipped the Greek polytheism that he himself was bringing in. This happened by the providence of God, so that he would not be received in the church as a martyr and the flock of Christ be harmed as a result. For if even now there are some who admit his fall and yet champion his [?] [gap in text], how would they not have defended his views as those of a martyr and a father, had it happened that he was perfected without worshipping the idols? For no one who holds fast to the truth falls away from God or is forsaken by him, as the divine Scripture says: “Look at the generations of old and see: who trusted in the Lord and was forsaken? Or who hoped in him and was disregarded?” But the impious Origen did not keep his blasphemies to himself; through his own writings he passed his error on to many others. So the voice of the holy apostle Paul fits him very well, when it says that “the sins of some men are

conspicuous, going before them to judgment, but the sins of others follow after them.” For the succession of his error, creeping through the souls of the weaker, causes the sins he committed at the beginning to follow after him. Those who hold Origen's views seem to find the impiety about the pre-existence of souls not enough, nor his other idle talk and his blasphemies about the Holy Trinity. Led on by his perverse words, they add this further error: they say that the punishment of all impious men, and of demons as well, has an end, and that the impious and the demons will be restored to their former rank. By saying this they make people slack in fulfilling the commandments of God, turning them away from the narrow and hard way and leading them astray onto the broad and spacious one. They also flatly contradict what was said by our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ. For he himself teaches in the holy Gospel that the impious will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life. And again, he says to those on his right: “Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world”; and to those on his left: “Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.” Since, then, the Lord plainly proclaims in the holy Gospel that both the punishment and the kingdom are without end, these men stand exposed as preferring the fables of Origen to the pronouncements of the Lord. On this point too their folly is refuted. For if anyone, following Origen's nonsense, should suppose that punishment has an end, he would be forced to put an end also to the eternal life promised to the righteous, since the word “eternal” is applied equally to both. And if both punishment and enjoyment have an end, why the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ? Why the crucifixion, the death, the burial and the resurrection of the Lord? What benefit is there for those who have fought the good fight and borne witness for Christ, if demons and the impious are to receive the same rank as the saints through the restoration? But may these things fall back on the heads of those who tell such fables. For the words of Christ remain unshaken in the souls of the faithful and in the very truth of things. Those who champion Origen's false teaching flee the unanswerable refutations on these matters and want to hide their error. So they wrongly pick out certain sayings of the holy fathers, twist them to their own meaning and fit them to their own disease, as they also do with the divine Scriptures. But we will show from the holy fathers themselves that these arguments of theirs are also vain. Gregory the Theologian among the saints says the following in his Apologetic Oration: “But for us, for whom what is at stake is the salvation of the soul, the blessed and immortal soul, which is to be immortally punished or praised for its vice or virtue, how great must we consider the contest, and how much skill does it require!” And a little later: “What false defence, what plausibility of [?], what device against the truth will lead astray the tribunal and rob of right judgment that which places everything in the balance for everyone, deed, word and thought, and weighs

the better against the worse, so that whichever side tips the scale may prevail [?] and the verdict go with the greater? After that there is no appeal, no higher judge, no defence through later deeds, no oil from the wise virgins or from those who sell it for lamps that are going out, no repentance for the rich man wasting away in the flame and seeking amendment for his family, no appointed time for change. The tribunal is lasting, fearful and final, and more just than it is fearsome, or rather more fearsome for this very reason, that it is just. Then thrones are set, and the Ancient of Days takes his seat, and books are opened, and a river of fire is drawn forth, and the light is before them, and the darkness is made ready. Those who have done good go forth to the resurrection of life, the life now hidden in Christ that will later be revealed together with him; but those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment, by which those who do not believe have already been condemned by the Word who judged them. The ineffable light receives the former, and the grace of the holy and royal Trinity, shining more clearly and purely and mingling wholly with the whole mind; and this alone I take to be the kingdom of heaven. But for the others, among other torments, or rather above all others, there is being cast away from God, and the shame in the conscience that has no end.”

Of Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, from his canonical book. Question: Since in one place it says, “he will be beaten with many blows,” and in another, “with few,” how can some people say that there is no end of punishment for those who are punished? Answer: Things in certain places of the divinely inspired Scripture that are ambiguous and seem to be said obscurely are made clear by what is plainly acknowledged in other places. The Lord declared that “these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.” At another time he sends some away “into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.” Elsewhere he names the Gehenna of fire and adds, “where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched.” And long before, through the prophet, he had foretold of certain people that “their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched.” Since these and similar things are said many times in the divinely inspired Scripture, this too is one of the devil's schemes: that many people, as though they had forgotten so many and such great pronouncements of the Lord, dare to prescribe for themselves an end to the punishments of sin in the age to come. For if eternal punishment is ever to have an end, eternal life too will certainly have an end. But if we do not accept this understanding of the expression in the case of life, what reason is there to give an end to eternal punishment? For the addition of “eternal” applies equally to both: “These,” he says, “will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.” — Of the same, from the Exhortation to Baptism: For a passing pleasure of sin they are tormented immortally; for the pleasure of the flesh they are handed over to the eternal fire. — Of John among the saints, bishop of Constantinople, from the first letter to Theodore the monk: Ponder these things continually, and the river of fire: “For a river of fire was drawn before his face.” One who has been handed over to that fire cannot hope for an end of punish-

ment. The unseemly pleasures of this life are no different from shadows and dreams, for before the sinful act is completed the pleasure is extinguished; but the punishments for them have no end. — Of the same, from the commentary on the First Letter to the Corinthians: The question before us here is no small one; it concerns matters of the greatest necessity, which all people ask about: whether the fire of Gehenna has an end. That it has none, Christ declared when he said, “Their fire will not be quenched, and their worm will not die.” And Paul too, showing that it is immortal, says, “Those who sin will pay the penalty of eternal destruction.” — Since, then, the divine Scripture and the holy fathers clearly teach us that there is no end to the punishment of the impious and of the demons whom they serve, what sort of restoration do those who hold Origen's views imagine, when the punishments have no end? For just as the holy church of Christ proclaims to the righteous an eternal life without end, so it hands down to the impious a punishment without end. So much on these matters. We have decided to bring forward a few of the many things said by the divine Scripture and the holy fathers, in order to refute the impiety of the Origenists. We wish to drive every stumbling block out of the most holy church, so that no stain may be left in it, and we follow the divine Scriptures and the holy fathers, who cast out this Origen and his abominable and impious doctrines and justly placed him under anathema. We therefore address this present letter to your Beatitude, and by it we urge you to assemble all the most holy bishops staying in this imperial city and the most God-beloved abbots of the holy monasteries here, and to have them all anathematize in writing, in every way, the aforesaid impious enemy of God Origen, also called Adamantius, who was a presbyter of the most holy church of Alexandria, together with his abominable and impious doctrines and all the chapters set out below. We also urge you to send copies of what your Beatitude does in this matter to all the other most holy bishops and to the abbots of the holy monasteries, so that they too may anathematize by their own signature Origen and his abominable doctrines, together with all the heretics who will be named. From now on no one is to be ordained bishop or abbot of a monastery unless he first anathematizes, together with all the other heretics customarily anathematized in the libelli submitted, namely Sabellius, Arius, Apollinaris, Nestorius, Eutyches, Dioscorus, Timothy Aelurus, Peter Mongus, Anthimus of Trebizond, Theodosius of Alexandria, Peter formerly of Antioch, Peter of Apamea and Severus formerly of Antioch, also the aforesaid Origen, who was sick with the madness of the Greeks and of Arius, together with his abominable and

impious doctrines. For everyone must be told in advance that no one is to dare in any way to champion this heretic or his expositions. Rather, each person must hate, abhor and anathematize them with all his soul and all his mind, since they are alien to the Christian tradition and do great harm to the souls of simpler people. We have written these same things not only to your Holiness but also to the most holy and most blessed Pope and Patriarch of elder Rome, Vigilius, and to all the other most holy bishops and patriarchs, that is, those of Alexandria, Theopolis and Jerusalem, so that they too may attend to the matter and bring it to completion. Since we wish all Christians to know that Origen's writings are utterly alien to the true faith of Christians, we have decided to set out, in his own words, a few of his many countless blasphemies. They are as follows. That the Son is less than the Father, and the Spirit less than the Son: from the first book of On First Principles. God the Father, who holds all things together, reaches to each of the things that exist, imparting to each its being from his own being, for he is He Who Is [?]. But the Son, being less than the Father, reaches to rational beings alone, for he is second to the Father; and the Holy Spirit is still less, extending to the saints alone. So in this respect the power of the Father is greater than that of the Son and the Holy Spirit, and the power of the Son greater than that of the Holy Spirit; and again, the power of the Holy Spirit is more surpassing compared with [?] in the saints [?].

That the power of God the Father is limited: from the second book of the same work. For we must say that the power of God too is limited, and we must not take away its limits on the pretext of speaking reverently. And a little later: For he made as many things as he could grasp, hold under his hand and keep together under his providence, just as he also prepared as much matter as he could set in order. Of the same, from the fourth book of the same work: Let no one take offence at the statement if we set limits even to the power of God. For it is by nature impossible to comprehend infinite things. And since the things that God himself grasps are, once and for all, limited, there must necessarily be a boundary to how many limited things his power suffices for. That the Son is a creature and has come into being: from the same fourth book. This Son, begotten from the will of the Father, “who is the image of the invisible God,” and “the radiance of his glory and the exact imprint of his being,” “the firstborn of all creation,” is a creature, wisdom. For Wisdom herself says: “God created me as the beginning of his ways for his works

That the Son too is encompassed by the Father along with the other things, that the Father is in every respect greater than the Son, and that he is incomprehensible [?] to him. From the fourth book of the same work, On First Principles. If the Father encompasses all things, and the Son is among all things, it is clear that he encompasses the Son as well. But someone else will ask whether it is true that God is known by himself in the same way as he is known by the Only-begotten; and he will declare that the saying, "The Father who sent me is greater than I," is true in every respect. So even in knowing, the Father is known by himself in a greater, clearer and more perfect way than he is known by the Son. From the first book of the same work. Since, then, we were made according to the image, we have the Son as our prototype, as the truth of the good patterns within us. And what we are in relation to the Son, the Son himself is in relation to the Father, who is truth. Of the same author, from the same book. So, then, I think that in the case of the Savior too it would rightly be said that he is an image of God's goodness, but not the good itself. And perhaps the Son too is good, but not good in the simple sense. And just as he is the image of the invisible God, and in this respect God, but not the one of whom Christ himself says, "That they may know you, the only true God," so he is an image of goodness, but not, as the Father is, unchangeably good. That, having called the Holy Spirit a creature along with the Son, he counted them among the other creatures, and therefore calls them ministering living creatures [?]. From the fourth book of On First Principles. That everything whatsoever besides the Father and God of all things is generated, we are persuaded from the same [?]. And after a little: The Hebrew used to say that the two six-winged seraphim in Isaiah, who cry out to one another and say, "Holy, holy, holy, Lord of hosts," are the Only-begotten of God and the Holy Spirit. And we think that in the ode of Habakkuk as well, "In the midst of two living creatures you will be known," is said of Christ and the Holy Spirit. From the second book of the same work, On First Principles, that he calls the Lord [?] a mere man. For this reason Christ also became man, having obtained this as the reward of his noble achievement, as the prophet testifies when he says, "You have loved righteousness and hated lawlessness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions." And it was fitting that the one who had never been separated from the Only-begotten should share the name of the Only-begotten and be glorified together with him. That the creatures of God are coeternal [?] with God, from the first book of On First Principles. How is it not absurd that he should once have lacked something of what befits him, when he was not almighty? The things on account of which he is almighty must always exist, and they must always have been ruled by him, having him as their ruler.

From the same book. All genera and species always existed; and someone else will say that even each individual in number did too. But either way it is shown that God did not begin to create after once having been idle. On the pre-existence of souls, from the first book of On First Principles. From a cause of their own, those who do not keep a wakeful watch over themselves fall away, sooner or later, to a greater or lesser degree; and from this cause, with the judgment of God measuring out what is deserved according to each one's better or worse movements, one will have in the ordering of the world to come an angelic rank, another a ruling power, another authority over certain beings, another a throne over those ruled, another lordship over servants. Those who have not fallen very far will have the stewardship of and the task of helping the aforementioned. And thus, for the most part from those under the principalities and authorities and thrones and dominions, and perhaps sometimes even in place of them, the human race will be formed in each [?]

From the same book, that if the demons should change for the better, they will one day make up humanity. I think it possible that from those subject to the worse principalities and authorities and world-rulers, in each world or in certain worlds, some, being benefited more quickly and wishing to change, will one day make up humanity. On the descent of beings from above into a body. Since the world is so very varied, then, and contains so many different rational beings, what else must one say was the cause of its coming into existence, if not the variety of the falling away of those who do not flow away from unity in the same way? And that the soul sometimes chooses the life of a water creature. From the second book of On First Principles. The soul, flowing away from the good and inclining towards evil, and sinking ever further into it, unless it turns back, is made brutish by its folly and turned into a beast by its wickedness. And after a little: And it chooses to become irrational and, if I may put it so, to live the life of a water creature; and perhaps, in proportion to its further fall into wickedness, it puts on the body [?] of some such irrational animal. From the same book, that there will be a complete [?] of bodies

But if the things subjected to Christ are in the end also subjected to God, all will lay aside their bodies; and I think that then there will be a dissolution into non-being, the nature of bodies coming into existence a second time if rational beings descend again. From the third book of the same work, on the [?]

[?] we can abandon wickedness, and God does not become all in all; nor can there be irrational animals, lest God come to be in wickedness too, and in irrational animals; nor inanimate things, lest God be in them as well when he becomes all things; and so neither bodies, which by their own nature are inanimate. From the second book of On First Principles. Through the falling away and the cooling from life in the spirit, what is now a soul came to be, which is also capable of returning to what it was in the beginning. This, I think, is what the prophet means in the words, "Return, my soul, to your rest," so that this whole thing was mind. How, then, did it become soul? And soul, when set right, becomes mind. From the same book, on the same subject. The Savior came to save what was lost, yet when the lost is saved it is no longer lost. In the same way the soul which he came to save, as one saves what was lost, no longer remains soul [?] once it is saved, just as what was lost does not remain lost. It must be further examined whether, just as what was lost once existed when it was not lost, and there will be a time when it will not be lost, so too the soul once existed when it was not soul, and will exist when it will not be soul. From the fourth book. It is necessary that the nature of bodies is [not?] primary, but comes into existence at intervals because of certain mishaps that befall rational beings, which then need bodies; and again, when the restoration is complete, these are dissolved into non-being, so that this happens perpetually. From the first book of the same work, that the sun, the moon and the stars are ensouled. That the soul of the sun is older than its being clothed in the body, I think I can show, after reasoning by comparing man with it, from the Scriptures as well. From the same book. "It is better to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better." For I think the sun would say, "It is better to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better." And Paul says, "But to remain in the flesh is more necessary for your sake," while the sun says, "To remain in this heavenly body is more necessary for the revelation of the children of God." And the same must be said about the moon and the rest of the stars. From the fourth book of the same work, that Christ must also be crucified for demons, and that this will happen many times in the ages to come. But even if someone inquires as far as the passion, he will seem to act rashly in inquiring about the heavenly place [?]. But if there are spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places, then, just as here we are not ashamed to confess him crucified for the destruction of what he destroyed through his

suffering, so too, granting that something similar happens there and in the ages that follow until the consummation of the whole age, we shall not be afraid. From the same book. Who with any sense will assert that a first, second and third day, and evening and morning, came to be without sun and moon and stars? These things being so, and the blasphemies uttered by Origen having become plain to all, it is fitting that the anathema against him be framed as follows. If anyone says or holds that human souls pre-exist, as having once been minds and holy powers, but that they grew sated with divine contemplation and turned to the worse, and on that account grew cold towards the love of God, and hence were named souls, and were sent down into bodies as punishment, let him be anathema. If anyone says or holds that the soul of the Lord pre-existed and was united to God the Word before the incarnation and birth from the Virgin, let him be anathema. If anyone says or holds that the body of our Lord Jesus Christ was first formed in the womb of the holy Virgin, and that afterwards God the Word and the soul [?], as having pre-existed, were united to it, let him be anathema. If anyone says or holds that the Word of God was made like all the heavenly orders, becoming a cherub for the cherubim and a seraph for the seraphim, and was made like, in short, all the powers above, let him be anathema. If anyone says or holds that at the resurrection human bodies are raised spherical, and does not confess that we are raised upright, let him be anathema. If anyone says that heaven and the sun and the moon and the stars and the waters above the heavens are ensouled and rational [?] powers of some kind, let him be anathema. If anyone says or holds that Christ the Master will be crucified in the age to come for demons, as he was for men, let him be anathema. If anyone says or holds that the power of God is limited, and that he created only as much as he could grasp, let him be anathema. If anyone says or holds that the punishment of demons and of impious men is temporary and will come to an end at some time, that is, that there will be a restoration of demons or of impious men, let him be anathema. Anathema also to Origen, also called Adamantius, who set out these things, together with his abominable, accursed and wicked doctrines, and to every person who thinks these things or defends them, or who at any time whatever dares in any way at all to lay claim to them. Letter of the Emperor Justinian to the holy synod concerning Origen and those of like mind with him. It has been and is our concern that the holy and apostolic Church of God be kept free from disturbance, as

is right, and that whatever springs up in any way contrary to the orthodox faith be condemned. Since, then, it has come to our knowledge that there are certain people in Jerusalem, monks no less, who follow and teach Pythagoras and Plato and Origen Adamantius, with their impiety and error, we thought it necessary to give this our attention and inquiry, lest by their pagan and Manichaean deceit they utterly destroy many. For they say, to mention a few things out of many, that there were minds without any number or name, so that all rational beings formed a unity by identity of substance and activity, and by their power and their union with and knowledge of God the Word. And that when they grew sated with divine love and contemplation, they put on finer or grosser bodies in proportion to each one's turning to the worse, and were allotted names; and that this is how the heavenly and ministering powers came into being. Moreover, that the sun and the moon and the stars, which also belong to the same unity of rational beings, became what they are through turning to the worse. That the rational beings which grew colder towards divine love were named souls and were thrust into grosser bodies such as ours, while those which had gone to the extreme of wickedness were bound into cold and dark bodies, and became and were named demons. And that from the angelic state comes the state of souls, and from the state of souls the demonic and the human. That out of the whole unity of rational beings only one mind remained unshaken and unmoved from divine love and contemplation, and that this mind became Christ, king, God and man. That there is a complete destruction of bodies, the Lord himself first laying aside his own body, and then all the rest; and that all are brought back again into the same unity and become minds, as they were in their pre-existence; the devil himself evidently being restored to the same unity as well, and the rest of the demons, and impious and godless men along with divine and God-bearing men and the heavenly powers, all having the same union with God that Christ has, just as they had in their pre-existence; so that there is no difference whatever between Christ and the other rational beings, neither in substance, nor in knowledge, nor in power, nor in activity. For Pythagoras said that the first principle of all things is the monad. And again Pythagoras and Plato, speaking of a certain populace of bodiless souls, say that those which fall into some sin are sent down into bodies as punishment. Hence Plato called the body a bond and a tomb, as though the soul were bound and buried in it. Then, concerning the future judgment and recompense of souls, he says again: "The soul of one who has loved boys, and of one who has lived guilelessly with philosophy, is allowed to be punished for a third thousand-year period, and so, having grown wings, it is set free in the three-thousandth year and departs. But the others, when they finish this life, some go to the places of judgment beneath the earth and pay the penalty and render account, while others, lifted up by Justice to some heavenly place, will live in a manner worthy of the way they lived." It is not hard to see the absurdity of this statement.

For who taught him the cycles of years and the thousands, and that when a thousand years have passed each soul then departs to its own place? And what lies between these it would not be fitting even for the most utterly licentious to say, let alone so great a philosopher. For he yoked the licentious and the pederasts together with those who had achieved a pure way of life, and said that these and those alike would enjoy the same things. So Pythagoras and Plato and Plotinus, and those of their band, while agreeing that souls are immortal, said that they pre-exist bodies, that there is a populace of souls, and that those which sin fall into bodies, as I said: the sluggish into donkeys [?], the rapacious into wolves, the deceitful into foxes, the women-mad into horses. But the Church, following the divine words, declares that the soul was created together with the body, and not the one first and the other later, as Origen's derangement would have it. Because of these wicked and ruinous doctrines, or rather this drivel, we exhort your most holy selves, gathered together in one place, to read carefully the exposition set out below, and to condemn and anathematize each of its chapters, together with the impious Origen and all who think such things or will think them, to the end.

In the name of God the Father, and of his only-begotten Son, Jesus Christ our Lord, and of the Holy Spirit. The Emperor Caesar Flavius [?] Justinian, Christ-loving, Alamannicus [?], Gothicus, Francicus [?], Germanicus, Anticus, Alanicus, Vandalicus, Africanus, pious, fortunate, glorious, victor, triumphant, ever-august Augustus, to the whole fullness of the catholic and apostolic Church. We know that nothing so pleases the God who loves mankind as that all Christians should think one and the same about the right and blameless faith, and that there should be no schisms in the holy Church of God. We have therefore thought it necessary, removing every pretext from those who take offense at, or cause offense to, the confession of the right faith proclaimed in the holy Church of God, to make that confession plain through the present edict, so that those who confess the right faith may keep it firmly, and those who contend against it may learn the truth and hasten to be united to the holy Church of God.

We confess, then, that we believe in Father, and Son, and Holy Spirit, a consubstantial Trinity, one Godhead, that is [?] A written statement, that is, a teaching and accurate exposition concerning the blameless [?] and orthodox faith

nature and substance and power and authority, glorifying it in three hypostases, or persons, into which we have been baptized, in which we have believed, and to which we have been joined; separating the properties, but uniting the Godhead. For we worship unity in Trinity and Trinity in unity, which has a paradoxical division and union: a unity according to the principle of substance, or Godhead, and a Trinity according to the properties, or hypostases, or persons. For it is divided indivisibly, if we may so speak, and joined dividedly. For the Godhead is one in three, and the three are one, in whom the Godhead is, or, to speak more precisely, who are the Godhead. Each is God if contemplated alone, when the mind separates what is inseparable; the three are God when thought of together, by the identity of their movement and nature. For we must both confess the one God and proclaim the three hypostases, that is, three persons, each with its own property. And we neither produce confusion in [confessing] the union, as Sabellius does, who says that the Trinity is one person with three names, the same being Father and Son and Holy Spirit; nor, by dividing [the properties], do we estrange the Son and the Holy Spirit from the substance of God the Father, as in the madness of Arius, cutting the Godhead up into three different substances. There is, then, one God the Father, from whom are all things; and one only-begotten Son, through whom are all things; and one Holy Spirit, in whom are all things. We confess that the only-begotten Son of God himself, God the Word, who was begotten of the Father before the ages and timelessly, not made, in the last days came down from heaven for us and for our salvation, and was incarnate of the Holy Spirit and of the holy and glorious Theotokos and ever-virgin Mary, and was born of her; and that he is the Lord Jesus Christ, one of the holy Trinity, consubstantial with God the Father according to the Godhead, and the same consubstantial with us according to the humanity; capable of suffering in the flesh, the same incapable of suffering in the Godhead. For it is not someone other than God the Word who underwent the passion and death; rather, the impassible and eternal Word of God himself, having submitted to birth in human flesh, fulfilled all things. Therefore we do not acknowledge one, God the Word, who worked miracles, and another, Christ, who suffered; but we confess one and the same, our Lord Jesus Christ, the Word of God incarnate and made man, and that both the miracles and the sufferings which he willingly endured in the flesh belong to the same one. For it was not some man who gave himself for us; God the Word himself gave his own body for us, so that our faith and hope might not be in a man, but that we might have our faith in God the Word himself. And so, confessing him to be God, we do not deny that he is also man; and calling him man, we do not deny that he is also God. For if he were God only, how did he suffer? How was he crucified, and how did he die? For these things are foreign to God. But if he were man only, how did he conquer through the passion? How did he save? How did he give life? For these things were beyond man. But as it is, the same one suffers and saves, and conquers through the passion: the same is God, the same is man, the [?]

[?] both, so each is one, as if alone. Hence, when we say that Christ is one and composite, from each nature, that is, from divinity and humanity, we do not bring confusion into the union. And when we know our one Lord Jesus Christ, the Word of God incarnate and made man, in each nature, that is, in divinity and humanity, we do not bring any division into parts or any cutting into his one hypostasis. Rather, we signify the difference of the natures from which he was composed, a difference not abolished by the union, since each nature is in him. For once composition is confessed, the parts exist in the whole, and the whole is known in the parts. The divine nature was not changed into the human, nor was the human nature turned into the divine. Rather, we say that the union according to hypostasis was brought about while each nature is understood and exists within the definition and principle of its own nature. The union according to hypostasis shows that God the Word, that is, one hypostasis of the three hypostases of the Godhead, was not united to a man who already existed. Instead, in the womb of the holy Virgin, he fashioned for himself from her, in his own hypostasis, flesh animated by a rational and intellectual soul, which is human nature. The divine Apostle also teaches us this union of God the Word with the flesh according to hypostasis when he says: "Who, being in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant." By saying "who, being in the form of God," he showed that the hypostasis of the Word exists in the essence of God. By saying "he took the form of a servant," he signified that God the Word was united to the essence of man, and not to a hypostasis or person. He did not say, "he took one who existed in the form of a servant," so as not to suggest that the Word was united to a man who already existed. That is what Theodore and Nestorius impiously blasphemed, calling the union a relation.
