But we, following divine Scripture and the holy fathers, confess that God the Word became flesh, which means that he united human nature to himself according to hypostasis. Therefore our Lord Jesus Christ is one, having in himself the fullness of the divine nature and the fullness of the human nature. He is the Only-begotten and the Word as begotten of God the Father, and the same one is the firstborn among many brothers once he became man. For the Son of God became the Son of Man, and remaining what he was, he was not changed by what he became. Hence we also confess two births of the same only-begotten God the Word. One was from the Father before the ages, without a body. The other was in the last days, when the same one was made flesh and became man from the holy and glorious Theotokos, the ever-virgin Mary. For he who shone forth from the Father beyond understanding rose from his mother beyond reason. Being true God, he truly became man. For this reason we confess the holy, glorious and ever-virgin Mary to be properly and truly Theotokos. This is not because God the Word took his beginning from her. It is because in the last days the only-begotten God the Word, who is before the ages, was made flesh from her and became man without change. Invisible in what is his own, he became visible in what is ours. Being impassible God, he did not disdain to become passible man,

and the immortal one did not disdain to be subject to the laws of death. He was born in Bethlehem of the seed of David according to the flesh, was made like men, and was crucified for us men under Pontius Pilate. The holy apostles proclaimed that he is God, that the same is man, that the same is Son of Man, that the same is from heaven and from the earth, that the same is impassible and passible. For the Word, who was begotten from above of the Father ineffably, inexpressibly, incomprehensibly and eternally, is himself born in time below of the Virgin Mary. He did this so that those who were first born below might be born a second time from above, that is, of God. So he has only a mother on earth, and we have only a Father in heaven. For he took the mortal father of men, Adam, and gave men his own immortal Father, as it is said: "He gave them power to become children of God." Hence the Son of God also tastes death according to the flesh because of his fleshly father, so that the sons of man may share in his life because of their Father according to the Spirit, who is God. He is Son of God by nature, and we are sons by grace. And again, he became son of Adam by the economy and for our sake, while we are sons of Adam by nature. God is his Father by nature but ours by grace. God became his God by the economy, because he became man, while he is our Master and God by nature. For this reason the Word, who is Son of God the Father, was united to flesh and became flesh, so that men, united to the Spirit, might become one spirit. He, the true Son of God, bears us all, so that we may all bear the one God. Even after he became man, the only-begotten Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, is one of the holy Trinity, composite of each nature. We confess that Christ is composite because we follow the teaching of the holy fathers. In the mystery of Christ, the union by composition rejects both confusion and division. It preserves the distinct property of each nature, while showing one hypostasis or person of God the Word even with the flesh. He is one and the same, perfect in divinity and perfect in humanity. He is known not as two hypostases or persons, but in a divine nature and a human nature. So in both respects he is one: perfect God and perfect man, the same our Lord Jesus Christ, the One of the holy Trinity who is glorified together with the Father and the Holy Spirit. For the holy Trinity did not receive the addition of a fourth person even when God the Word, one of the holy Trinity, was made flesh. We guard this good deposit, which we have received from the holy fathers. We live and conduct ourselves in it, and may we take it with us as our companion when we depart: the confession of the Father, and of Christ the Son of the living God, and of the Holy Spirit. Confessing these things in this way, and in addition to the other teachings of Cyril, among the saints, on the orthodox faith, and [?]

[?] "incarnate." Accepting this, we confess that one Christ was brought into being from the divine nature and the human nature, and not one nature, as some try to say because they take the expression wrongly. Indeed, whenever the father himself spoke of one nature of the Word incarnate, he used the word "nature" here in place of "hypostasis." In the passages where he used this expression, he mostly added [?] sometimes "Son," sometimes "Word" or "Only-begotten." These terms indicate not a nature but a hypostasis or person. So the hypostasis of the Word, once made flesh, produced not one nature but one composite Christ, the same God and man. For those who confess that Christ is God and man, it is impious to speak of one nature or essence in him. It is impossible for our Lord Jesus Christ to be both before the ages and in time, or both impassible and passible, according to one and the same nature or essence. We rightly confess these things of his one hypostasis or person. We will show his very clear teaching about this expression from the words of the same Cyril among the saints. In the first letter to Succensus, after saying "one nature of the Word incarnate," he immediately added: "So as far as understanding goes, that is, simply seeing with the eyes of the soul how the Only-begotten became man, we say that the natures which were united are two. But we say that the Son and Christ and Lord is one, the Word of God the Father made man and incarnate." With these words the father wished to set out the manner in which God became man, while preserving what is undivided and unconfused. He showed the number of the natures that came together and proclaimed one Christ, but not one nature of divinity and flesh. In the second letter to the same Succensus he teaches similar things and writes as follows: "If we had said one nature of the Word and then fallen silent, without adding 'incarnate,' as though setting the economy aside, they would perhaps have a not implausible argument when they pretend to ask: where is the perfection in humanity, or how does our essence subsist? But since the perfection in humanity and the indication of our essence have been brought in by saying 'incarnate,' let them stop propping themselves up on a reed staff. One who casts out the economy and denies the incarnation could rightly be accused of depriving the Son of perfect humanity. But if, as I said, saying that he was made flesh is a clear and unambiguous confession that he became man, then nothing more prevents us from understanding that Christ is one and the only Son, and that the same is God and man, perfect in divinity and likewise perfect in humanity. Your Perfection has set out the account of the saving passion most correctly and very wisely. You maintain that the only-begotten Son of God himself, insofar as he is understood to be and is God, did not suffer the things of the body in his own nature, but rather suffered in the earthly nature. Both must necessarily be preserved for the one who is truly Son: that he does not suffer as God, and that he is said to have suffered as man. For his own flesh suffered." And in the thirteenth chapter of the Scholia the same Cyril among the saints

likewise rejects both those who introduce two sons and those who speak of one nature of the divinity and the flesh of Christ, and writes as follows: "So we must not divide the one Lord Jesus Christ into a man by himself and God by himself. We say that Jesus Christ is one and the same Lord, knowing the difference of the natures and keeping them unconfused with one another." As Cyril among the saints teaches, our Lord Jesus Christ is one, perfect in divinity and the same perfect in humanity. He did not suffer in the divine nature but in the earthly nature. Cyril also knows the difference of the natures, and that they are kept unconfused with one another in one hypostasis. If all this is so, the father clearly says that the same one is known in the divine nature and the human nature, and that each of the natures from which he was composed is in him. No one could be so mad as to think that those who say that the flesh and divinity of Christ are one nature or essence, at once divine and earthly, passible and impassible, think rightly. Some also try to establish from another quarter that the divinity and humanity of Christ are one nature. They put forward the example of man and argue as follows: just as man, made up of soul and body, which differ in kind, is called one nature, so too, when we say that Christ is from two natures, divinity and humanity, we ought to speak of one nature in him. To them we will say this. Man, even though he is made up of different things, that is, soul and body, is nevertheless called one nature because that nature is predicated in common of all the hypostases or persons that fall under the same species. However much each hypostasis or person, Peter and Paul for example, is set apart from the others by his own properties, they are still not divided in nature, for both are men. Again, neither soul without body nor body without soul [is a man] [?] of humanity; man was created from soul and body, brought from non-being into being. And every creature, even if it is made up of different things, is still said to have the one nature in which it was created by God. But Christ is not like this. He does not signify one nature or essence predicated in common of many hypostases or persons, as man does. If that were so, there would be many Christs of whom the common nature was predicated, which it is impious even to say. Nor was Christ created from the beginning out of divinity and humanity, as man is out of soul and body, so that this would be the nature of Christ. Rather, the Word was God before the ages, of the same nature or essence as the Father and Creator of all things. In the last days he united human nature to himself according to hypostasis and became man, without ceasing to be

[?] So Christ is one hypostasis or person, and he has in himself the fullness of the divine and uncreated nature and the fullness of the human and created nature. Since two natures are known in him, uncreated and created, how then is it

possible to speak of one nature or essence in this case? For even if Christ is one hypostasis or person, the same one is consubstantial with God the Father and consubstantial with us, though not according to one and the same nature or essence. If Christ were one nature or essence, there are only three possibilities. Either he would be without flesh and consubstantial only with God the [Father] and the Spirit, since the Godhead has one essence or nature. Or he would be a mere man and consubstantial only with us, since humanity has one nature. Or each nature would have been changed and would have produced something of a different kind, besides the natures that came together. On their view, then, Christ neither remained God nor became man, and so the same one is consubstantial neither with the Father nor with us. To think this way is full of every impiety. We say these things knowing that some of the holy fathers also used the example of man for the mystery of Christ. But they did so to show that a man is one, made from soul and body, and not two men, and in the same way Christ, composed of divinity and humanity, is one and is not divided into two Christs or two sons. These people, however, have used the example of man to introduce one nature or essence of the divinity and humanity of Christ, which we have shown is foreign to true religion. When they are refuted on this point, as people who make up for themselves a nature or essence of divinity and flesh contrary to the correct teaching of the fathers, they move on to other arguments. They say that one must not speak of a number of natures in Christ, since number introduces division. So let them know this. When number is used of different persons or hypostases, the things themselves are actually separated into parts, as in the case of [?] several men. But when it is used of things that are united, the division is only in reason and contemplation, not in the things themselves. An example is the one hypostasis of a man made up of soul and body. Here too two natures are contemplated, that of the soul and that of the body, and yet he is not for that reason divided into two men. We know the man as one, and his hypostasis as one. So too in the mystery of Christ, once the union has taken place, the things united may be contemplated as different, yet the things from which our Lord Jesus Christ was composed are not actually separated from one another into parts. Still, because we perceive the difference and wish to signify it, we use number and say that the natures in him are two, and the one Christ is not for that reason divided into two Christs or sons. Gregory the Theologian, among the saints, bears witness to what we have said. In the first discourse to Cledonius he writes as follows: "If anyone introduces two sons, one from God the Father and a second from the mother, and not one and the same, may he fall away from the adoption promised to those who believe rightly. The natures are two, God and man, just as soul and body are also two. But there are not two sons, nor two gods. Here too there are not two men, even though Paul spoke in this way of the inner and the outer man. To put it briefly, the things from which the Saviour is made are one thing and another, since the invisible is not the same as the visible

and the timeless is not the same as what is subject to time. But he is not one person and another, God forbid." With these words Gregory among the saints clearly teaches that in the mystery of Christ, whoever applies number to persons is condemned as impious. But whoever applies it to the natures from which the one Christ was composed confesses rightly, since he uses it to signify the difference of the natures that came together and in no way makes a separation into parts. The nature of the soul is one thing and that of the body another, and yet by composition one man results, not two. In the same way, even if two natures are contemplated in Christ, one of divinity and the other of humanity, two Christs or two sons are not introduced on that account. So those who refuse to speak of the number of the natures in Christ, in the sense described, are clearly denying their difference and bringing confusion into the economy. But if they confess the difference, they must also speak of the number of the natures that came together without confusion into one hypostasis. For wherever difference is preserved, number certainly follows. To confirm what we have said, we will use the testimony of the holy fathers. We will show that they say the terms in the mystery of Christ are distinguished according to the difference of the natures, divinity and humanity, from which he was composed, and that they apply number to them. But they do not actually divide the natures into parts, as two hypostases or two persons. Cyril among the saints says this in the Interpretation of Leviticus: "See again in these things, clearly, the mystery of our Saviour and the cleansing through holy baptism. He commands that two small birds, living and clean, be taken. Through the birds you are to understand the heavenly one, man and God together, divided into two natures as far as the account proper to each is concerned. For he was the Word from God the Father who shone forth in flesh born of a woman, yet he was not divided, for the one Christ is from both." Again, the same Cyril among the saints writes as follows in the second letter to Succensus: "But they did not know that things which are usually divided in contemplation alone do not by any means also depart from one another entirely and separately [?] into otherness, part by part." Basil among the saints, in the fourth discourse against Eunomius, interprets "The Lord created me … and before all the hills he begets me" and writes as follows: "So we must take 'he begot' as said of the Son of God, and 'he created' as said of him who took the form of the servant. In all these we do not speak of two, God by himself and man by himself, for he was one. We are only reckoning, in thought, the nature of each." And Gregory the Theologian among the saints, in the second discourse on the Son, teaches us how the natures in our Lord Jesus Christ must be distinguished in thought, and writes as follows: "When the natures are distinguished in thought, the names are divided along with them. Hear Paul saying: 'That the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of

[?] of glory: of Christ, God; but of glory, Father. For even if the two together are one, they are one not by nature but by their coming together.” And Gregory, bishop of Nyssa, who is among the saints, teaching us the same things in the fourth book Against Eunomius, writes as follows: “And so that no one might attach the suffering of the cross to the undefiled nature, he corrects such an error more clearly in other passages, calling him mediator between God and man, and naming him both God and man. In this way, since two things are said of the one, what fits each may be understood: impassibility belongs to the divine, and the economy of suffering to the human. Thought, then, divides what is united by love for humankind but distinguished in reasoning. So when he proclaims what is transcendent and surpasses all understanding, he uses the loftier names, calling him God over all, and great God, and power of God, and wisdom, and the like. But when his words describe the experience of sufferings, which was necessarily taken on along with our nature because of our weakness, he names the two together from what is ours and calls him man. He does not use the word to make the one it signifies common with the rest of nature, but so that piety may be preserved concerning each.” Since these things have thus been demonstrated through the teaching of the fathers, let them stop making the number of natures in Christ a pretext for their own error, and stop trying to introduce confusion by denying the difference on this ground. For how is the number not necessary, when the fathers used it to signify the difference of the natures united into one hypostasis, and not to divide them into parts? Since it has been demonstrated from every side that it is impious to speak of one nature, or essence, of the Godhead and of the flesh of Christ, we will also say this: in the way we speak of one hypostasis of the Godhead and humanity of Christ, it is not possible also to speak of one nature of Christ, because nature and hypostasis are not the same thing. For all the holy fathers teach us that nature, or essence and form, is one thing, and hypostasis, or person, another; and that nature, or essence and form, signifies what is common, while hypostasis, or person, signifies what is particular. If some say that just as one composite hypostasis has been spoken of in Christ, so one must also speak of one composite nature, we will show that this too is foreign to piety. For when we speak of one nature, or essence, of the Godhead, we glorify three hypostases in it, recognizing the same nature, or essence, in each hypostasis; and we piously say that out of the three hypostases one hypostasis, that of the Word, was compounded with the flesh. No one in the catholic church has ever dared to say that just as there are three hypostases of the holy Trinity, so there are also three natures, such that one could say that a nature out of the three natures was compounded with flesh. Arius alone dared to speak of three natures in the holy Trinity, and he was condemned as a blasphemer. For this reason, then, right reasoning leads us to speak of a union of two natures, and of one hypostasis. For the Son of God, being other in hypostasis

than the Father but of the same nature as the Father, fashioned for himself in his own hypostasis flesh animated by a rational and intellectual soul. This shows that the Word of God was united to human nature, and not to the hypostasis, or person, of some particular individual. The Word of God, then, even when incarnate, is one hypostasis, recognized in each nature: in the divine, in which he existed, as in “who, being in the form of God,” and in the human, as in “being made in the likeness of men.” For this reason one may piously speak of a composite hypostasis of God the Word, but not of one composite nature. When nature is spoken of simply by itself, with no particular person attached to it, it denotes something indefinite and without hypostasis, and what is indefinite cannot be compounded with anything. Even after such arguments someone may look only to contention and try to object, saying that by the account of nature just given, the human nature of Christ must also have its own hypostasis, or its own person. Such a person plainly says that the Word was united to a man who already existed, and that the union came about by relation. For a union according to hypostasis of two hypostases, or persons, is impossible. Whoever says these things, then, is striving to empty the power of God with words of human wisdom, and is ignorant of the great mystery of piety, which is believed with the heart for righteousness and confessed with the mouth for salvation. For the human nature of Christ is never spoken of simply by itself, nor did it have its own hypostasis or person; it received the beginning of its existence in the hypostasis of the Word. Hence we confess that God the Word himself became man without change, and not that he came into some man. We confess that the birth from the virgin belongs to the same God the Word incarnate, and that for this reason the holy, glorious, ever-virgin Mary is Theotokos. For this reason too, both before the incarnation of God the Word and after it, we speak of three hypostases, of the Father, the Son and the Spirit, since the holy Trinity has not admitted the addition of a fourth hypostasis, or person. All this refutes those who speak of two natures before the union, since they speak of a man who existed beforehand and was then united to God the Word, after the madness of the impious Theodore and Nestorius. It also refutes those who say that one must not speak of two natures in Christ after the union, but of one nature; they introduce confusion and illusion, after the impious Apollinarius and Eutyches. So much for them. But the holy fathers contemplated, after the Word became man, the things from which Christ is, and saw that the natures have remained unconfused. So they have most rightly said that the two natures, the divine and the human, are in Christ. For there were not two natures of the Lord before he became man, nor did the two become one after he became man, even though they are recognized in one hypostasis. We have been taught these things both from the divine scriptures and from the teaching of the fathers, and so we have rightly written them to overthrow those who

confuse the mystery of the divine economy and those who cut it apart. By clarifying the things from which Christ is and in which he is recognized, we introduce neither confusion nor division into the divine economy. Indeed, offering a doxology and the account of the union [?], we confess and worship one Christ and Son and Lord, God the Word incarnate and made man, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit. Since these things are confessed in this way by the catholic church of God, we want all Christians to know that just as we have one God and Lord, so we also have one faith. For there is one definition of faith: to confess and rightly glorify the Father, and Christ the Son of God, and the Holy Spirit. We keep this confession, into which we were also baptized. Our great God and Savior Jesus Christ gave it to his holy disciples and apostles, and they proclaimed it in the whole world. The three hundred and eighteen holy fathers who assembled at Nicaea against Arius condemned him along with his impiety, and handed down this same confession, or creed and [holy] teaching of the faith, to the holy church of God. After them came the one hundred and fifty holy fathers who assembled in Constantinople against Macedonius, the fighter against the Spirit, and Magnus the Apollinarian. They condemned these men along with their impiety and, following in every respect the same holy creed handed down by the three hundred and eighteen holy fathers, clarified what concerns the divinity of the Holy Spirit. Further, the holy fathers who first assembled at Ephesus against the impious Nestorius, and the holy fathers at Chalcedon against the impious Eutyches, followed the said holy creed, or teaching of the faith, in every respect. They condemned the heretics already named along with their impiety, together with those who held or still hold views like theirs. Besides this, they anathematized those who hand down another definition of faith, or creed and teaching, to people coming to holy baptism or turning back from any heresy whatever, other than the one handed down, as has been said, by the three hundred and eighteen holy fathers and clarified by the one hundred and fifty holy fathers. These things being so, we have seen fit also to append chapters that contain in brief both the right confession of the faith and the condemnation of the heretics. If anyone does not confess Father, Son and Holy Spirit, a consubstantial Trinity, one Godhead, that is, nature and essence, and one power and authority, worshipped in three hypostases, that is, persons, let such a one be anathema. If anyone does not confess that God the Word, begotten of the Father before the ages and outside time, in the last days [came down from the heavens and] was made flesh of the holy [glorious] Theotokos and ever-virgin Mary, became man and was born of her; and that therefore the two births, the one before the ages without a body and the one in the last days according to the flesh, belong to the same God the Word, let such a one be anathema. If anyone says that God the Word who worked the miracles is one, and the Christ who suffered is another,

or says that God the Word is with Christ born of a woman, or is in him as one in another; and does not confess one and the same our Lord Jesus Christ, God the Word incarnate and made man, to whom belong both the miracles and the sufferings that he willingly endured in the flesh, let such a one be anathema. If anyone says that the union of God the Word with a man came about by grace, or by operation, or by worth, or by equality of honor, or by authority, or by reference, or by relation, or by power; or by homonymy, by which the Nestorians call God the Word Christ and separately name the man Christ, and speak of one Christ by the name alone; or if anyone says that the union came about by good pleasure, as Theodore the heretic says in these very words, as though God the Word were pleased with the man because he thought well and favorably of him; and does not confess that the union of God the Word with the flesh animated by a rational and intellectual soul is according to hypostasis, and that therefore his hypostasis is one and composite, let such a one be anathema. If anyone calls the glorious ever-virgin Mary Theotokos by reference or in an improper sense, or calls her “man-bearer” or “Christ-bearer,” as though Christ were not God; and does not confess her to be Theotokos properly and in truth, because God the Word, begotten of the Father before the ages, was in the last days made flesh and born of her, let such a one be anathema. If anyone does not confess that our Lord Jesus Christ, who was crucified in the flesh, is true God and Lord of glory and one of the holy Trinity, let such a one be anathema.

If anyone says “in two natures” but does not confess our one Lord Jesus Christ, God the Word incarnate, as being in Godhead and in humanity; and does not use the phrase to signify the difference of the natures from which he was compounded, but takes it, in speaking of the mystery of Christ, to mean a division into parts, as though the natures were separate and each had its own hypostasis, as Theodore and Nestorius blasphemously say, let such a one be anathema. If anyone confesses the number of natures in our one Lord Jesus Christ, that is, God the Word incarnate, but does not take the difference between the natures from which he was compounded as something grasped in contemplation and not abolished by the union, and instead uses the number to divide them into parts, let such a one be anathema. If anyone says “one nature of God the Word incarnate” and does not take it to mean that from the divine nature and the human one Christ was formed, consubstantial with the Father in his Godhead and the same one consubstantial with us in his humanity, but takes it to mean that one nature, or essence, of the Godhead and of the flesh of Christ was formed, after the false belief of Apollinarius and Eutyches, let such a one be anathema.

For the catholic church turns away from and anathematizes equally those who divide or cut into parts the mystery of the divine economy of Christ and those who confuse it. If anyone does not anathematize Arius, Eunomius, Macedonius, Apollinarius, Nestorius, Eutyches, and those who hold or have held views like theirs, let him be anathema. Theodore of Mopsuestia said that God the Word is one and Christ another. He said that this Christ was troubled by passions of the soul and desires of the flesh, improved by progress in works, and baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Through baptism, he said, Christ received the grace of the Holy Spirit and was counted worthy of adoption; he is worshipped in the person of God the Word just as an imperial image is; and after the resurrection he became unchangeable in his thoughts and entirely sinless. Theodore said too that the union of God the Word with Christ was like what the apostle spoke of regarding husband and wife: “The two shall become one flesh.” Besides his other countless blasphemies, he dared to say that after the resurrection, when the Lord breathed on the disciples and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit,” he did not give them the Holy Spirit but only made a show of breathing on them. He also said that Thomas's confession “My Lord and my God,” made when he touched the Lord's hands and side after the resurrection, was not said about Christ. For Theodore says that the Lord is not God; rather, Thomas was astonished at the marvel of the resurrection and praised the God who raised Christ. Worse still, in his so-called commentary on the Acts of the Apostles, this same Theodore compares Christ to Plato, Mani, Epicurus and Marcion. He says that just as each of them devised his own doctrine and caused his disciples to be called Platonists, Manichaeans, Epicureans and Marcionites, so in the same way Christ devised his doctrine, and Christians are called after him. If anyone, therefore, defends Theodore, who blasphemed in this way, and does not anathematize him and his writings and those who hold or have held views like his, let him be anathema. Theodoret set forth writings on behalf of Nestorius the heretic and against the right faith, against the first holy synod of Ephesus, and against Cyril, who is among the saints, and his twelve chapters. In these impious writings he says that the union of God the Word with a certain man is a union by relation. Speaking blasphemously of this man, he says that Thomas touched the one who rose and worshipped the one who raised him. For this reason he calls impious the teachers of the church who confess the union of God the Word with the flesh according to hypostasis, and besides this he denies that the holy, glorious, ever-virgin Mary is Theotokos. If anyone, therefore, defends or praises these writings of Theodoret and does not anathematize them, let him be anathema. It was for these blasphemies that he was expelled from his bishopric, and afterward, at the holy synod

of Chalcedon, he was compelled to do everything contrary to the writings of his that we have mentioned, and to confess the right faith. There is an impious letter said to have been written by Ibas to Mari the Persian, the heretic. It denies that God the Word became man, and says that it was not God the Word, made flesh of the virgin, who was born, but a mere man who was born of her, whom it calls a temple, as though God the Word were one and the man another. Besides this, it insults the first synod of Ephesus as having condemned Nestorius without inquiry or trial; it calls Cyril, who is among the saints, a heretic, and his twelve chapters impious; and it praises and defends Nestorius and Theodore along with his impious writings. If anyone, therefore, defends this impious letter, or says that it or any part of it is correct, and does not anathematize it, let him be anathema. This letter has been justly anathematized because of the blasphemies it contains. Yet those who impiously hold the views of Nestorius and Theodore try to say that it was accepted by the holy synod of Chalcedon. In saying this they slander the holy synod, and under cover of it they strive to free Theodore and Nestorius from the condemnation they deserve, and with them the impious letter. Yet Ibas, though often accused over it, did not dare to own it, because of the blasphemies it contains. We will show this from the various proceedings held about it. In the proceedings conducted by Photius and Eustathius at Tyre, the Ibas already mentioned was accused over his insults against Cyril, who is among the saints. He plainly declared that after the union of the Easterners with Cyril he had said nothing insulting about him. But the letter, full of the blasphemies mentioned and the grounds of the charge against Ibas, contains many insults against Cyril, and it shows that it was written after the union with the Easterners. This shows that Ibas disowned it. Hence Photius and Eustathius, whom we have mentioned, laid down in writing, to satisfy the accusers, that Ibas should do everything contrary to the letter, as the decision they gave on the matter shows. But Ibas did not fulfill what they had decided, and so he was expelled from his bishopric because of the blasphemies of that letter. Nonnus was ordained in his place, and he also sat in the holy synod of Chalcedon. At Chalcedon, then, Ibas was again accused on the same matters. After the impious letter was read, he did not dare to own it, but immediately added, in these very words: “I am a stranger to what is brought against me.” Hence the holy synod, not content with Ibas's disavowal of the impious letter, compelled him to do the opposite of what it says. He had to confess the right faith that the letter rejects, accept the first holy synod of Ephesus, and acknowledge as father and teacher Cyril, who is among the saints, whom the impious letter insults. He also had to anathematize Nestorius and his impious doctrine, which the impious letter praises and defends. If, then, Ibas himself, accused on several occasions over the impious letter, did not dare to own it, but also

…the holy synod at Chalcedon made him do everything contrary to it, how could that same holy synod have accepted the said letter and fallen under condemnation for the impiety it contains, when it was eager to free Ibas from that impiety? The heretics pass over all the blasphemies contained in the letter and bring forward from it only the phrase its writer used to deceive simpler people, namely "two natures, one power, one person." We will therefore show that even here he mixes in his own impiety. For of whom could a man speak of two natures and one person, when he denies that God the Word was made flesh of the holy and glorious Theotokos and ever-virgin Mary and was born of her? It is plain, rather, that he assigns each nature its own person, as Theodore and Nestorius set out in their blasphemous writings, and the writer of the letter defends them together with their impiety. For they openly speak of two persons, one of God the Word and one of Christ, whom they call a mere man. They also say that one person appears by a relational conjunction and by the same dignity and honour. The writer of the letter also speaks of one power, or authority, of the two natures, and in this too he plainly follows these heretics. Theodore says it in the various discourses on the incarnation that he impiously set out. Nestorius says it in many writings, above all in the letter he wrote to Alexander, the heretic of Hierapolis: that the two natures have one sovereignty, one power or might, and one person by virtue of one dignity and the same honour. This shows that the writer of the letter followed their false doctrine and used the word "natures" in place of "persons." For one sovereignty, one power or might, one dignity and the same honour are said not of different natures but of different persons of the same substance, which is what we confess of the Holy Trinity. This is why the holy fathers anathematized those who say that God the Word was united to Christ (whom the followers of Theodore and Nestorius call a mere man) by sovereignty, or power or might, or dignity, or equality of honour, and who do not confess that the union of the Word with flesh animated by a rational and intelligent soul took place according to hypostasis. This would be enough to refute the impiety of those who defend that abominable letter. Yet toward the end of the same letter its writer shows his own false doctrine again, saying that one must believe in the temple and in the one who dwells in the temple, and in this he plainly introduces two persons. This impiety too the writer of the letter learned from Theodore and Nestorius. The catholic Church, however, condemns such false doctrine. It teaches us to confess and believe not in the temple and in the one who dwells in the temple, but in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Word of God made flesh and made man. Nor is it surprising that the writer of that impious letter used the word "natures." Heretics make a habit of using, to deceive the simpler, expressions that the orthodox use piously, and they turn the pious

meaning and interpretation of these words into their own impiety. For sometimes the same expressions are consistent with piety when they are rightly interpreted and understood, but contain impiety when heretics explain them wrongly and put them forward. Nestorius, for instance, spoke of two natures and one person but did not confess their union according to hypostasis. The first holy synod, over which Celestine and Cyril of holy memory presided, therefore did not accept him but condemned him. We follow the teaching of the holy fathers in all things, and we have shown more clearly above both the union of the two natures, from which our Lord Jesus Christ, one of the Holy Trinity, God the Word made flesh, was composed, and the fact that their difference was not abolished by the union. What we have said would be enough to convince those who do not wish to be contentious. But once these people have turned aside to impiety they try other arguments as well, so we must also show that such pretexts of theirs are empty. They say that the impious letter ought not to be censured because it is found in certain books. But anyone who accepts this, in keeping with their folly, must also accept Eutyches and Nestorius, since much about them too is contained in the acts of the synod. No one of sound mind, however, will pay attention to what they say. Whatever is brought forward about heretics in synods and becomes part of the minutes is taken up not to acquit them but to refute them, and to condemn all the more both them and those who think as they do. Moreover, as has been said, the minutes that contain the impious letter are included in certain books, but they are nowhere found in the authentic copies to which the most holy bishops subscribed. Those who search for the truth must also bear this in mind. In synods, individuals present often say things out of partiality, or opposition, or ignorance [?], but no one pays attention to what individuals say, only to what is defined by all with common consent. If anyone chose, as they do, to pay attention to such contradictions, every synod would be found to overturn itself. For these reasons, if they truly accepted the holy synod, they ought not to fasten such censures on it. They should rather follow the teachers of the catholic Church, and above all Athanasius among the saints. He was bishop of the church of Alexandria and took on many great struggles for the right faith of Christians against every heresy, especially against the most impious Arians. These same Arians, to deceive the people, tried to draw to their side Dionysius, who had been bishop of Alexandria many years before Athanasius among the saints, and claimed that this Dionysius held the same views as they did. Athanasius, the great teacher of the Church, then showed in writing and in many ways that Dionysius had preached the right faith from the beginning and had in no way shared in the impiety of the Arians. But these men, holding the views of the heretics, are eager to fasten their own impiety on the synod. What kind of condemnation there is, and what curse falls

on those who sin against their fathers, divine Scripture also teaches us. Ham, the son of Noah, saw his own father naked. He did not cover his father's bodily nakedness but went out and reported it to his brothers, and they covered it with a garment. Ham himself and those born of him came under a curse, while those who covered it were counted worthy of a great blessing. If so, how much greater and fuller a condemnation do these men deserve, who are eager to fasten on the synod, through the impiety of the letter and of Theodore, a dishonour that in no way belongs to it? Yet this will not let the impious letter, or those who champion it, escape condemnation for their impiety. Nor will Theodore escape, who surpassed Greeks, Jews and all heretics in impiety. Besides his other blasphemies, he was not content to twist the creed of the three hundred and eighteen holy fathers to suit his own error. Despising that creed, he set out another, full of every impiety, in which he dared to anathematize those who think or teach otherwise. So, as far as their madness goes, all the holy apostles and fathers stand condemned. This impious creed of Theodore was brought forward at the first synod of Ephesus and read at Chalcedon, and each synod condemned it together with the man who set it out and those who accepted it. When Theodore's impious writings are produced, some who plead his cause pretend to agree that they are impious because of the blasphemy in them, yet they refuse to anathematize the man himself who spewed out such impiety. We marvel at their folly in daring to oppose divine Scripture, which plainly says, "Equally hateful to God are the ungodly man and his ungodliness." And indeed, "what was done will be punished together with the one who did it." If the ungodly man is as hateful to God as his ungodliness, it is plain that such a man has been separated from God and is justly placed under anathema. For anathema means nothing other than separation from God, as the judgment of anathema in the Old and New Testaments shows. The Lord says that those who do not abide in the word of his truth are separated from the Church. Speaking to the Jews in the Gospel according to John, he says this: "Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin. The slave does not remain in the house forever; the son remains forever." And the apostle testifies in the First Letter to Timothy that divine Scripture calls the house the Lord spoke of "the church of the living God." Some say that Theodore ought not to be anathematized after his death. Let those who defend such a heretic know that every heretic who persisted in his own error to the end is all the more justly placed under perpetual anathema, even after death. This has been done with many heretics, both older and more recent: [?], Basilides, Marcion, Cerinthus, Mani, Eunomius and Bonosus. The same was done with Theodore, who was accused in his lifetime and, after his death,

anathematized by the holy fathers. If those who champion him, being heretics, will not obey the fathers, let them at least believe the impious letter they defend. Although that letter defends Theodore as far as it possibly can, it still openly says that holy fathers anathematized him in church, and that from then on there was much inquiry into his writings, evidently because they were full of impiety. The members of the catholic Church did this at the time so that simpler people who came across his impious writings would not be turned away from the right faith. The holy synods show that the impious are anathematized by the catholic Church after death, even if they did not receive anathema in person during their lifetime. The synod at Nicaea anathematized, without naming them, those who championed the impious doctrine of Arius, and the synod at Constantinople likewise anathematized the most impious heresy of Macedonius. Yet the holy Church of God anathematizes Arius and Macedonius by name even after their death. Many proofs show that those who champion Theodore and his impiety are impious to no purpose. Refuted, they take refuge in another empty pretext and say that he ought not to be anathematized because he died in the communion of the churches. But they ought to know that the ones who die in the communion of the churches are those who have held to the end the common doctrine of piety proclaimed in the catholic Church. This man died in his own impiety and has been cast out of every church. Indeed, the whole body of the church of Mopsuestia, where he is said to have been bishop, struck his name from that time on from the sacred diptychs of the church. They did so because of the blasphemies for which the holy fathers numbered him with Greeks, Jews and Sodomites, as the minutes drawn up about him in that same city before the provincial synod show. We marvel, then, at those who defend Theodore and make him and his impiety their own, when the very church in which he was bishop cast him out as a heretic many years ago. The fearful judgment that fell on Judas also shows that those who defend Theodore put forward such a pretext to their own condemnation. Judas thought he could escape the notice of the one who knows people's secrets, and he shared in the mysteries with the apostles. Yet that hypocritical communion did him no good. After his death the disciples were still called the Twelve, as John the evangelist says: "Thomas, called the Twin, one of the Twelve, was not with them when Jesus came." But this neither released Judas from condemnation nor caused him to be counted among the apostles. Indeed, after the Lord's ascension the apostles by their own vote condemned that same Judas even after his death and brought in another in his place. That they put forward an empty pretext in saying that heretics who have died ought not to be anathematized, we will show from the very words of the Lord. He calls the ungodly dead even while they are still alive, saying, "Let the dead bury their own dead," just as he calls the righteous who have died living.

For he says of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob that God is not the God of the dead but of the living. If, then, by their argument, heretics who have died must not be anathematized, neither will living heretics be anathematized. The Lord calls them dead because they are separated from him, and he said, "I am the life." So by their reasoning heretics will be anathematized neither living nor dead. By their account, the apostolic teaching handed down in vain that those who teach contrary to what we received are to be anathematized. The holy synods condemned heretics in vain, and the other holy fathers and teachers of the Church anathematized heretics in vain. Let them also find fault with the prophet Jeremiah, who says, "Cursed is the one who does the works of the Lord negligently," and with the prophet David, who said, "Cursed are those who turn aside from your commandments." In short, let them find fault with the whole of divine Scripture, which in many places brings such condemnations on the ungodly. If those who do the Lord's works negligently and sin against his commandments are subject to such condemnations, how much more justly has the impious Theodore been condemned and anathematized? He uttered such blasphemies against our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ himself. These arguments, together with the proofs given above and in other treatises of ours on why heretics must be condemned even after death, would be enough to shame those who champion Theodore and to stop them from such impiety. But because they contentiously persist in the same views, we will say more. Some of those who gathered at the holy synod of Nicaea subscribed to the definition, that is, the creed of faith, that it set out. When they were later found to hold contrary views, they were anathematized, some while they were alive and others after death, by Damasus of holy memory, pope of elder Rome, and by the synod at Sardica, as Athanasius among the saints also testifies. Moreover, the holy synod at Chalcedon condemned after his death Domnus, who had been bishop of Antioch, simply because he had dared to write that the twelve chapters of [?] among the saints should be passed over in silence.

The heretics who champion Theodore have failed in every proposition and argument. So, to deceive the ignorant, they have tried to claim that Cyril of holy memory praised him in some part of a letter. Many things show that their claim does not agree with what Cyril among the saints said against the ungodly Theodore in various treatises. In these he showed Theodore to be more impious than all the other heretics. Unable to bear the number and magnitude of the blasphemies Theodore uttered against our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ, he cried out: "'Heaven was astonished at this and shuddered exceedingly,' says the Lord. O unspeakable perversity! O tongue that speaks injustice against God and lifts up its horn!" And again: "Set a door and a bar on your tongue, O man. Stop lifting up your horn on high and speaking injustice against God. How long will you leap upon Christ, who bears it patiently? Keep in mind what was written

by the inspired Paul: 'When you sin in this way against the brothers and wound their weak conscience, you sin against Christ.' And to quote the prophetic books as well: 'Sodom was justified by you.' You have outdone the unbridled insults the Greeks hurled against Christ when they counted the cross foolishness. You have made the charges of Jewish madness look like nothing." These things, then, were said by Cyril among the saints to condemn the impious Theodore. Even if one granted their claim that Cyril among the saints said something in Theodore's favour, not even this would exempt him from condemnation. For we find that many of the holy fathers accepted certain heretics: Damasus, Athanasius and Basil among the saints accepted Apollinarius, and Leo of holy memory accepted Eutyches. Yet once the impiety of these heretics became plain, that acceptance did not let them escape the condemnation and anathema that afterwards fell on them personally and on their impiety. So great is the madness of those who defend Theodore that they dare to tell lies even about Gregory the Theologian and John of Constantinople, claiming that these men sent Theodore letters full of praise. This is entirely false. Gregory struggled for the truth in Constantinople and turned the people from the error of the Arians to the orthodox faith, and then returned to his own homeland. The letters that the heretics maliciously bring forward were written by him not to Theodore of Mopsuestia but to Theodore, bishop of Tyana, the metropolis of Second Cappadocia. Nazianzus, of which Gregory among the saints became bishop, belongs to the same region, as does Arianzus, the village he came from. The letters themselves show this clearly. They mention peoples and synods, that same village of Arianzus and other places in the same province, and months named in the local dialect of the Cappadocians. They also mention Bosporius, bishop of the city of Colonia, who was subject to Theodore, and other bishops, chorepiscopi and monasteries under that same Theodore, whose names are preserved to this day. What connection did Cappadocians have with the people of Second Cilicia, then or now, when the administration of these provinces is separate? Or what bishops could the bishop of Mopsuestia have under him, when he himself was subject to the metropolitan of Second Cilicia? John of Constantinople did write a letter to Theodore of Mopsuestia, but it was full not of praise but of reproaches and rebukes, since Theodore had fallen away from godliness. John had lived the monastic life with him in one and the same monastery, and he reminds him of the life they shared there. Sozomen, Hesychius and Socrates testify to this, as does Theodoret, who wrote many treatises and eulogies on Theodore's behalf. And if they bring forward testimonies given by John of Antioch and the Eastern synod under him in favour of Theodore and his impiety, they must also accept what John and his party, as far as it lay in their power, dared to do to condemn Cyril among the saints and set aside the right faith, and what they wrote, Nestorius…

[?] …defending his own heterodoxy for a very long time. This is shown by various speeches and letters of theirs, written to Theodosius of pious memory and to various others. So much for that. But so that we leave out nothing that bears on accuracy, we thought it necessary to mention also what was written by Augustine of holy memory, who was a bishop in Africa. A dispute had arisen about Caecilian after his death, on the grounds that he had departed from the tradition of the Church, and some had separated themselves from the catholic Church on this account. Augustine of holy memory wrote to Boniface that no one ought to separate himself from the catholic Church for this reason. For if the charges brought against Caecilian had been true, and he had been shown to hold views contrary to the catholic order, they would have subjected him to anathema even after his death. Moreover, a canon of the holy synod in Africa declares that bishops who pass on their property to a heretic, whether by will or by intestacy, must be anathematized even after death. Besides all this, who does not know what was done in our own times in the church of elder Rome against Dioscorus? Though he had committed no sin against the faith, he was anathematized after his death by the most holy church of Rome itself, solely over a matter of church order. If, then, bishops who did not err at all in the faith are subjected to anathema even after death over church order and over money, how much more Theodore, who committed impiety against God himself? As for the folly of those who say that people who died in their own impiety ought not to be anathematized after death: by that reasoning, neither ought fathers who were unjustly condemned to be restored after death. Yet this is what happened in the case of John of holy memory, who was bishop of Constantinople and was restored by the catholic Church after his death, and in the case of Flavian of holy memory, who was likewise bishop of Constantinople, unjustly condemned in his lifetime but justly restored after his death by Leo [?] of holy memory and by the holy synod at Chalcedon. On their argument, then, it follows that heretics are counted among the holy fathers, as though released from the condemnation they deserve, while holy fathers who were unjustly condemned are joined to the heretics, as though the unjust condemnation against them were never lifted. But the most trustworthy teacher of all is our Lord and God Jesus Christ, who says of himself: "For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life. For God did not send his Son into the world to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through him. Whoever believes in him is not judged; but whoever does not believe in him has already been judged, because he has not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God." And the Holy Spirit says through the prophet David that the ungodly will not rise up in the judgment. Since, then, such a sentence of the Lord has been pronounced against every ungodly person, and it makes no distinction

between living and dead heretics, how do they dare to oppose this sentence and say that those who have once committed impiety, and have for that reason already been condemned by the Lord, ought not to be condemned after death? The divine apostle too, who had Christ speaking within him, pronounced such a sentence not only against men but even against angels, saying in the Letter to the Galatians: "But even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be anathema. As we have said before, so I now say again: if anyone preaches to you a gospel contrary to the one you received, let him be anathema." And who is so impious as to dare to say that what Theodore impiously wrote [?], or any part of it, was ever handed down to the holy Church of God? Was not anyone who dared to utter such a thing at once subjected to anathema by the holy fathers? If, then, after this correct confession and condemnation of the heretics, with the pious meaning preserved, anyone fights over names or syllables or words and separates himself from the holy Church of God, as though our piety lay in names and words alone and not in realities, such a man, as one who delights in schisms, will give account for himself and for those deceived by him, or who will yet be deceived, to our great God and Savior Jesus Christ on the day of judgment. Amen.

Letter [?] of the Emperor Justinian to the holy synod concerning Theodore of Mopsuestia and the rest.

The orthodox and our fathers who reigned piously have always taken care to cut off, through synods of most holy priests, the heresies that sprang up from time to time, and to keep the holy Church of God in peace, with the right faith purely proclaimed. So when Arius blasphemed, saying that the Son is not consubstantial with God the Father but a creature that came into being from nothing, Constantine the Great gathered the three hundred and eighteen fathers at Nicaea and attended in person. Once Arius had been condemned and anathematized, he worked to strengthen the orthodox faith. In that faith the divine fathers confessed that the Son is consubstantial with God the Father, and not a creature that came into being from nothing, and it is sung to this day [?]. When Macedonius denied the divinity of the Holy Spirit, and his disciple Apollinaris blasphemed against the economy of God the Word, claiming that the Word of God did not take on a human mind but was united to flesh that had an irrational soul, Theodosius the Elder gathered the one hundred and fifty fathers at Constantinople and took part in the synod himself. Once these heretics had been deposed and anathematized, together with their impious doctrines and those who shared their views, he saw to it that the orthodox faith was proclaimed. And when the impious Nestorius said that God the Word was one and Christ another, impiously bringing in one who was Son of God the Father by nature and another who was son by grace, and denied that holy Mary is Theotokos, Theodosius the Younger convened the first synod of the two hundred holy fathers at Ephesus. He sent officials to attend the synod and ordered Nestorius to be present and to be judged.

After a careful examination they condemned Nestorius, anathematizing him together with those who shared his views. When things had gone this far, those of the accursed party of Nestorius rose up against the most holy [?Cyril] and tried, as far as it lay with them, to overturn the judgment passed against Nestorius. But Emperor Theodosius upheld what had truly and rightly been judged against Nestorius and his evil doctrines, and saw to it that the judgment passed on him stood firm [the Latin translator read "thus"]. Since these men also spouted some other nonsense against the divine Cyril, Cyril wrote to the emperor as follows:

"Most pious emperor, I have learned that some of those who love to talk are buzzing about like wild wasps and belching out wicked words against me. They claim that I say the divine body of Christ was brought down from heaven and not from the holy Virgin, and they have also prated that we confess two sons [?] in the manner of Nestorius. So we thought it necessary to say a few words to them on this matter, as follows: O foolish men, who know only how to slander, how were you led to this opinion, and how did you fall sick with such madness? You ought to have understood clearly that almost our whole struggle for the faith was fought to establish that holy Mary is Theotokos. But if we say, as they claim, that the divine body of Christ was born from heaven and not from her, how could she be understood to be Theotokos? Whom did she bear at all, if it is not true that she gave birth to Emmanuel according to the flesh? Let those who have prated these and similar things against me be laughed at. For the blessed Isaiah does not lie when he says: 'Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel, which means God with us.' And the archangel Gabriel certainly spoke the truth when he said to the Virgin: 'Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor with God. Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. For he will save his people from their sins.' When we say that our Lord Jesus Christ is from heaven above, we do not say this as though his holy flesh had been brought down from heaven above. We are following the holy Paul, who says: 'The first man was from the earth, earthy; the second man is the Lord from heaven.' We also remember the Lord himself saying: 'No one has ascended into heaven except the one who came down from heaven, the Son of Man.' And yet, as has been said, he was born according to the flesh from the holy Virgin. But God the Word, who came down from heaven above, emptied himself, taking the form of a slave, and was called son of man while remaining what he was, that is, God, for by nature he is unchangeable and unalterable. Since he is now understood as one together with his own flesh, he is said to have come down from heaven, and he is also called the man from heaven. He is perfect in divinity, and the same is perfect in humanity, and he is understood as in one person. For there is one Lord Jesus Christ, even if we do not ignore the difference of the natures from which, we say, the ineffable union was made. We therefore confess that the only-begotten Son of God, God the Word, is perfect God and perfect man, of a rational soul and a body. He was begotten from the Father before the ages according to his divinity, and in the last days the same [was born] for us and for our salvation from Mary the Virgin

according to his humanity. The same is consubstantial with the Father according to his divinity and consubstantial with us according to his humanity. For a union of two natures has taken place, and so we confess one Christ, one Son, one Lord. And we confess the holy Virgin to be Theotokos, because God the Word became flesh and became man, and from the very moment of conception united to himself the temple taken from her. If you please, let us take as an example our own composition, by which we are human beings. We are composed of soul and body, and we see two natures, one of the body and another of the soul. Yet from both there is one human being by union. Being composed of two natures does not make the one man be thought of as two men; he is one man by composition, as I said, made of soul and body. For if we do away with the fact that the one and only Christ is from two different natures, while remaining undivided after the union, our opponents will say: 'If the whole is one nature, how did he become man, or what flesh did he make his own?' As for those who say that a mixture, confusion or blending of God the Word with the flesh took place, may your Piety see fit to silence them openly."

After this, when Cyril had died, there sprang up a monk and archimandrite named Eutyches, who drew no small part of the people after him. He confirmed [?] the views of Nestorius and his own evil doctrine, saying that the Lord's flesh is not consubstantial with us. And shortly afterwards, when the devil's hand again prevailed, another synod was held at Ephesus, a robber synod and not a holy one. Flavian of Constantinople was also sent there, and Dioscorus of Alexandria held all authority. The divine Flavian was murdered while fighting for the orthodox faith, and the first synod of Ephesus was overturned, after some bishops signed under murderous coercion, among them Basil of Seleucia. Then, as the evil doctrines of Nestorius, Dioscorus and Eutyches were spread abroad and great turmoil arose, especially in the East, Proterius, the great priest, was murdered, along with very many others. This being the state of affairs, the Emperor Marcian was raised up by God. He convened the synod of the six hundred and thirty fathers at Chalcedon concerning Dioscorus and Eutyches, and went there himself [?]. Dioscorus and Eutyches were condemned, and Nestorius was anathematized again. Theodoret, Ibas and Basil of Seleucia were received after they had signed, and once the robber synod had been overturned and anathematized, the divine fathers brought everyone into one concord. These four synods having been held, confirmed and accepted as authoritative in the Church of God, those who held the views of Nestorius tried once more to strengthen their heresy by using Theodore of Mopsuestia as a pretext, a man whose blasphemies were far worse than those of his disciple Nestorius. So we too, following our fathers and wishing to keep the right faith unharmed, urge you to examine his blasphemies as well and to pronounce against him and those who share his views. For besides his countless other blasphemies against Christ our God, he said that God the Word is one and Christ another, who was troubled by the passions of the soul and the desires of the flesh, and

who, withdrawing little by little from what is worse, advanced to what is better through progress in works and became blameless by a most excellent way of life. He said that Christ was baptized as a mere man in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, that through baptism he received the grace of the Holy Spirit and was deemed worthy of adoption as son, that Christ is worshipped with reference to the person of God the Word in the way an imperial image is, and that after the resurrection he became unchangeable in his thoughts and sinless. Besides this he said that the union of God the Word with Christ was of the kind the apostle spoke of concerning husband and wife: "The two shall become one flesh." I further urge you to examine also what was wickedly written by Theodoret and Ibas against the first holy synod of Ephesus, and likewise to pronounce against it.

After investigating these matters in the same way, the divine fathers replied: The divine synod at Chalcedon, having loudly denounced Theodoret and Ibas, did not receive them until they had first anathematized their own wicked writings, and Theodore and Nestorius. We, for our part, condemn and anathematize, in addition to all the other heretics condemned and anathematized by the four holy synods already mentioned, Theodore, who was bishop of Mopsuestia, and his impious writings. We also condemn what Theodoret wickedly wrote against the right faith, against the twelve chapters of Cyril, who is among the saints, and against the first holy synod of Ephesus, and whatever he wrote in defense of Theodore and Nestorius. In addition, we anathematize the impious letter said to have been written by Ibas to Mari the Persian. It denies that God the Word, incarnate of the holy Virgin Mary the Theotokos, became man. It slanders the divine Cyril as a heretic, finds fault with the first synod of Ephesus for deposing Nestorius without trial or inquiry, spurns the twelve chapters of the blessed Cyril, and defends Theodore and Nestorius and their God-hated writings and doctrines. Therefore we rightly number the unbridled tongues of these heretics and of all heretics, together with their most impious writings and the heretics themselves who persisted to the end in their own heterodoxy and wickedness, with the father of lies, the devil, and we say: "Walk in the light of your fire and in the flame that you have kindled."

[?] … and his evil doctrines, and the so-called letter of Ibas, and the writings of Theodoret written against the right faith.

We have received your letter. On reading it we were amazed that you have not taken to heart the teaching of the Lord, who says: "Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart." Instead you have been lifted up to such arrogance that you despise all the priests of the Church of God and justify yourselves alone out of everyone, like that Pharisee who was not justified even though he condemned the tax collector. We had hoped that you thought as the other priests do, but contrary to our hopes we found you defending things that are opposed both to God and to the right faith. And while defending such impiety, you supposed yourselves equal to the apostles, saying that no one ought to reproach you as rustics, since God also commanded rustics to preach the gospel. We did indeed, as is said, call you rustics, and we said so for this reason: because, being ignorant of the order and tradition of the Church and of the orthodox faith, you defend such impiety. But the apostles, whom you call rustics, God chose for himself, filled with his own Spirit, grace and wisdom, and sent out so that they might lead the nations who did not know God onto the way of truth. That is why he said to the apostles alone: "You are the light of the world." It is evident, then, as the apostle said, that you understand "neither what you are saying nor the things about which you make confident assertions," since you have dared to make yourselves equal to the apostles and to insult the patriarchs and all the priests. You have kept so little of the order of the Church that you have dared to do what Christians have never done at any time. For while all the most blessed patriarchs are in union with one another, no one has ever separated himself from the catholic Church unless he was plainly gripped by heretical madness, and this is what you have now set about doing. Yet even though you have done this, we do not cease doing and writing whatever may serve to set you right. You wrote that we were eager to have these three chapters condemned, that is, Theodore with his writings, the so-called letter of Ibas, and the writings of Theodoret, in order to satisfy the wishes of those who had separated themselves from the catholic Church. Know, then, that we did not do this on their account. We did it first because of the impiety of these chapters, and second because certain people, while pretending to keep silent about the name of Nestorius, were trying by means of these chapters to bring in Nestorius himself and his heterodoxy, attaching the impiety of these chapters to the catholic Church.

For this reason, although the impiety of these chapters was evident, we nevertheless asked the priests of God's church what they thought about them. Wishing to show that the catholic church never held such impiety and does not hold it now, they too condemned this ungodliness, which had been condemned from the beginning by the holy fathers. Not even those who are separated from the catholic church make any argument about these chapters, since they know that no one who bears the name of Christian can defend them. What they oppose is the definition of the holy synod at Chalcedon, the definition of the faith put forward to condemn Nestorius and Eutyches and their unbelief. Those who oppose the right doctrines of the church would rather have the holy church of God defend the impious chapters we have mentioned, so that on this pretext they may deceive the simpler folk and separate the Christian people from the church. Now, you wrote two things about whether that impious letter ought to be accepted [?]. The first was that it fought rightly, so it is said, against Apollinaris. The second was that, even if the writer of the letter seemed to disparage Cyril, who is among the saints, he nevertheless removed this stain of insult at the end of the letter, and that for this reason, so it is said, this impious letter ought to be judged orthodox. You have made it plain that you understood neither the style nor the sense of this impious letter. It contains nothing against Apollinaris. Instead it calls Cyril himself, who is among the saints, an Apollinarian. Nor did this impious letter retract at its end what had been said against that same Cyril. On the contrary, in its closing parts it said even worse things against him. As we go on, however, we shall expose both the whole impiety of the so-called letter of Ibas and the emptiness of the chapters you sent. When everything you had written was read out, we were deeply grieved that you had fallen into such error, men from that very region where the right faith has always been kept blameless, down to your own day. We therefore thought it necessary to reply to those chapters of yours and to urge you to turn away from this impiety and from your impious teacher, the man who composed these chapters. Wishing to deceive you, he brought forward certain words from the divine Scriptures, understood them wrongly, and tried to fit them to certain words of that impious letter. This is what all heretics do: they misinterpret certain words of the divine Scriptures and bend them to their own perverse meaning. It seems to us that your impious teacher either has not read that anonymous letter, or else has read it but maliciously quoted a few of its words and kept silent about the many worse ones. That letter says of blessed Cyril and the impious Nestorius that each wrote harmful words against the other. It says that Nestorius denied that blessed Mary is the Mother of God, so that many thought he belonged to the heresy of Paul of Samosata, while Cyril, wishing to overturn the words of Nestorius, slipped and fell into the doctrine of Apollinaris. So it is clear that the writer of the letter shows himself held fast by the madness of Nestorius. Of Nestorius, though he denied that the holy virgin

Mary [?] is the Mother of God, he says only that he came under the suspicion of some, not that this showed him to be a heretic. But Cyril, who is among the saints and is the teacher of the church, he insists slipped and fell into the doctrine of Apollinaris, because Cyril said that God the Word himself was made flesh and became man. As we have said, your teacher left these words out, because he knew that whoever says Cyril slipped and fell, and calls his words heretical, condemns the whole church, which rightly holds Cyril as its father and teacher. How did he not shudder to say that Cyril is a heretic because he said that God the Word himself became man, and that by saying so he fails to acknowledge the distinction between the temple and the one who dwells in it? With these words he blames not only Cyril but also the evangelist who says, "The Word became flesh," and all the prophets who proclaimed that God the Word himself would come in the flesh. Above all he blames Jeremiah, who says, "This is our God; no other shall be reckoned beside him. Afterward he appeared on earth and lived among men." He also blames Isaiah, who says, "The child... mighty God" (Isaiah 9:6). Besides these he blames the apostle Paul, who says in the Letter to the Ephesians, "He who descended is the very one who also ascended far above all the heavens, that he might fill all things." For if your teacher's ravings were right, the prophets, evangelists and apostles would all deserve blame for saying that God the Word himself became man, as though these words meant that the Godhead had been changed into manhood. Those who do not confess that God the Word himself became man are plainly saying that Christ is a mere man who is called Son of God by grace, as the false doctrine of Nestorius and his teacher Theodore holds. The divine Scriptures, and the holy fathers who follow them, say that God the Word himself came down, was made flesh and became man: the invisible and incorporeal one, light from light, begotten of the Father before the ages and outside time. Gregory, who is among the saints, speaks this way in his oration on the Theophany: "The very Word of God, the pre-eternal, the invisible, the incomprehensible, the incorporeal, the beginning from the beginning, the light from light, the source of life and immortality, the impress of the archetype, the unmoved seal, the unchanging image, the Father's definition and word, comes to his own image. He bears flesh for the sake of flesh and is mingled with a rational soul for the sake of my soul, cleansing like by like. He becomes man in every respect except sin, conceived of the virgin, whose soul and flesh had first been purified by the Spirit. For it was fitting both that childbearing should be honoured and that virginity should be honoured above it."

In much the same way, Athanasius, who is among the saints, says this in his discourse on the Holy Spirit against the Arians: "He who was begotten from above, of the Father, ineffably, inexpressibly, incomprehensibly and eternally, is himself born in time, here below, of the virgin Mary." Again, Basil, who is among the saints, writing to Amphilochius, said this in the eighth chapter: "Heaven and earth, the vast expanses of the seas, the creatures that live in the waters and the animals of the dry land, the plants, the stars, the air, the seasons and the varied order of the whole universe do not show the surpassing greatness of his power so much as this: that God, whom nothing can contain, was able to grapple with death through the flesh without suffering, so that by his own suffering he might grant us freedom from suffering." Augustine too, who is among the saints, a bishop from the land of the Africans, says this in his exposition of the creed: "You too, prophet Habakkuk, speak your testimony about Christ. 'Lord,' he says, 'I have heard your report and was afraid; I considered your works, O God, and was amazed.' What works of God did he marvel at [?]? The creation of the world? Far from it. Hear instead what amazed him. 'In the midst of two living creatures,' he says, 'your works will be made known.' For you, God the Word, became flesh: in the midst of two animals you will be made known. Who are you, that you came down so far? You have amazed me, for the Word through whom all things were made was born in a manger."
