Likewise Leo, who is among the saints, pope of Rome, said this in his letter to Flavian, archbishop of Constantinople: "The impassible God did not disdain to be a man capable of suffering, nor the immortal one to be subject to the laws of death." This is what the divine Scriptures and the holy fathers have said. Yet by your reasoning they deserve to be accused of introducing a confusion of the flesh with the Godhead, since they said that God the Word himself became man. After all, you have said that Cyril, when he says that God the Word himself became man, introduces confusion by these words. Now let us show that the writer of the letter, held fast by the madness of Theodore, denied that God the Word became man. We shall show it from the very things that this same heretic Theodore wrote against the impious Apollinaris. In his fourth book he writes: "You said that some of our people granted you what would never be granted by anyone who has been eager to hold to the church's doctrine. 'We asked them,' you said, 'whether they confess that God the Word became man, and they granted it.' But who in his right mind would say that God the Word became man, as you say? No one, unless he had first caught the same folly as you. We do indeed emphatically say that God the Word assumed a man. But that he became man, as you say, we could never bring ourselves to say." These quotations have shown that the impiety of the letter agrees with Theodore's heretical madness. How then could anyone who places his hope in God the Word, who was made flesh and became man, fail to condemn, and rightly, both Theodore and that impious letter alike? [Note: Perhaps read apantēsin ("answer") instead of eipōn epēn. — Ed.]

You also praise the impious letter for holding that whoever says God the Word himself was made flesh and became man abolishes the distinction between the temple and the one who dwells in the temple. Know, then, that the holy church of God rightly proclaims a distinction of the natures from which the one Christ, our Lord and God, was composed. But a distinction between the temple and the one who dwells in it was taught by none of the holy fathers. Only the impious Nestorius and Theodore spoke of it, because they wanted to introduce two persons by this means. The divine Scriptures and the holy fathers do use the word "temple", but when they say it they mean the body of the only-begotten Son of God, as the evangelist said: "But he was speaking of the temple of his body." No one says that the one person of Christ is distinct from itself, as if one were inside another. There is a distinction only of the natures, from which the one Christ was formed without confusion and without division. So you, by defending the impiety of the letter that denies that God the Word himself became man, have made it plain that you introduce two persons and think of Christ as a mere man. You apply to him what the apostle said of the faithful: "You are God's temple, and the Spirit of God dwells in you." By your error, then, there would be no difference between us human beings and Christ. This is just what the heretic Theodore himself says, the teacher of the man who wrote the letter, raving in his third book against Apollinaris, where he speaks as though in the person of Christ: "I whom you see can do nothing by my own nature, since I am a man. But I work, because the Father, abiding in me, does all things. For since I am in the Father," he says, "and the Father is in me, and God the Word, the only-begotten of God, is in me, it is clear that the Father too, together with him, abides in me and does the works. And there is nothing remarkable in thinking this about Christ, since he clearly says of the rest of men: 'Whoever loves me will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him.' If the Father and the Son make their dwelling with each such person, what wonder is it if both are thought to abide together in Christ, the Lord according to the flesh? For their communion in essence, it seems, admits a communion of [?] as well." Since the ungodly Theodore said such things, it is no wonder that one who has fallen away from God has foolishness yoked to his impiety, as the prophet Isaiah says of the impious: "The fool will speak foolish things, and his heart will devise vain things." He insists that the Father and the Son abide in Christ just as they do in other men, and does not confess that Christ is God the Word made flesh and become man. How then can he speak of Christ "according to the flesh"? The holy fathers confess that Christ is God the Word made flesh and become man, and so whenever they say something lowly about him, they rightly add "according to the flesh". Now, it would have been fitting for those who defend Theodore

to turn away from his ungodliness because of this extreme blasphemy alone. Yet because of their shamelessness, let us bring forward other blasphemies of his as well, by which he introduces two persons. He finds fault with those who say that God the Word, who is before the ages, became man in the last times, and in his fourth book against Apollinaris he puts it this way: "'He who is before the ages,' he says, 'came into being in the last times.' Again he says this as though some had granted it, though no one eager for piety would choose to catch this folly and say that he who is before the ages came into being in the last times." And further on: "So then, let us follow your laws and accept the conversion, or rather the subversion, that your shrewdness lays down. Come, let us confuse everything into one, and let there be no distinction any more: not between the form of God and the form of a slave; not between the temple that was assumed and the one who dwells in the temple; not between the one who was destroyed and the one who raised him up; not between the one who was perfected through sufferings and the one who perfected him; not between the one who was remembered and the one who remembered him; not between the one who was visited and the one who visited him; not between the one who was made a little lower than the angels and the one who made him lower; not between the one who was crowned with glory and honour and the one who crowned him; not between the one who was set over the works of God's hands and the one who set him there; not between the one who received them in subjection and the one who granted the subjection." Let those who champion him and the impious letter blush at these impious words of Theodore and at his blasphemy, so obvious as it is. For when he shamelessly and repeatedly says that God the Word is one and Christ another, that one is the benefactor and the other the one who receives the benefit, that one saved and the other was saved, he openly denies the salvation that has come to us through our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ. How can one who received a benefit from another, that is, who was saved, save others? So those who defend the man who uttered these blasphemies: whose body and blood do they think they receive, that of the one who received the benefit or that of the benefactor? If it is the body and blood of God the Word, the benefactor, how can they say so when they do not confess that he was made flesh and became man? If it is that of the one who received the benefit, their hope is vain, for they promote the worship of a man: they have acted impiously and worshipped the creature rather than the Creator. But all of us who belong to the catholic church confess God the Word, made flesh and become man, who is one of the holy Trinity, and we receive his body and his blood for the forgiveness of sins and for eternal life, as the Lord himself says: "Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day. For my flesh is true food, and my blood is true drink. Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in [him]. As [the living Father] sent me [Note: Perhaps read: "'He who is before ... in the last times,' again, as though some were teaching and saying this, though no one..." — Ed.]

and I live because of the Father, so whoever eats me will also live because of me." This is what we believe and confess. And how full of falsehood is what that same impious letter says about the twelve chapters of Cyril, who is among the saints! It slanders him by claiming that in them he speaks of one nature of the Godhead and the manhood of Christ, and for this reason it says that these chapters are full of every impiety. Your teacher craftily interprets this, saying that the letter called the chapters full of every impiety not because of the twelve chapters as such, but because they are said to teach one nature of Godhead and manhood. This is an obvious falsehood. Cyril, who is among the saints, nowhere appears to have spoken of one nature of Godhead and manhood: not in his other writings, not in the letter to which the twelve chapters are appended, not even in the chapters themselves. What he teaches is that there is one hypostasis, that is, one person, of the Godhead and the manhood of Christ. This is what the holy church of God proclaims and what all the fathers taught, and they anathematized those who speak of one nature of the Godhead and the manhood of Christ. For nature is one thing, and hypostasis, or person, is another. Nature signifies what is predicated commonly and generically of all persons, while hypostasis, or person, denotes what is particular, for one person is not seen within another person. That the abominable letter says of Cyril's twelve chapters that they are full of every impiety you can find for yourselves in what follows in that same impious letter, where it plainly says that these twelve chapters are contrary to the right faith. That same impious letter, said to be by Ibas, also blames Cyril, who is among the saints, for denying the distinction between the expressions used of Christ. Know that on this point too both the writer of the impious letter and your teacher are lying. In all his writings, when Cyril teaches about our Lord Jesus Christ, he does speak of a distinction between the expressions. The lofty ones refer to his Godhead and the lowly ones to his manhood, yet all of them are spoken by one and the same God the Word made flesh, and about him alone. What Cyril forbids is assigning them to two different persons. But you, no doubt because you wish to assign the expressions to two persons, claim for that reason that Cyril denied the distinction between the expressions. Your teacher, wishing to deceive you on this point too, also said that the same impious letter said to be by Ibas writes against the impiety of Apollinaris, and that it ought therefore to be considered orthodox. You must know that here too he lied. As we said above, the letter was not written against Apollinaris. And even if, as you claim, this were true, the letter would not on that account escape condemnation. When one heretic speaks against another, that does not prove him orthodox. Arius spoke against Sabellius [?], Apollinaris against Arius, and Eutyches against Nestorius. And though all these men were held fast by very different [errors?], none of them

…is judged orthodox on the strength of such a refutation. But [?] all are condemned by the catholic Church. From this too it is evident that the man who wrote the impious letter already mentioned brings in two persons, for he said: "How is it possible for the Word who was in the beginning to be understood of the temple born of Mary?" These words clearly show that he does not say that God the Word was made flesh and born of the holy Virgin Mary, but that Christ, whom he calls a temple, was a mere man. That the writer of that loathsome letter took this impiety too from the teaching of Theodore is clear from what the same impious Theodore wrote in the third book against the heretic Apollinaris, where he says: "But he who is God from God and consubstantial with the Father was, my good sir, present in the one born of the Virgin, who was formed by the Holy Spirit according to the divine Scriptures and received his constitution in the woman's womb. He was present in him, as is fitting, since at the very moment of being formed he had also received being the temple of God. Yet we must not think that God was born of the Virgin, unless indeed we are to think that what was born and what was in the one born are the same, the temple and God the Word in the temple. Nor, as you put it, must we by any means declare that the one born of the Virgin is God from God, consubstantial with the Father. For if, as you say, the one born of the Virgin is not a man who was assumed but God made flesh, how could the one born be called God from God and consubstantial with the Father, when the flesh cannot admit this expression? For it is senseless to say that God was born of the Virgin. This is nothing other than saying that he was born of the seed of David, from the substance of the Virgin, and formed in her; since what we say was born of the Virgin is what came from the seed of David and from the substance of the Virgin, was constituted in a mother's womb, and was formed by the power of the Holy Spirit." Since Theodore blasphemes in this way and repeatedly insists that it is impossible for him who is God from God and consubstantial with the Father to be made flesh and born of the Virgin, because the flesh is not consubstantial with the Father either, how can those who champion such a heretic not blush? He loathsomely set out things contrary both to the divine Scriptures and to the holy fathers, whereas it is clear to all that from the beginning, from the time God founded the Church on the right confession, all the priests of God proclaimed that God the Word, who is from God, was made flesh of the holy and glorious Virgin Mary, in flesh animated by a rational and intelligent soul, and became man and was born of her. And in teaching this they neither introduced a change of the Godhead into flesh, nor denied on account of the flesh that he is consubstantial with the Father, as Theodore babbles. Rather, they taught that one and the same, our Lord and God Jesus Christ, is consubstantial with the Father according to the Godhead and, the same, consubstantial with us according to the humanity.

Again, in the book already mentioned, the impious Theodore says this too, in blasphemy: "But it was not the divine nature that was born of the Virgin; what was born of the Virgin was he who was constituted from the substance of the Virgin. It was not God the Word who was born of Mary; the one born of Mary was he who was of the seed of David. It was not God the Word who was born of a woman; the one born of a woman was he who was formed in her by the power of the Holy Spirit. It was not the one consubstantial with the Father who was brought forth from a womb, for he is without mother according to the saying of the blessed Paul. It was he who was formed in later times in a mother's womb by the power of the Holy Spirit, who for this reason is also called without father." So says the impious Theodore, using false reasoning to twist the apostle's teaching on this matter, for in the Epistle to the Hebrews the apostle says of the Lord: "First, by interpretation, king of righteousness, and then also king of Salem, that is, king of peace; without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life." The apostle said of one and the same person, "without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life," but the impious Theodore calls one person without father and another without mother. We shall refute the impiety of those who think this way from the teaching of the holy fathers as well. Gregory, bishop of Nazianzus, among the saints, says this in his oration on the Theophany: "Who does not worship the one who is from the beginning? Who does not glorify the one who is last? Again the darkness is dispelled, again the light is established; again Egypt is punished with darkness, again Israel is lit by a pillar. Let the people that sat in the darkness of ignorance see the great light of knowledge. The old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new. The letter withdraws, the Spirit speaks openly; the shadows pass away, the truth comes in. Melchizedek is fulfilled: he who was without mother becomes without father, without mother the first time, without father the second. The laws of nature are dissolved; the world above must be filled. Christ commands; let us not resist." In addition, Proclus, bishop of Constantinople, among the saints, says this in his sermon on the Theotokos: "He who by nature is impassible became, out of compassion, subject to many sufferings. Christ did not become God by advancement, God forbid! Rather, out of compassion God became man; this we believe. We do not proclaim a man made God, but confess God made flesh. He who in essence is without mother, and in the economy without father, enrolled his own handmaid as his mother. Otherwise, how is the same one, according to Paul, without mother and without father? If he were a mere man, he would not be without mother, for he has a mother. As it is, the same one is without mother as Creator and without father as creature." And Augustine among the saints says this in his work on the exposition of the Creed: "We believe in his Son Jesus Christ, born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary. Why, unbeliever, are you astonished at this birth? Do not believe it if the one born was only a man. But if he was God and man, he was born of whom he willed, since he was born as he willed. Marvel rather at this: that the Word took flesh and was not changed into flesh; that while remaining God he became man. Yet why do you marvel that she who gave birth bore her own Creator, that the thing made

bore its Maker? The Most High willed to be born lowly in this way so that in his very lowliness he might display his majesty." That is what the holy fathers say. It is also evident that the divine Scriptures, which the holy fathers followed, teach that God the Word himself was made flesh, was born of the holy Virgin Mary, and became man. First the prophet Isaiah says: "Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel," which translated means "God with us." Then the prophet David says in the hundred and sixth Psalm: "He sent his word and healed them, and delivered them from their corruptions." And the holy apostle Paul says: "But when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons." This being so, who is mad enough to dare to say that a man was in the heavens, and that this man was sent to be born of a woman and under the law? For human beings were under the law before the Word became flesh. But God the Word himself, the only-begotten Son of God, who was not under the law but had himself given the law, was sent from the Father, and being born of a woman came under the law, to redeem us who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption. If, then, as the writer of that impious letter and the heretic Theodore madly claim, the one born of a woman was not truly and properly the Son of God, how could he bestow adoption on us? Moreover, the same impious letter contains the claim that "You made him a little lower than the angels" cannot be said of the Godhead of the Only-begotten. You too have put this forward as rightly said, claiming that it can be said about the man and not about God the Word made flesh. That the writer of the letter uttered these blasphemies because he had learned this impiety too from the heretic Theodore, let us make plain from what that same Theodore said in his fourth book against Apollinaris. It runs as follows: "The blessed Paul clearly shows that the man of whom the prophet says these things is the man assumed by the Only-begotten. For having said, 'But someone has testified somewhere, saying: What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son [?] a little lower than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honour, and set him over the works of your hands; you put all things in subjection under his feet,' he adds, 'But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honour because of the suffering of death.' In this he clearly shows that Jesus is the man of whom the blessed David speaks, astonished that the divine nature then [?] made mention of him and deemed him worthy of its own visitation, made him a little lower than the angels by causing him to taste death,

and clothed him with glory and all honour, so as even to declare him lord of all things through his conjunction with itself." And again, in his interpretation of the eighth Psalm, on the same text, the same impious Theodore says: "For this reason, then, the psalm shows us how great the difference is between God the Word and the man who was assumed. These are found kept distinct in the New Testament. The Lord applies to himself the first parts of the psalm, which say that he is the maker of creation, that his majesty is exalted above the heavens, and that he is marvelled at in all the earth. The apostle applies to Jesus the second parts, which concern the man deemed worthy of so great a benefaction. How then is it not plain that the divine Scripture clearly teaches us that God the Word is one and the man another, and shows us that the difference between them is great? For the one is mindful, the other is deemed worthy of being remembered; the one visits, the other is deemed worthy of this too and is called blessed; the one, as benefactor, makes him a little lower than the angels, the other is the recipient of benefaction even in such a lowering; the one crowns with glory and honour, the other is crowned and is called blessed for these things; the one set him over all the works of his hands and put all things in subjection under his feet, the other was deemed worthy to be master of these things, over which he previously had no authority." So the impious Theodore and that loathsome letter openly blaspheme, saying that God the Word is one and Christ another. And you, following them, have written that "You made him a little lower than the angels" was said about a man and not about God the Word made flesh. Yet you ought to understand that every man is lower than the angels, and that this was said on account of the only-begotten Son of God. For though he was God, he deigned to become man, condescending to our weakness. The apostle teaches us this too when he says: "But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honour because of the suffering of death." If, then, as you say, Jesus who was made a little lower than the angels is one, and the Word of God who was not lowered is another, then beyond doubt the Christ who endured the passion is a mere man. On your view the apostle too is lying when he says, "For if they had known, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory." For who is the Lord of glory if not God the Word made flesh, whom the Jews, not knowing him to be God, asked: "Why do you, being a man, make yourself God?" Your teacher too, through this wicked interpretation, followed the Jews instead and spoke against our God. To confirm your arguments you added to your chapters the claim that the apostle's words, "who, being in the form of God, emptied himself, taking the form of a servant," agree with your interpretation, and were said not about God the Word made flesh but about a man only. But even if you, following the error of the heretics in this too, insist that the apostle said of a man that he emptied

himself, it is nevertheless clear to all the orthodox that the apostle says it was God the Word himself who emptied himself. For being in the form of God, that is, in the divine nature, he deigned to take the form of a servant; and the form of a servant signifies the human nature, which God the Word united to his own hypostasis in the Virgin's womb and from her. He was not united to a man formed beforehand, as the impiety of Nestorius and Theodore has handed down to their followers. Nestorius says that God the Word was together with the man born of Mary; Theodore says that he was present, as is fitting, in the one who was born. That "You made him a little lower than the angels" and "He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant" were said about God the Word made flesh, we also learn from other words of the apostle, who says: "For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, he became poor for our sake, so that we through his poverty might become rich." Who, then, will dare to say that a man was rich and became poor to make us rich? You also say that if anyone says of God the Word made flesh, the only-begotten Son of God, that he himself was lowered or emptied, he introduces a change in the divine nature in the manner of Apollinaris's impiety, or brings in a passible Godhead in the manner of Arius's madness. To you it is fitting to apply that saying of the Gospel: "You are mistaken, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God." For what can you say about the Lord's saying, "No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven"? Do you say that a man came down from heaven? No: it is plain that God the Word himself emptied himself, coming down from the heavens, was made flesh of the holy Theotokos and ever-virgin Mary, became man, and was born of her. The one who descended is the same as the one who ascended, and the lowering and the emptying are ascribed to him because of his descent. In another place in the Gospels the Lord also said, "My Father is greater than I." Do you suppose, then, that some man said this about himself, and not God the Word who became man? It is evident that the one who said, "My Father is greater than I," himself also said, "I and the Father are one." In saying "I and the Father are one," he shows the equality he has with the Father according to the divine nature. In the same one's saying "My Father is greater than I," he shows the lowering that came about for our sake in the economy. Both the equality and the lowering are said of one and the same, our Lord and God Jesus Christ, that is, God the Word made flesh. The Arians, with wicked intent, use the lowly sayings to deny that the Son is consubstantial with the Father, and so they insist that he is lesser. You, refusing to accept the lowly sayings as referring to God the Word made flesh, bring another person into the Trinity, following the impiety of Theodore and Nestorius. But we, saying both

the lofty and the lowly things of one and the same God the Word made flesh, our Lord Jesus Christ, introduce neither confusion nor division of the natures from which we confess the one composite hypostasis of our Lord and God Jesus Christ; nor do we bring a fourth person into the Holy Trinity. The holy fathers and teachers of the Church who interpreted the holy Scriptures have also taught us that "You made him a little lower than the angels" was written, as has already been said, about the only-begotten God the Word made flesh. Cyril among the saints said this in his letter to the Empress: "How, then, was he made lower than the angels, he who is worshipped by them? The reason is clear. He was held within the measures of humanity. Having taken a body naturally subject to death and made it his own, he suffered in it willingly, and because of his suffering he is crowned with the highest glories, as having through it abolished death and rendered corruption powerless, since he is indeed incorruption and life. Whenever, then, Scripture names Jesus and says that he was made lower than the angels, we understand not a man taken separately and individually, but the Only-begotten himself, yielding precedence to the holy angels in the economy, because he truly became man and so fell short of their superiority. The holy angels are superior in that they are outside the flesh and death, while the Son came to be in these through his voluntary [?]. But he who was made a little lower than the angels because of the measure of humanity, being supreme in Godhead, is worshipped by them and is seated on thrones which they surround, ever glorifying him and naming him Lord of the powers." That the emptying also belongs to God the Word himself made flesh, the same Cyril among the saints says in what he wrote against the objections Theodoret raised against his fourth chapter: "That all human things are small to the Word who sprang from God I would say without any hesitation. But I ask whose emptying this should be understood to be, and who it was that underwent it willingly. If, as they say, it was the form of the servant, that is, what is of the seed of David, how or in what way was it emptied, if it was taken up by God? But if the Word himself, who exists in the form of God the Father and equal to him, is said to have emptied himself, how again or in what way was he emptied, if he should refuse the emptying? For God the Word, who cannot undergo change, the emptying consists in doing and saying some of the things that belong to human beings, because of his union with flesh in the economy." And again the same Cyril among the saints says this in the same book against the Nestorians: "Has the divine Paul, then, deceived those sanctified through faith when he says most plainly of the Only-begotten that, though he was rich, he became poor for our sake? God forbid! For the herald of the truth certainly speaks the truth. But who is the rich one, and in what way did he become poor? Let our discourse examine this now too. If, as they have dared to think and say, a man was assumed by God, how did the one who was assumed, and made glorious with honours beyond nature, become poor? For he has been glorified, or, if this is not true, [?]

…would be [?] by them, as though it had brought the measure of humanity down to the lesser, and indeed to the more inglorious. But it is absurd to think this. So the one who was assumed did not become poor. It remains, then, to say that he who was rich as God came to be in poverty like ours." Likewise St Gregory the Theologian, in his oration on the Theophany, says this: "God came forth with what he had assumed, one thing out of two opposites, flesh and spirit, of which the one deified and the other was deified. O the new mingling! O the paradoxical blending! He who is comes to be, and the uncreated is created, and the uncontainable is contained, through the mediation of an intellectual soul standing between the Godhead and the grossness of flesh. And he who makes rich becomes poor, for he becomes poor in my flesh, so that I may be made rich by his Godhead. And he who is full is emptied, for he is emptied of his own glory for a little while, so that I may share in his fullness." St Athanasius too, interpreting the words of the Apostle, who says, "who, being in the form of God, emptied himself, taking the form of a servant," says this: "What could be clearer and more conclusive than this? For he did not become better from a lesser state. Rather, being God, he took the form of a servant, and in taking it he was not advanced but humbled himself." And a little later: "What does this mean, except that he who is in the form of God, the Son of a noble Father, humbled himself and became a servant in our place and on our behalf?" And a little later: "For the Word became flesh, and such a man is said to be from heaven and heavenly, because the Word came down from heaven." St Gregory, bishop of Nyssa, also says this in the third book Against Eunomius: "These things we have believed concerning the Crucified, and for this reason we do not cease to exalt him according to the measure of our power: that he who can be contained by no one, because of his ineffable and unapproachable majesty, except by himself and the Father and the Holy Spirit, was able to come down even to share in our weakness. But they make this a proof that the Son is alien in nature to the Father, that the Lord was made manifest through flesh and the cross. They argue that the nature of the Father remains purely in impassibility and can in no way admit any share in suffering, while the Son, because his nature has been altered toward the lower, is not incapable of coming to the experience of flesh and death." And after other things: "For this reason the cross is said to be the cross of the Lord of glory, and every tongue confesses that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father. And if we must also divide the rest in the same way, let us consider what it is that dies, and what destroys death, and what is renewed, and what is emptied. For the Godhead is emptied, so that it may become containable by human nature; and the human is renewed, becoming divine through its blending with the divine." These passages from the teaching of the holy fathers

we have set out so that, considering them, you may know that the things you have put forward are what both the Arians and the Nestorians impiously say against our Lord and God Jesus Christ. For the Arians, eager to prove that the Son is a creature and alien to the Father's substance, attach the suffering and the other lowly things to his Godhead alone. The Nestorians, wishing to bring in two sons, speak of God the Word separately and of Christ, a mere man, separately, and assign the lowly things to the man alone. But this is not what the holy fathers teach. They do not speak of a change in the Son's Godhead because of the lowly things, nor do they separate the humanity from the Godhead because of the lofty things. Rather, they hand down that both the lofty and the lowly things belong to the one and same only-begotten God the Word, who became flesh and was made man.

You have also put into your chapters, from the same letter, the claim that it rightly said "two natures, one power, one person." So let us refute the impiety of the letter's writer on this point too. If someone does not confess that God the Word himself, made flesh from the Virgin, became man, whose two natures is he talking about? It is obvious that, following Nestorius and Theodore, whom this impious letter praises, he takes [?] the two natures in place of persons. For even if the letter seems to speak of one person and one [son?], Theodore and Nestorius say this too. They say that Christ, a mere man, holds the person of God the Word, has the dignity and honor of God the Word and the grace of adoption, and is worshiped in his place. For this reason they pretend to speak of one Son and one person of the Word and of Christ, though Christ shares only in the name of sonship. This is shown plainly by the letter's speaking of one power of the two natures, as you yourselves wrote. For "one power" is said not of different natures but of different persons, as we confess in the case of the Holy Trinity. That is why the holy fathers anathematized those who say that the man was united to the Word by power, or dignity, or authority, or relation, or honor, and who do not confess that the union of the two natures came about by hypostasis. The followers of Nestorius, whose unbelief began with Theodore, impiously take even this statement, which the holy fathers rightly made about the difference of the two natures, and speak of natures in place of persons. Championing a relational union of persons, they pretend to speak of one person. The impious Theodore himself shows how they do this, in the fourth book of his work against Apollinaris the heretic, where he writes: "Through these words, then, it shows us sufficiently the difference of the natures, since it is amazed at the one as having chosen, out of excess of love for mankind, to remember and visit one so mean, and it counts the other most blessed for having been deemed worthy of such things (sic). In this way divine Scripture makes the division of the natures, and indeed shows us the difference between the nature of the one who assumed and that of the one who was assumed. But it also takes care to show us the union that came to the one who was assumed, and so it often speaks, by way of the union, of the properties of each of the natures as belonging to one [?], so that it might indicate to us the union with the one who assumed

of the one who was assumed, and all that came to him from his conjunction with that one." We have now shown that the irreligious Theodore speaks of natures in place of persons. Let us bring forward a still greater blasphemy of his, which shows what kind of union he means, to the condemnation of those who defend him. For in the eighth book On the Incarnation he says this: "It is evident that the principle of union fits. For through it the natures, brought together, produced one person by the union. So what the Lord says about husband and wife, 'so that they are no longer two, but one flesh,' we too might fittingly say according to the principle of union: 'so that they are no longer two persons, but one,' while the natures, of course, remain distinguished. For just as there the flesh being called one does no harm to the number two (for it is evident in what sense it is called one), so here too the union of the person does no harm to the difference of the natures. When we distinguish the natures, we say that the nature of God the Word is complete and his person complete (for it is not possible to speak of a hypostasis without a person), and that the nature of the man is complete, and likewise his person. But when we look to the conjunction, then we say one person." It is dreadful for Christians to utter such things. Nevertheless we have been compelled to bring them forward because of the madness of those who defend Theodore and that impious letter, and we beseech God to be merciful to us. By all this it has been proven that that accursed letter is full of all the impiety of Theodore. All this we have given in answer to what is contained in your list of chapters (sic), by which you have tried to defend that impious letter, and through it to revive the false doctrine of Theodore and Nestorius, whose impiety that same letter praises. But you have left out many parts of this letter written to Mari the heretic, and you did not dare to put them into your chapters, so that the Christian people among you would not learn from them as well the impiety you are defending. So we have thought it necessary to make these parts known too, briefly. For the words of the impious letter that you left out include this: "that Cyril held fast the ears of all the bishops who had gathered at the synod in Ephesus with the drug that blinds the eyes of the wise, and that he found his occasion in his hatred of Nestorius; and that the synod at Ephesus deposed Nestorius from the episcopate without any trial or inquiry having taken place." The letter also contains this: "that the bishops gathered at Ephesus put forward, confirmed and agreed with the twelve chapters written by Cyril, which are contrary to the right faith, as though they accorded with the right faith; and that Nestorius, since he was hated in his own city and by its leading men, was unable to return there." In all of this the writer of this impious letter not only defends and

praises the heretics but also censures the orthodox. For concerning the blessed Rabbula, bishop of Edessa, a man distinguished among bishops, whose tomb works miracles to this day, he says this in that impious letter: "that the tyrant of our city, whom you yourself also know, under pretext of the faith persecutes not only those living with him but also those who long ago departed to the Lord. One of these is the blessed Theodore, the herald of the truth and teacher of the Church, who not only struck the heretics in his own lifetime by his own faith, but also after his death left spiritual weapons in his books to the children of the Church, as your piety knows, having spoken with him and come to believe from what he wrote. This is the man whom he who dares all things dared to anathematize openly in church." The same impious letter to Mari also contains this about St Cyril: "that the heart of the Egyptian was softened, and that without any trouble he agreed with the right faith"; and "that, having rushed in disorderly fashion against the living and the dead, they are now in shame, making excuses for their own blunders and teaching the opposite of their first teaching"; and "that one must confess in the temple and in him who dwells in it." We have been eager to make plain to you these things contained in the letter we have mentioned, so that even now, late as it is, you may read them and withdraw from this false doctrine. The impiety of this abominable letter is so great that not even you, as has been said, dared to put everything it contains into the chapters you sent, even though you tried to interpret some of it in a distorted sense. Who can be counted among Christians who does not call impious a letter that contains blasphemies of this kind and of this number? Whoever defends the letter that calls St Cyril a heretic and rejects the first synod of Ephesus openly accepts Nestorius and his impiety. The same letter says that Nestorius was condemned without trial or inquiry, and that he did not return to the church because of the hatred of the citizens, not because of his doctrines. And this is not the only way in which the defender of the impious letter sins. He also condemns Pope Celestine, who said of Cyril that Cyril's faith is our faith. Whoever says that the twelve chapters of St Cyril are contrary to the right faith condemns not only St Cyril himself, Celestine of blessed memory and the first synod at Ephesus. He also condemns the synod of Chalcedon, which inscribed Cyril as its own father and teacher. At the same time he likewise condemns St Leo, pope of Rome, who, writing to the synod at Chalcedon, said of the twelve chapters of St Cyril: "Let the definitions put forth against Nestorius by Cyril of holy memory remain firm." But though the abominable letter is full of impiety, there is one truth it could not hide: that Theodore was anathematized from the church by orthodox and holy men

even after his death. This impious Theodore, who blasphemed beyond all the heretics, is the man the same impious letter calls teacher of the Church and herald of the truth. In another letter we have already made known to you a very small part of his blasphemies, in his own words. There we also showed what the holy fathers Cyril, Proclus and Rabbula wrote against Theodore and his impious words, condemning him together with that impiety. For Theodore's blasphemies are such that not even you dared to defend them, even though you defend the man who set them forth. Yet it is plain that no one who condemns evil teachings defends the man who set them forth, unless that man repented, departed from his error and condemned those teachings. To the other insults against St Cyril in the same letter this too is added: that St Cyril himself was [shameless?], and that he changed his mind and set forth things contrary to his first teaching. This shows that the writer of the letter is full of all folly. Where did St Cyril set forth anything contrary to his first teaching, or repent? How could the holy synod at Chalcedon have inscribed him as its father, if he had changed his mind, as the letter says? For one who repents is not counted among the teachers but is received as one who has turned back from error.

The writer of the letter made this its conclusion, saying "that one must confess in the temple and in him who dwells in the temple." By these words, as far as it lies with the impiety of the letter and of those who defend it, the whole right faith is overturned. For the catholic Church confesses one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God. It does not teach us to believe in or confess the temple and him who dwells in the temple. That is why those who are deemed worthy of holy baptism are taught to confess and believe in one Father almighty, and in one Lord Jesus Christ, his only-begotten Son, and in the Holy Spirit. They are not taught to believe in two sons or two Christs, which is what the letter to Mari the Persian means when it says that one must confess in the temple and in him who dwells in the temple, and so brings a fourth person into the Holy Trinity. From all this, then, it has been shown that whoever praises or defends the aforementioned impious letter is alien to the orthodox faith. You also say that the Easterners accepted St Cyril because he interpreted his own chapters. We are not surprised that you were deceived in the same way in the chapters you sent, since you do not even know what was written at the first synod in Ephesus. For St Celestine and the first synod at Ephesus, and St Leo and the holy synod at Chalcedon, accepted and confirmed the chapters of St Cyril as they stand, and [required?] no interpretation of them [?]. The interpretation was made not for the orthodox but for the heretics, who defended Nestorius and [opposed?] the chapters we have mentioned. For by your reasoning, neither

the holy Gospels, nor the Apostle, nor the other divine Scriptures would be acceptable unless the holy fathers had interpreted them. You ought to blush when you say that the Easterners who defended Nestorius accepted St Cyril because he interpreted his own chapters. On the contrary, the apostolic see of Rome and St Cyril received into communion the Eastern bishops who condemned Nestorius and his impiety. St Sixtus, pope of Rome, writing with his own synod to St Cyril and praising the labors he had undertaken for the union, said this among other things: "The brothers have returned to us. To us, I say, who drove out the disease by our common effort and took care to heal souls." And again: "Rejoice, beloved brother, and exult with us over the brothers who have been gathered [?]. The Church was seeking those whom it has now received back. If we wish none of the little ones to be lost, how much more ought we to rejoice at the health of those who lead? We have read how much joy one sheep gave when it was brought back. We ought to consider, then, how much praise it deserves to have called together so many shepherds. In each of them whole flocks are seen. The matter at stake here is not one person, whenever action is taken for the health of many." And again: "I rejoice that your holiness now calls the priest of the church of the Antiochenes a most reverent man and lord. He is fittingly called lord, since he [acknowledges] the common Lord, and with us he confesses the [mystery] of his incarnation with an orthodox voice." And again: "Afflictions are always to be desired by one who preaches the faith. For a rich reward, along with blessedness, is prepared in heaven for those who are appointed to endure insults, persecutions and every evil for the sake of righteousness. You endured falsehood so that you might make the truth prevail. For this reason we must now rise up against falsehood, so that no one may be lost to the truth." And again: "The holy brotherhood with me has written this in reply to your reverence. It accepts and confirms your labors in every respect. They have not been heavy or bitter, since they were spent for him whose light burden and kind yoke we bear." This is what St Sixtus wrote to St Cyril about the Easterners. You have also said, without understanding, that the condemnation of the impious letter to Mari damages the reputation of the holy synod at Chalcedon. We ask you on what grounds you ventured to write this. Do you perhaps think that the definition of the holy synod at Chalcedon contains anything like the impious letter? God forbid that a Christian should say so. For it is plain that everything in that impious letter and in Theodore's writings is contrary to the definition of the faith issued by the synod at Chalcedon. Theodore and the letter say that God the Word is one and Christ is another. But the holy synod at Chalcedon says that our Lord Jesus Christ is one, God the Word made flesh and made man without change. The letter and Theodore do not confess that God the Word was made flesh from the holy and glorious Theotokos and ever-virgin Mary and was born of her, and for this reason they deny that she is Theotokos

…that the holy Virgin Mary is; but the holy fathers who assembled in synod at Chalcedon confessed that the holy Virgin Mary is the Mother of God. The impious Theodore and the anonymous letter speak of two persons and then invent one person by a relational union. The synod speaks of the union of the two natures according to hypostasis, and so proclaims one person, that is, one hypostasis of Christ, the only-begotten God the Word. Again, that impious letter condemns the first synod at Ephesus and Cyril, now among the saints, and calls his chapters impious, while it defends and praises Nestorius and Theodore. The synod at Chalcedon, by contrast, follows that same first synod at Ephesus in everything. It names Cyril as its father and teacher, and confirms his synodical letter, to which the twelve chapters are appended. It condemns the impious Nestorius. Besides this, it likewise condemns, together with its author, the Jewish creed composed by Theodore, which had been condemned at the first synod of Ephesus and was later brought forward at the synod of Chalcedon itself. The holy synod at Chalcedon set these things out in its definitions. It introduced no novelty into the orthodox faith, but followed in everything the confession of faith which the Lord gave through the holy apostles, which the holy apostles proclaimed, which the three hundred and eighteen holy fathers handed down to the church of God, and which the hundred and fifty fathers confirmed when they clarified the doctrine of the divinity of the Holy Spirit. The holy fathers who had earlier assembled at Ephesus also followed this confession. The holy synod at Chalcedon also anathematized those who hand down any other creed or exposition of faith besides the one handed down by the three hundred and eighteen holy fathers. Since this is the truth of the matter, consider now at last, however late: who is rightly defending the holy synod at Chalcedon? Is it the one who shows that it followed the holy fathers we have named and set out everything rightly, or the one who is eager to attach the impious words of heretics to it? Those who accept with a pure conscience and an upright intention the first synod at Ephesus, the holy fathers Celestine, Cyril and Leo, and the definition of the synod at Chalcedon cannot also accept the abominable letter to Maris, which opposes them in every respect. For who can accept at the same time the teachers of the church and those who teach the opposite, or the orthodox and the heretics, or those who condemned and those who were condemned? So that you may know more fully what was done in the cases of Ibas and Theodoret, we thought it necessary to make this clear to you as well. Know, then, that at various times Ibas was accused because of the impiety of Theodore and Nestorius contained in that letter, and because of the insults uttered against Cyril, now among the saints, and against his chapters. He was accused before Theodosius, the emperor of pious memory, and before Proclus, now among the saints, archbishop

of Constantinople, and before various archbishops of Antioch. Finally the same emperor, together with Flavian, now among the saints, who became archbishop of Constantinople after Proclus, assigned the case brought against Ibas to Photius, bishop of Tyre, and Eustathius, bishop of Berytus. Before them Ibas was accused both on matters of faith and over the insults against Cyril, now among the saints. In his defence he replied that after the union reached between the Easterners and Cyril, now among the saints, he had said or written nothing insulting against him. But this abominable letter, produced by his accusers, shows that it was written after the union. So Ibas's own deposition shows that he was disowning the letter in question. The bishops we have mentioned saw the impiety of the letter, and so, although Ibas did not admit that it was his, they nonetheless gave a sentence that was in every respect contrary to the impiety it contained. They decreed that Ibas should anathematize Nestorius, his impious doctrines and those who defend him, all of which the impious letter defended. He was likewise to accept the faith of the three hundred and eighteen holy fathers, and the first synod at Ephesus as assembled by the Holy Spirit in the same way as the three hundred and eighteen holy fathers. Yet this same impious letter insults that synod at Ephesus, together with Cyril himself, now among the saints, and his twelve chapters.

Since Ibas did not carry out what the judges had decided, he was deposed from his bishopric. After this the holy synod at Chalcedon assembled. Ibas was not summoned to it and did not attend as a bishop, because Nonnus had already been ordained in his place, and Nonnus was summoned to the holy synod at Chalcedon. But after the definition of faith had been issued, Ibas came in and asked for his case to be examined, the case for which he had been deposed from his bishopric. He produced the sentence of Photius and Eustathius mentioned above. When it had been read, his accusers also came in and produced the proceedings held at Tyre, which contained this same impious letter. When it had been read, Ibas knew that if he admitted the letter was his he would be condemned for its impiety. So he interrupted the reading of the proceedings and said: "Order the letters of the clergy of Edessa to be read, so that you may learn from them that I have nothing to do with the charges brought against me." When these had been read, the bishops considered the sentence of Photius and Eustathius and the accusation that had been brought against Ibas. They then required him to carry out what Photius and Eustathius had decided, and to accept and sign the definition which this holy synod had pronounced. By doing so he also accepted the first synod at Ephesus, Cyril, now among the saints, and Cyril's teaching, all of which, as we have said, that abominable letter insults. All this shows that the holy synod at Chalcedon had Ibas do these things in order to condemn and overturn that impious letter. We are amazed at you, then, for defending that abominable letter, which not even

Ibas himself dared to call his own or to defend, whether at Tyre or later at the holy synod at Chalcedon. Instead he used the letters of the clergy of Edessa and the sentence of Photius and Eustathius to escape the accusation brought against him concerning the impious letter. Besides everything else that you have interpreted wrongly, you have also twisted the statement Eunomius made about Ibas into a false meaning, asserting that Eunomius made it in favour of the impious letter. For that statement is said to mean that Ibas insulted Cyril, now among the saints, in the earlier parts of the letter, but corrected himself in the last parts. Yet it is clear that Eunomius's statement was made not about that impious letter but about the deposition Ibas made at Tyre before Photius and Eustathius. In the proceedings before them, as we said above, Ibas openly admitted that earlier, together with the other Eastern bishops, he had insulted Cyril, now among the saints, at a time when there was discord between them, but that after the union reached between them he had said nothing insulting against Cyril. From this admission Eunomius found that Ibas had first insulted Cyril, now among the saints, and had afterwards defended himself by saying that he had said nothing insulting against Cyril after the union. It was on that basis that he made the statement in question. No one doubts that the impious letter we have spoken of, which is said to be by Ibas, is full of every impiety and of insults against Cyril from beginning to end. Nor is it reasonable to believe that Eunomius censured the first parts of the letter as bad and praised the last parts, which are worse. No one in his right mind approves of a man who praises and blames the same thing at once, on one and the same matter. So if anyone dares to say that Eunomius's statement agrees not with Ibas's deposition at Tyre but with the text of the impious letter in question, he does not keep to the thread of the truth. Rather, like a heretic, he is eager to heap insult on the fathers. We were also amazed that you were bold enough to write that the chapters of Cyril, now among the saints, are obscure, while you praised the impious letter as having been accepted through the mediation of the Holy Spirit. It is clear that you produced these words not from the Holy Spirit but by the working of the evil spirit, since you called the fathers and teachers of the church obscure, while blasphemously praising the false doctrine of the letter. So what the holy apostle Peter said about those who misunderstand the letters of holy Paul fits you well, and the others who think as you do about the holy fathers: "These things the ignorant and unstable will twist [or: twist], as they do the other scriptures also, to their own destruction." In the same way, then, to you also, who think wrongly,

what has been set out by the teachers of the church and by the divine scriptures seems obscure. These proceedings concerning Ibas and that impious letter, which went as we have described, are found in certain books. But you must know that the proceedings containing that impious letter are not attached to the authentic acts which the bishops signed, authentic copies of which they deposited in the most holy church of Rome, in Constantinople, and in our sacred palace. This impious letter is shown on every side to be full of every impiety and contrary to what the holy synod at Chalcedon defined. So those who say that the holy synod at Chalcedon accepted it are not only eager to defend their own false doctrine, but also to heap insult on that holy synod. For the things which that holy synod accepted and confirmed are named one by one in the definition of faith it issued. We also want you to know that Theodoret had written against the twelve chapters of Cyril, now among the saints, in defence of Nestorius and his false doctrine. For this reason, after the definition of the holy synod at Chalcedon, he was compelled first to anathematize Nestorius and his impiety and to confess the holy, glorious, ever-virgin Mary as Mother of God, and only on those terms was he received. So Ibas and Theodoret were both received, not as teachers and fathers, but as penitents. They anathematized the false doctrine of which they had been accused, and accepted and signed the definition of the synod at Chalcedon. For it is the custom in the catholic church that all heretics who abandon their own error and return to the orthodox faith are received into communion, but they are not counted among the fathers as teachers. In the same way the other Eastern bishops had opposed the first synod at Ephesus and Cyril, now among the saints, in defence of Nestorius. Since they afterwards anathematized Nestorius and his false doctrine, the apostolic see of Rome and Cyril, now among the saints, received them, and for this reason the holy church of God also receives them. We also want you to know that Ibas and Theodoret were not the only ones expelled from their bishoprics for opposing the twelve chapters of Cyril, now among the saints. Domnus, archbishop of Antioch, was also condemned for this reason, because he had written that those twelve chapters should simply be passed over in silence. The synod at Chalcedon accepted and confirmed this condemnation of Domnus even after his death. That this is true Theodoret himself testifies, writing to John, bishop of Germanicia, as follows: "Why on earth do they lie so openly and say that no innovation in doctrine has taken place? For what murders and sorceries was I expelled? What adulteries did so-and-so dare to commit? What tombs did so-and-so break into? It is clear even to barbarians, I beg you [sic], that they expelled me and the others for the sake of doctrines. For the lord Domnus, as one who had not accepted the

chapters, was deposed by those excellent men, who called them altogether praiseworthy and confessed that they abide by them. I have read their depositions myself. Me they proclaimed the ringleader of the heresy." This shows that Domnus, Theodoret himself, Ibas and some others were expelled because of the chapters that Cyril, now among the saints, set forth against Nestorius. Theodoret and Ibas repented and accepted those chapters and the other things for which they had been expelled, and the holy synod at Chalcedon received them. The others, who did not repent, were not received, and the condemnation of Domnus was confirmed even after his death. You wrote that you anathematize the blasphemies of Theodore that we sent you, whoever wrote them, but that you hesitated to anathematize Theodore himself because, as is said, he had already died in the communion of the churches. Know, then, that those who say it is not permissible to anathematize Theodore, and that he should be counted among the bishops because, as you put it, he died in the communion of the church, ought also to count Judas among the apostles. Judas thought he had escaped the notice of God, who knows the secrets of men, and he received communion from him along with the other disciples. As far as those who say such things are concerned, the apostles too deserve blame, for after his death they passed sentence against him, condemning him and putting another in his place. Again, since his name is read in the holy Gospels among the other apostles, does that mean he is to be received as an apostle, or ought to be freed from the condemnation of anathema? Understand, then, that the one who dies in the communion of the churches is the one who has kept the orthodox faith to the end of his life. Suppose a Manichaean, an Arian, a Nestorian, a Eutychianist, any other heretic whatever, or someone in the grip of pagan madness secretly takes communion in the church and dies in that state, and after his death is shown to be a heretic, whether from his writings or in some other way. Even so, the orthodox faith is not harmed by this, nor is that man freed from condemnation, if [in the manuscripts:] he is said to have died in the peace of the churches. In general, death frees no heretic from condemnation for his false doctrine. On the contrary, it condemns him precisely because he did not repent while he lived. Many cases show that heretics who did not repent in their lifetime were condemned even after death. Eunomius, Apollinaris and Bonosus, and in more ancient times Valentinus, Basilides, Marcion, Cerinthus and many others, were not anathematized in their own lifetime but were condemned after death, and the catholic church anathematizes them because they died in their own error. In the same way, those who were unjustly condemned in their own lifetime were, after death, by the

catholic church restored, namely John and Flavian, archbishops of Constantinople, now among the saints. By your reasoning, heretics who died in their own error must be set free, while the orthodox who were unjustly condemned must not be restored after death, and that is full of every impiety. These examples have made it clear that it is the tradition of the church that heretics are condemned and anathematized even after death. But this is also shown by the Constitutions of the holy apostles. For when they say that it is fitting to give alms for the repose of the departed, they add the following: "We say these things about the pious. But as for the impious, even if one gives all the world's goods to the poor, it will not profit him at all. For the one to whom the divine was opposed while he lived, it clearly remains opposed when he has departed." Since the apostles laid this down about the pious, who would say that heretics must be freed after death from the condemnation of anathema, and Theodore above all? The holy fathers counted him among Jews, pagans, Sodomites and all the heretics, as one whose blasphemies were worse than theirs, and they condemned him together with his impiety. That heretics must be anathematized even after death, as we said before, is also stated by Augustine, now among the saints, a bishop from the land of the Africans, in his letter to Boniface: "Even if what they allege against Caecilian could be shown to be true, we and you alike would anathematize him even though he is dead. Nevertheless, we ought not to abandon the church of Christ for the sake of any man whatever. For the church is not changed by contentious [?] but is confirmed by divine testimonies." So says Augustine, now among the saints. Moreover, the holy fathers anathematize after death not only those who sin against the faith but also bishops who, in their last will or by dying intestate, leave their property to heretical relatives or to outsiders. The eighty-first canon of the synod in Africa says this: "It was further decreed that if any bishop prefers to the church heirs from outside his own family, or heretics, even if they are his own relatives, or pagans, he is to be anathematized even after death, and his name is not to be read among the priests of God. Nor is he exempted from condemnation if he dies intestate, since once he had become a bishop he ought by no means to have put off disposing of his own property in a way befitting his profession." If, then, as the church's canon has defined, bishops are anathematized even after death for failing to dispose rightly of their own property, how much more ought those to be anathematized who sin against God himself? For holy scripture says: "If a man sins against a man, they will pray for him; but if anyone sins against God, who will pray for

We have shown that in earlier times the holy fathers decreed that those who sinned against the faith or against the canons must be anathematized even after death. We have judged it necessary also to make plain to everyone what has happened in our own times, in order to remove every pretext from those who defend manifest heretics and their impiety. Laurentius and Dioscorus, at different times, usurped the priesthood of the apostolic see. Although they did not sin against the faith, they strove to seize the bishopric by intrigue, and for this the apostolic see condemned and anathematized them after their death. You also added in your letter that if anyone anathematizes a heresiarch and, in condemning him, adds "and those who think as he does," he includes everyone who has ever held those views. On that basis you argue that, since you anathematize Paul of Samosata, Photinus, Bonosus and Nestorius, you need not also anathematize by name Theodore, who held views like theirs. Know, first of all, that those who are anathematized without being named are the ones who followed the heresiarchs out of error, not those who deceived others. For the church of God anathematizes the leaders of heresies by name. Theodore, moreover, was not only the teacher of Nestorius's impiety but also deceived many through his impious writings. The true teachers of the church are known and praised through their own expositions, and in the same way, conversely, all the leaders of false doctrine are refuted and anathematized through their own impious writings. Since Theodore became a heresiarch and spewed out countless blasphemies in his books, you have no just pretext for refusing to anathematize him. As for the exposition of faith which you included [?] in your letter, we had much to find fault with in it. Nevertheless, because of your ignorance and simplicity, we thought it best to pass over it for the time being. In some places you wrote carelessly. In some you have used words known neither to the divine scriptures nor to the holy fathers. In others you have condemned the teachers of the church, as far as it lay with you. Besides this, you have also left out certain things that bear on the orthodox faith. So you must follow the advice of the holy fathers: either speak when you know, or keep silent when you do not, and learn from those who understand. You wrote to us about how we ought to answer the Egyptians. We are amazed that you defend that impious letter, and Theodore and Nestorius and their false doctrine, and yet presume to advise us on how we ought to answer others who oppose the church. For if anyone follows [?] what you have written, he will advise the Egyptians to do nothing other than accept the heretics Theodore and Nestorius, and

…to condemn all the holy fathers, who condemned those men and their unbelief as well, and besides this to fall from one error into another, when you wrote to us, in answer to those opposed to the Church, that that loathsome letter was good and orthodox. Make haste, therefore, first to correct yourselves, and then to teach others. For if anyone defends Theodore, or the so-called letter of Ibas, or the writings of Theodoret set forth against the right faith, he numbers himself among the heretics and makes himself a stranger to the catholic Church, whose head is the only-begotten Son of God, our Lord and God Jesus Christ. From him you separate yourselves by defending the impious letter and Theodore, and for this reason it is right for you to keep away from the impiety of the letter and from defending Theodore, so manifest a heretic. For if the holy apostle Paul forbids anyone to be called either by his own name or by the names of the other apostles, and rebukes those who say,

[In doing a thing not unaccustomed to the imperial power, we too have come to the present law. For as often as the decree [?] of the priests has cast down from the priestly thrones men unworthy of the priesthood, such as Nestorius and Eutyches, Arius and Macedonius and Eunomius, and certain others no less wicked than they, so often has the imperial power joined its vote to the authority of the priests, so that things divine and human, running together, have made one harmony with right decrees. We know that something of this kind happened lately in the case of Anthimus. He was driven from the throne of this royal city by Agapetus of holy and celebrated memory, who was president of the most holy Church of elder Rome, as one who had leapt, against all the holy canons, into a throne that in no way belonged to him. By common decree, first of that man of holy memory himself and then of the holy synod held here, he was condemned and deposed, because he had departed from the orthodox doctrines; and what he had earlier seemed in many ways to cherish, he later evaded by various subtleties. He pretended to follow the four holy synods: that of the fathers at Nicaea, that of the 150 in this blessed city, that of the 200 who first assembled at Ephesus, and that of the God-loving fathers at Chalcedon, 630 in number. Yet he did not follow their doctrines. Nor was he willing to accept our clemency and the condescension we showed for the sake of his salvation, nor would he himself anathematize the leaders of impious doctrines cast out by the earlier holy synods; instead he thought it necessary to treat the condemned and those who condemned them on the same and equal footing. For once he had been enslaved to notions alien to the most holy Church and estranged from orthodox doctrines, he naturally could not return to their correctness, even though he was urged and guided by us, who spared no effort for his salvation. For all these reasons, therefore, our majesty confirms the sentence of deposition passed against him by the holy synod, on the grounds both of his unlawful seizure of the priestly throne of this royal city, which the holy canons do not support, and of his deviation from the right and true doctrines; and to this end it writes the present law. We forbid him to stay in this blessed city and its environs, or in any other of the notable cities, and decree that he remain in quiet and content himself with those things to which he has deservedly subjected himself, and that he neither communicate with anyone nor draw them away into the ruin of the forbidden doctrines. Nor do we leave without imperial confirmation the sentence justly pronounced against Severus, which proceeded from practically all the archiepiscopal and patriarchal thrones with the consent of the monks, and which lays anathema upon him. Having earlier seized, against the sacred ordinances, the throne of the most holy Church of the Theopolitans, he threw everything into such confusion and so filled it with turmoil as to cast a common and truceless war

among the most holy churches against one another. This was written also by the sceptres before us concerning him: that he had used various subtleties and blasphemies in doctrine, alien to orthodoxy, had thrown everything into confusion, and clung only to the foul and unholy doctrines of the error of each of the heresiarchs, Nestorius and Eutyches, and of the leaders of each of them, who seem somehow to be opposed to one another but hasten toward one goal of impiety; and that he had stamped upon himself their characteristic statements. For there are two doctrines contrary to one another, each of which equally leads to the ruin of the soul, that of Nestorius and that of Eutyches, as we said before, which arose out of the defilements of the Arians and of Apollinarius; and he, by a strange fate, fell into both alike. Championing now this, now that, he made himself and his words, it seemed, a common receptacle for such great offences. Let him therefore also be under the said anathema, which the whole patriarchal, priestly and monastic order of our commonwealth, so to speak, has justly laid upon him. He has been cast out of Theopolis, because the throne there shook him off, as one who had not rightly taken hold of it from the beginning, but while the man who held the priesthood before him was still living and being proclaimed in the most holy churches, he had [?] fallen upon the priesthood. Nor did he stop at this alone, but he has now come under the common anathema of the orthodox and catholic Church, and has filled our commonwealth with many books, blasphemous and forbidden. We therefore forbid anyone to possess any of his books. And just as it is not permitted to copy or possess the books of Nestorius, because the emperors before us decided in their constitutions that they were like what Porphyry said against the Christians, so too let nothing that Severus has said or written remain in the hands of any Christian; let these writings be profane and alien to the catholic Church, and let those who possess them burn them with fire, unless those who have them wish to be in danger. And henceforth let no one copy them, neither calligraphers nor shorthand writers nor anyone else at all, knowing that the penalty for those who copy his writings will be the cutting off of the hand. For we do not wish the blasphemy that comes from them to be spread [?] in time to come. Likewise we forbid him altogether to set foot in the royal city or its environs, or in any other of the notable cities; he is to sit in some solitude and quiet, and not corrupt others, nor lead them into blasphemy, nor be forever devising something new against the true doctrines by which to throw the most holy churches into confusion once again.

Nor does the imperial power receive Peter, formerly bishop of Apamea, who was deposed and at the same time came under the said anathema for the same things as Severus; rather, let what was decreed against him also stand. And since he has been placed under the common anathema,

let him know that he is under it, the decree issued against them by the most holy high priests remaining in force. We do not permit him either to live in this royal city or its environs, or in any of the more distinguished cities; let him imitate the way of life of those whose error he followed, banished as far away as possible and hiding himself, since for such men it is more profitable to be hidden than to be seen. For while they are out of sight they will harm only themselves, but by publishing their doctrines they give many of the simpler folk occasion for ruin, which it is not right should happen in any way in the Christian flock of God and among the orthodox people, nor is it permitted by the imperial power. And since the most reverend bishops, judging justly, also saw fit to place Zooras wholly under anathema, as being a kind of appendage to such evils, in which he has been disgraced [?], having thereby gained at least some memory at all, let Zooras too know that he is a paltry appendage of this wicked party—of Anthimus, Severus and Peter, I mean. Let him too be ranked among the anathematized, since the priestly decree has condemned him. That decree is valid in itself, and the imperial power makes it more valid still, expelling him from this royal city and its environs and forbidding him altogether to dwell in cities, so that he may live and take counsel only with those we have named above, who blaspheme alike, have suffered alike, and are confined alike. And if anything else is contained in the decree of the most holy bishops deposing and anathematizing the aforesaid, we make this valid too and confirm it by our divine and imperial laws, as if it had proceeded from the imperial power itself. And if any of them should henceforth be caught doing anything contrary to what has been ordained, let him know that he will also fall under the imperial laws, which pass over the lesser penalties and inflict greater displeasure. We also forbid anyone who attempts to rend the catholic Church of God, whether following the guidance of the brain-damaged Nestorius, or the senseless tradition of Eutyches, or the blasphemy of Severus, who held the same views as they, or anyone of their followers, to stir up disturbances in the most holy churches or to say anything about the faith. We decree instead that each such person keep quiet, and neither call anyone together to himself, nor receive those who come to him, nor dare to rebaptize, nor defile the holy communion and give it to anyone, nor expound the forbidden teachings, whether in this our royal city or in another, but rather expect every danger if they do any such thing. We also forbid everyone to harbour them. We decree, then, that they be driven out of the cities they disturb, knowing the penalties already contained in our divine constitutions, which also assign to the most holy churches the very houses in which any such thing is done and the estates from which they are supplied with their sustenance, taking these from their owners, since they become a cause of harm to the simpler folk; and under the most holy and orthodox churches

these properties are justly brought. These things we legislate for the common peace of the most holy churches [?]; these we decree, following the [teachings?] of the holy fathers, so that the whole priesthood may remain undisturbed for us henceforth. For when it is kept in peace, our commonwealth too will flourish henceforth, having peace from above, which our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ, one of the Trinity, the only-begotten [Son?] of God, proclaims to all and bestows on those deemed worthy to glorify and worship him genuinely and truly.
