Let your Blessedness, therefore, guard what has rightly been determined, sending it down by your God-loving letters to all the most holy metropolitans under you, each of whom shall take care to make it known to the most holy churches under them, so that no one at all may be unaware of what the high priesthood has resolved and the imperial power has confirmed…

The divine signature. Since Justinian, who was our emperor, composed a dogmatic treatise drawn from the divine Scriptures and the holy Fathers, addressed to the monks of the Enaton of Alexandria, we have thought it necessary to make it known to your Blessedness. It runs as follows: We hold that the first salvation for all people is the confession of the right faith, and especially for those who have taken up the solitary life. For if they are zealous to discipline the body, much more ought they to train the soul in faith toward God, through which we hope to enjoy eternal life. For unless faith, the more perfect work, is joined to action, it follows, as it is written, that work without faith is dead; for no one, it says, is crowned unless he competes according to the rules. To fall sick belongs to our common nature and to human weakness, which touches everyone, even those very strong in mind; but to be healed, to recognize the right faith, and to embrace the unity and peace of the Church belongs to reason and to grace. For God both is and is called peace, so that this belongs to God, and those are near to God

and to divine things who are seen to embrace the good of faith and peace. We say this to your God-belovedness because we have learned from what the most blessed archbishop and patriarch of Alexandria, Zoilus, wrote to us, that you have embraced the peace dear to God and hastened to the holy Church of God, having found the doctrines preached in it to be correct. By them every heresy has been driven out; condemned and cast out is the division of Paul and Nestorius, who are blind in the eyes of the soul and, like the madness of the Jews, deny the divinity of Christ; and likewise condemned and cast out is the conflation, that is, the confusion, of Apollinarius and Eutyches, who reject the true humanity of Christ. We therefore exhort your God-belovedness to show henceforth the fruits of faith, to guide to the truth those still held by error, and to bring them to the holy Church of God, whose true and saving preaching we shall demonstrate as we proceed from the divine Scriptures and the traditions of the Fathers, refuting at the same time the malice of the said impious heretics. For the holy Church of God proclaims Unity in Trinity and Trinity in Unity: for there is one God the Father, from whom are all things; and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things; and one Holy Spirit, in whom are all things. The 'from whom', 'through whom' and 'in whom' do not divide natures but characterize the properties of one unconfused nature. For we worship one essence in three hypostases, contemplating the same essence in each hypostasis. We proclaim each of the hypostases singly; but when we must count them together, we are not carried away by an ignorant counting into the notion of polytheism. For we do not count by addition, increasing from one to a multitude, but, confessing what is proper to the hypostases, we remain within the monarchy, not scattering theology into a severed multitude, [?] the one form, as it were, being contemplated in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, united by the unvarying identity of the nature. And so we confess each to be God if contemplated alone, the mind alone separating what is inseparable; and we conceive the three together as God, by the identity of their movement and nature. The Trinity, then, is truly a Trinity; and the three are not an enumeration of unequal things but a gathering together of things equal and equal in honour, the name uniting what is united by nature and not allowing what is undivided to be scattered by a divided number. We confess that the only-begotten Son and Word of God, who is glorified and worshipped together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, who was begotten of the Father timelessly and incorporeally, the light from light, the source of life and immortality, the impress of the Archetype, the unmoved seal, the unvarying image, the Father's definition and Word, did not overlook humanity when it was pitiably separated from God its maker by the envy of the devil and the bitter taste of sin. Rather, working our salvation, he comes to his own image and takes flesh

for the sake of my flesh, and is united with a rational soul for the sake of my soul, cleansing like by like, and becomes man in all things except sin. And he who had ascended to the heaven of heavens, toward the east of his own glory, is glorified in the west of our weakness. For the divine and surpassing power is not shown so much by the vastness of the heavens, the brightness of the luminaries, the ordering of the universe and the continual governance of all that exists, as by his condescension to the weakness of our nature: how the lofty came to be in the lowly and is seen in the lowly, and yet the Godhead does not descend from its height; for, interwoven with human nature, it both becomes this and is that. Therefore we confess the same one to be perfect God and perfect man, on behalf of the whole that had suffered, so that he might grant salvation to the whole of me, having loosed the whole condemnation of sin. For the full one is emptied—emptied of his own glory for a little while—so that I may partake of his fullness; and he who makes rich becomes poor. How he becomes poor though he is rich, Athanasius among the saints tells us in his discourse on the saving appearance: 'He took the impoverished nature into himself, putting it forward in his own righteousness, suffering on behalf of men, being from men, manifested above men, and become wholly God's, so that God might truly be man and man truly God; the only-begotten God being pleased, by the fullness of his Godhead, to raise up for himself from the Virgin's womb the fashioning of the archetypal man and a new creation, by natural birth and indissoluble union.' Following these words, then, we know that the miracles and the sufferings, which he willingly endured in the flesh, belong to the same one. For the holy Trinity does not admit the addition of a fourth person when God the Word, one of the Trinity, became flesh and became man; and we do not know God the Word as one and Christ as another, but we confess one and the same God the Word, the Lord Jesus Christ. To put it briefly, the elements of which the Saviour is composed are one thing and another, since the visible is not the same as the invisible, nor the timeless the same as what is subject to time; but he is not one person and another—God forbid! For he is one from both, and both are through one. Hence, when we speak of 'one thing and another' in the one and the same only-begotten Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, we do not introduce two sons or two hypostases or two persons, but we recognize that he exists in those things of which he is composed. For in this way we both set forth the difference between his Godhead and his flesh, abolishing the fusion of essence taught by Eutyches, and confess his one hypostasis, abhorring the division of Nestorius. For Cyril among the saints also says this in the third tome against Nestorius: 'For he will never lose his being God because he has become as we are; nor, because he is God by nature, does he reject likeness to us and refuse to be man. But just as he has remained God in humanity, so too, while being in the nature and supremacy of the Godhead, he is no less [man]. Both, then, are in him, and he is one, God and man together, Emmanuel.'

Here too we must pay attention to what the Father has said. He teaches us to confess the preposition "in" with respect to the two natures, the divine and the human, in which the one Christ is known. The heretics refuse to apply this preposition to the divinity and humanity of Christ, on the pretext that it produces a division. They do not know that this very preposition keeps the union unconfused and undivided. That is why divine Scripture itself uses this preposition of the divinity and humanity of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ. The inspired apostle Paul says: "Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus, who, being in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men; and being found in fashion as a man." When the Apostle says that the only-begotten Son of God was in the form of God, and adds that he took the form of a servant, was made in the likeness of men, and was found in fashion as a man, he is teaching us nothing other than that the Lord is in each form, that is, in divinity and in humanity. Indeed, Cyril among the saints, interpreting this very text in his discourse to Theodosius, writes as follows: "God the Word, coeternal with God the Father, having taken the form of a servant, is perfect in humanity just as he is perfect in divinity. He is not composed into one Christ, Lord and Son from divinity alone and flesh, but is wondrously bound together from two perfect things, humanity, I mean, and divinity, into one and the same." See how plainly the Father again confesses that Christ exists in divinity and humanity. Just as "from divinity and humanity" means "from two natures," so "in divinity and humanity" shows that Christ exists and is known in two natures. For it is clear that whatever is said to be composed from certain things causes the confusion and obliteration of the things that came together, unless it is known in the very things from which it was composed. On this point the same Cyril among the saints says, against the Synousiasts: "But if they say that the flesh and the Word have been mixed with one another in the manner of liquids, how have they failed to recognize that liquids blended with one another, wine and honey for example, are no longer purely what they were, but rather change into something else by taking on a quality of a different kind? So if they say that the flesh has been blended with the Word, it is altogether necessary [?] to say that each of the things named has ceased to be what it was, and that from both one thing has been produced, an intermediate, surely of a different nature from what each was separately." Since it has been shown, then, that confusion arises where the components are not preserved after the composition, it is clear that where there is no confusion or obliteration of the things that came together, what has been composed from certain things is also known in them. And it is evident that those who confess that from two natures,

that is, from divinity and humanity, our one Lord Jesus Christ was brought into being, and who say that no confusion of the substances that came together took place in him, will be bound to confess that he is also known in those very two natures from which he was composed, that is, in divinity and humanity. In this way the difference of the natures in Christ is not abolished, and their union is kept unbroken. For of what things do they speak of a difference, unless they grant that the things which made up Christ are preserved in him? And yet Cyril among the saints writes in the twenty-fourth discourse of the Thesaurus: "He says these things as man, and he also says them as God, having authority in both. Speaking humanly he said, 'Now my soul is troubled.' Speaking divinely, again, he said, 'I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again.' Being troubled, then, is a passion proper to the flesh, while having authority to lay down the soul and take it up again is a work of the power of the Word." And again the same Cyril among the saints says in his commentary on the Gospel according to John, in the sixth chapter of the second book: "For since he was now clothed in the form of the servant, having become man because of his union with flesh, he did not make his discourse free or entirely given over to the boldness befitting God. Rather, for the sake of the economy, he sometimes used such speech as would befit God and man together, for he truly was both at once." When the Father says that Christ is both at once, and has authority in both, he is showing nothing other than that he exists and is known in two natures. For the terms "God" and "man," when said of Christ, signify substances. And yet the enemies of the truth, passing over all the teachings of the Fathers, and above all those that Cyril among the saints set forth for the condemnation of Nestorius the blasphemer and that were confirmed by a synod, take a few things from his memoranda to Succensus alone and misinterpret them to suit themselves, namely "one incarnate nature of God the Word" and the example of man. What is customary with all heretics, twisting certain words of the holy Scriptures to their own error, they too do. But we will show from the very words of the Father that their error on these matters is also vain. For they skip over what comes before such expressions, cut off what follows, and strive to establish their own error. The Father said: "After the union we do not separate the natures from one another, nor do we cut the one and indivisible into two Sons, but we say one Son." Having shown that after the union the natures must not be divided but must be confessed as united in Christ, he is passed over by them in silence,

and they fabricate one nature of flesh and divinity. Yet the Father among the saints does not speak of one nature of flesh and divinity, as they imagine. Having spoken of the one nature of the Word as of one without flesh, he did not stop there, but added "incarnate," so that by "incarnate" he might set before us the other nature, that is, the human. Indeed, not content with this expression, and wishing to set out his meaning more clearly, he immediately added what they once again leave out: "So far, then, as it is a matter of understanding, and only of seeing with the eyes of the soul how the Only-begotten became man, we say that there are two natures, but one Christ and Son and Lord, the Word of God made man and incarnate." What could be clearer than this? Or what dispute remains for right-minded people about the confession of the two natures in Christ, when the Father has handed down such things to us? But they, striving to pervert what is right at every turn, add this too to their idle talk: that what is seen in the understanding and with the eyes of the soul must not be confessed with the mouth. Nothing is more irrational than this trickery of theirs. By their madness they will not confess God with the mouth either, since we know him only in the understanding and with the eyes of the soul. Moreover, the Father himself spoke of the very things he contemplated with the eyes of the soul, and set them out in writing; we know what he contemplated in no other way than through his words and writings. If, by the folly of the heretics, it is not fitting to confess what is contemplated by the mind alone, how will they confess the preeminence of the divinity of our Lord Jesus Christ, since his incarnation is visible but his divinity is contemplated by the mind alone? If, according to the divine Apostle, "with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth one confesses unto salvation," it is evident that what is contemplated by the mind is also confessed with the mouth. As Gregory the Theologian says: "An unspoken thought is the motion of men asleep. For it is shameful, shameful and utterly irrational, for those strong in soul to quibble over the sound, and to hide the treasure as if begrudging it to others, [?] fearing to sanctify the tongue as well." Since this is so, all who receive the great mystery of godliness of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ must also confess with the mouth the two natures of Christ, the divine and the human. For in the second memorandum to the same Succensus, Cyril among the saints, both accepting Succensus's orthodox faith concerning the incarnation and setting out his own view more distinctly, teaches as follows: "Your Perfection sets out the account of the saving passion most rightly and very wisely, maintaining not that the only-begotten Son of God himself, insofar as he is understood to be and is God, suffered the things of the body in his own nature, but rather that he suffered in the

earthly nature. For both must necessarily be preserved in the one and true Son: that he does not suffer divinely, and that he is said to have suffered humanly, for it was his own flesh that suffered." It is clear, then, from what has been said, that the two natures, the divine and the human, are preserved in the one hypostasis, that is, in the one person of the only-begotten Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ. For he says that both must be preserved in the one and true Son. [?]

[?] to suppose. For we have been taught to confess the suffering and the impassibility of one and the same hypostasis of our Lord Jesus Christ, but not according to the same nature, since it is impossible for one and the same nature to signify contrary things at the same time. But the enemies of the truth, who oppose the doctrines of the Fathers, fail to make these distinctions and fall again into another folly. They say that those who confess Christ as God and man, and do not say that he is of one nature like a man, ought to speak of not two natures in Christ but three, for the nature of the Word is one thing, that of the soul another, and that of the body yet another. Let these new inventors of evils, who themselves agree with us that Christ is from two natures, tell us how they understand this. Do they mean that he assumed a soul without a body, or a body without a soul? They will certainly have to offer one of these absurdities. But if, to avoid this absurdity, they say that the Lord assumed both soul and body, they will be caught in their own snares and will plainly be forced to say that Christ is from three natures. They do not know that the name "man," when used without the individual properties, is taken in a general sense, signifies a substance or nature, and is predicated of many hypostases. But when the properties are added to what is common, then the hypostasis appears; and the difference of soul and body is also recognized. The apostolic tradition teaches us to say both. The divine Paul, speaking of the individual and wishing to signify both soul and body, names them the inner man and the outer man. James, on the other hand, indicating the common substance of humanity, says: "Every kind of beasts and birds, of reptiles and sea creatures, is tamed and has been tamed by human nature." The name "Christ," however, does not signify a substance, since it is not taken in a general sense, is not predicated of many hypostases, and is not confessed without the individual properties. This is what Cyril among the saints teaches us in his scholia on the incarnation, saying

that "The name 'Christ' has neither the force of a definition nor signifies the substance of anything, whatever it may be, as do, for instance, 'man' or 'horse' or 'ox.'" If, by the blasphemy of the heretics, the name "Christ" indicated a substance as "man" does, then on their view many Christs will be found, of whom they predicate the common substance of Christ. But if this is impious and wholly foreign to Christianity (for there is one Lord Jesus Christ), plainly "Christ" is confessed of a person, that is, of a hypostasis. Let us consider in another way, too, what difference the mystery of the economy has from the example of man. Man is composed of soul and body, both of them created. But our Lord Jesus Christ, being himself both God and man, is before the ages and uncreated according to his divinity, and created and in time according to his humanity. Hence the same one is uncreated and created, timeless and in time. And for this reason we confess all things as belonging to one and the same, but we reckon some to his divine nature and others to his human nature. Let us hear Proclus among the saints teaching us much the same in his discourse on the Theotokos. He says: "A wondrous birth, a beginning and not a beginning of the one born: for his humanity had a beginning, but his divinity remained without beginning." So let no one be deceived, and let no one deceive others, by spinning tales from the example of man that Christ is of one substance. Examples are not alike in every respect to the things for which they are taken as examples; if they were found to be alike in every respect, they would be the same things and not examples. Cyril among the saints uses the example of man for no other purpose than to drive out the blasphemy of Paul and Nestorius, who separate the natures from one another, take them as two persons or hypostases, and thereby speak of two Sons and two Christs, fabricating one Son from God the Father and another from the holy Virgin and Theotokos Mary. For this reason they do not even confess her as Theotokos, but call the one born of her a mere man, who by grace, by affinity, and by relation to the Son by nature was through progress deemed worthy of sonship. To prove that Paul and Nestorius did blaspheme in this way, we have set out a few of the impieties they wrote, exposing their madness publicly to all Christians. The impious Paul says in the acts of his case: "The Word came together with the one born of David, who is Jesus Christ, born of the Holy Spirit. And the Virgin bore this one through the Holy Spirit, but God begot that one, the Word, without a virgin and without anyone at all except God; and so the Word came into being." And again the same impious Paul says: "The Word was greater than Christ; Christ became great through wisdom; let us not lower the

dignity of wisdom." And again the same heretic Paul says: "For the Lord was in the prophets, and still more in Moses and in many, and still more in Christ as in a temple. For Jesus Christ is one, and the Word another." Then again the impious Nestorius says: "Nowhere, then, does divine Scripture say that God was born of the Christotokos Virgin." And again the same man-worshipper Nestorius says: "'Arise, take the child and his mother.' He did not say, 'Arise, take God and his mother.'" And again the same impious Nestorius says: "To be with the one who has been born is one thing, and to be born is another. 'For that which is born in her,' it says, 'is of the Holy Spirit,' that is, the Holy Spirit created the one in her. The Fathers, then, as men learned in the divine Scriptures, saw that if we put 'born' in place of 'incarnate,' God the Word is found to be the Son of the Spirit and to have two fathers; and if through the one Son, God the Word will be found to be a creature of the Spirit." And again the same impious Nestorius says: "But just as we called the Creator of all things God, and called Moses god ('I have made you a god to Pharaoh,' it says), and called Israel son of God ('Israel is my firstborn son,' it says), and just as we called Saul christ ('I will not lay my hand on him,' it says, 'for he is the Lord's christ'), and Cyrus likewise ('Thus says the Lord to my christ Cyrus,' it says), and the Babylonian holy ('I give them orders,' it says; 'they are sanctified, and I lead them'), so we call the Master Christ also God and [?] and holy and Christ." And again the same impious Nestorius says: "Because of the one who wears it I revere what is worn; because of the hidden one I worship the one who appears. God is inseparable from the one who appears; therefore I do not separate the honour of the one who is not separated. I separate the natures, but I unite the worship." And again the same impious Nestorius says: "God the Word is also named Christ, since he has a continuous conjunction with Christ." And again the same impious Nestorius says: "The blessed Virgin did not bear the Son of God, but bore the humanity, which is Son because of the Son conjoined to it." And

not to confess her as Theotokos, and to follow neither the prophets, nor the Gospels, nor the apostolic preaching. To refute their impiety we have set out a few scriptural testimonies out of many. For Jeremiah, etc. (1) [See p. 222.] The reader must pay attention to Cyril's words. When he says that no pouring of the natures into one another took place, but rather that each remains in the union, he is plainly teaching that the two natures, of divinity and of humanity, are preserved and confessed in the one person of our Lord Jesus Christ. Hard pressed by this, the heretics devise yet another impiety, wishing to overshadow the earlier one with it. For at times they fabricate one composite nature, not knowing that, as is shown by the teaching of the Fathers and as we ourselves said above, the name "nature" is said of something common, signifies something indeterminate, and is predicated of many hypostases. If, then, on their view, the two natures of divinity and humanity have become one composite nature, it is clear that something common and indeterminate has been produced. And one must ask of what kind of commonality, or of which hypostases, they say such a nature is predicated. This is contrary to the mystery of Christ. For Christ is not predicated as something common and of many hypostases, but is spoken of a single hypostasis, that is, one person, known in the different substances of divinity and humanity. We, speaking of two substances in Christ, know him to be consubstantial with the Father and the Holy Spirit according to his divinity, and recognize the same one as consubstantial with all men according to his humanity. But those who say that the two substances produced one composite nature, that is, that he is one of certain common things, grant this commonality. For according to their own words, something intermediate and of a different nature must have been produced, other than what each was separately. Their absurdity is exposed from this side too. If all agree that the nature of the Holy Trinity is simple and uncompounded, while they introduce a composite nature of the Son, then on their view the nature of the Son will be found to be different from that of the Father and the Holy Spirit. Moreover, the invention of the composite nature belongs to none other than the teacher of their error, Apollinaris, who sometimes speaks of one composite nature and at other times fabricates one nature of divinity and humanity. This can be found from the writings of that heretic. In the discourse he entitled "Against those who say that a man was assumed by the Word," he says this: "Christ is one man, as the Father is one God, which pertains to nature; so that this too belongs to a composite nature, intermediate between God and man." And again the same impious Apollinaris, in his discourse on the divine incarnation, in the thirteenth chapter, says this: "The flesh, being moved by another, is wholly moved by what moves and leads it, whatever that may be, and since it is not a complete living being by

…of itself, but so as to become a complete living being, composed [?] of the flesh.

Of the same, in the discourse On the Incarnation: “O new creation, O divine mixture! God and flesh have brought to completion one and the same nature.”

Of the same, to Peter: “We say that the Lord is God by nature and man by nature, but in one blended nature, at once fleshly and divine.”

[P. 224.] That the holy Cyril rejects those who speak of a composite nature and who fabricate one nature of flesh and Godhead, we shall at once demonstrate from the very words of the Father [?]. For in his discourse Against the Synousiasts he says this: “That we may believe that, even if his holy and all-pure body was of the same nature as our bodies, it is nevertheless venerable and divine, and far beyond our measures, inasmuch as it had become his own; for he acted through it. For this reason it was also named the bread of life. Indeed, it is even said to have come down from heaven and to give life to the world, because of the Word who came down from above and from heaven, whose own the flesh became. So then it is divine, as I said; yet no one would suppose that it was changed into the nature of Godhead, if he has a well-grounded mind and is skilled in precision of doctrine. For in the nature that is beyond all things and highest of all, there must be purely preserved its simplicity and its freedom from mixture with anything else, and that it should not be thought composite in what belongs to itself, or to need the addition of something not connatural with it [?] … to come into a communion of nature in identity, that is, of consubstantiality.”

By these words the Father clearly forbids us to speak of one composite nature in the case of the Godhead and the manhood of Christ, since the divine nature, when united to the human, does not admit of making up one nature with it. Now that the absurdity of our opponents has been refuted, it has become clear that the two natures, in coming together, produced not a composite nature but a composite Christ, since he is God by nature and man by nature, even though he is confessed to be one and the same. But the enemies of the truth, on top of their other absurdities, refusing to follow the doctrines of the Fathers and championing instead those of Apollinarius, leave no path of absurdity untried by which to corrupt the souls of the simpler sort. For they cunningly push away the name of Apollinarius, since it is a plain proof of impiety, and

attach the names of the holy Fathers to his writings and to their own fabrications, deceiving the simpler folk and running away from the path of truth. For they bring forward two letters falsely inscribed: one supposedly from Julius, bishop of Rome, written to Dionysius the presbyter, which runs as follows (see Muratori’s edition); and the other supposedly from the holy Athanasius, written to the emperor Jovian, which runs as follows: “We confess the Son of God, begotten [?] of the Father before the ages, and at the end of the ages, for our salvation, born according to the flesh of Mary the holy Virgin, as the divine Apostle teaches when he says: ‘But when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of a woman.’ And we confess that he himself is Son of God and God according to the Spirit, and Son of Man according to the flesh; not that the one Son is two natures, one worshipped and one not worshipped, but one nature of God the Word incarnate, worshipped together with his flesh with one worship.”

Since these things, then, are brought forward by the Acephali, the wisdom of God, destroying their wickedness from on high, did not allow the falsehood to remain unrefuted. For it granted us to come upon the writings of Apollinarius; and by setting these beside what these people bring forward, we shall plainly prove from Apollinarius’ own words that it is from him they have put these things forward. For Apollinarius himself writes this in his work Against Diodore: “That there should be one and the same worship of one substance and of another, that is, of Maker and of thing made, of God and of man, is unlawful. But the worship of Christ is one, and accordingly God and man are understood under the one name. Therefore God and man are not different substances, but one, by the composition of God with a human body.” And again in the same work: “For how is the matter not impious, that a different substance, created and servile, should have one and the same worship with the Creator and Master?” And again the same impious Apollinarius, in the discourse On the Incarnation: “It is impossible for the same one to know himself as both worshipped and not worshipped. It is impossible, therefore, that the same one should be wholly both God and man; rather he is in the singleness of a blended, incarnate divine nature.”

How well these agree with, and follow, the letters fraudulently brought forward by the Acephali under the names of Julius and Athanasius, our holy Fathers, is unknown to no one of sound mind. For saying “not two natures, one worshipped and one not worshipped,” and again, “that there should be one and the same worship of one substance and of another is unlawful,” and “that the created and servile substance should have one and the same worship with the Creator and Master,” shows no difference either in wording or in meaning. Having therefore proved that the two letters brought forward by the heretics belong to nothing other than the error

of Apollinarius, and are foreign to the catholic Church, let us show that the fabrications of the Acephali are also contrary to what has been set forth by our holy Fathers. (There follow … ) (Then p. 229.)

By all that has been said, I think, it has been clearly demonstrated that what the heretics bring forward is contrary to the teachings of the holy Fathers and foreign to the faith of Christians, since both the holy Athanasius and the holy Cyril plainly confess two natures, of the Godhead and of the manhood of Christ, calling the one uncreated and the other created, and teaching that our one Lord Jesus Christ is worshipped with one worship. What has been said is enough to expose the villainy of the Acephali. Still, there is nothing amiss in exposing their malice in another way as well, namely, that the letter they bring forward as supposedly by Julius, bishop of Rome, is shown to be forged on other grounds too. For the priests of elder Rome, having followed the apostolic tradition in all things, have never disagreed with one another, but have preserved the right and true doctrine to this day (3). Next, it is not the custom of the patriarch of elder Rome to use such a superscription as these people produce; we do not mean to presbyters, as they slanderously claim, but neither to bishops, nor even to patriarchs themselves. Third, when we sent to the archives of the episcopal residence of elder Rome, we found nothing of the kind written by Julius of holy memory.

As for the letter they bring forward as from the holy Athanasius to Jovian, it is shown in many ways to be utterly false. For it has neither the character of a letter, nor is it composed in language befitting an emperor. Moreover, in Jovian’s time no dispute had been raised about the Lord’s becoming man, but rather about consubstantiality in the Holy Trinity, since the Arian madness was then troubling the churches. On this matter the genuine letter of the holy Athanasius written to Jovian is extant, to which Gregory the Theologian bears witness in his funeral oration on St Athanasius, and which Timothy, the disciple of Apollinarius, sets down in full in his own history … [?]

[P. ?] Let us also show that Timothy Aelurus held views in agreement with the Manichaeans but contrary to those same holy Fathers, Athanasius and Cyril. For this same Timothy says the following in the eighth chapter of the third book, which he wrote in Cherson: “The nature of Christ is Godhead alone, even though he became incarnate.” And Mani, writing the same thing in his letter to Kundaros, says this: “The whole is one nature, even though the form of flesh was seen.” In reply we say that if, according to Timothy’s folly, the nature of Christ is Godhead alone, then Christ is also the Father and the Holy Spirit; for the nature of the Godhead is one,

that, I mean, of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. And by his madness the suffering will also be common to them.

(P. 236.) Again the blasphemer Timothy, as though not content with his earlier idle talk, reveals his disease more plainly in the second of his books of refutation. For he says this: “The incarnation of God the Word does not have the principle of nature, but of a dispensation carried out by God above nature, from our common and human nature or substance. For this reason he is said to be of like nature, of like kind, and consubstantial with us according to the principle of the dispensation, that is, his birth from a woman. But the undefiled body of God the Word, which is of like kind with us, has never been called the nature or substance of some ordinary man.”

From these words, then, it has become plain that Timothy denies that the incarnation of the Word has the principle of nature. And if it does not have the principle of nature, he is saying that it appeared in mere phantasm. For he says that God the Word was born “from our common and human nature or substance,” that is, from a woman, and that only in this respect is he said to be of like nature, of like kind, and consubstantial with us, and that God was born of a woman. Consubstantial with us, yes; yet he says that the Lord himself has nothing in common with men by nature or substance. For he adds: “The undefiled body of God the Word, which is of like kind with us, has never been called the nature or substance of some ordinary man.” By denying that the Lord’s body shares in our nature, he is clearly using the word “of like kind” [?] only to deceive, and understands nothing else by it than that he was born as a man in phantasm, and appeared as a man in seeming, not by nature. And if this is how things stand according to Timothy’s madness, it is clear that he says the passion, the cross, the death, and the resurrection of the Lord took place in phantasm, which is exactly what Mani says.

And again Timothy, adding worse things to his blasphemies, says this in the fourth chapter of the third book already mentioned: “Let the Dyophysites show us the difference between the two natures of Christ, as they call them, if they can.” See, he plainly denies the difference between the two natures in Christ; and in this, too, he likewise opposes all the other holy Fathers, and above all Athanasius and Cyril.

And again Timothy the heretic, devising still greater blasphemies for himself, puts forward a prophetic saying which runs thus: “Announcing his Christ to men; and the Lord God Almighty is his name.” Then, interpreting it wrongly, he adds: “He himself, then, announced it to men through himself; seeing him, the sun set at midday. But it did not admit of this taking place through a man, that is, through human nature; for human nature would have altogether and utterly dissolved the virginity. For if he who was to be brought to completion as man in the womb of the Virgin had been man according to nature and its law, he would not have been born of her without her virginity

first being dissolved.”

But may these words be turned back on the head of Timothy and of those who follow him! For he blasphemes, opposing both the divine Scripture and the holy Fathers, not perceiving that the wonder of the mystery of godliness lies above all in this: that the only-begotten Son and Word of God, being God by nature, and having become incarnate in the womb of the Virgin and become man by nature, was born of her and kept his mother a virgin.

[P. 238.] The holy Cyril, in the discourse That the Virgin Must Be Confessed as Theotokos (4), says this: “We acknowledge Christ as Lord and God. For the Word of God became man for our sake, sharing in human nature, and through his ineffable love for mankind he was born with it of the holy Virgin who knew not wedlock. For this reason, then, he is called man; and he is also called God, being one and the same Christ under either name.”

These things, then, we have set out from the divine Scriptures and from the holy Fathers to refute the heretics, so that all Christians may know that the heretics Dioscorus and Timothy Aelurus are shown to hold, quite plainly, the views of Mani and Apollinarius.

[P. 240.] Hear, too, how the holy Cyril clearly explains this in the discourse That the Holy Virgin Must Be Confessed as Theotokos. For he says this: “Nevertheless, let us consider this point as well: if the divine Apostle had not known Christ to be at once God and man, he would not have said ‘according to the flesh’; for this is plainly said of one who is not only man, but is also something else in substance. So indeed he went on: ‘who is God over all.’ For he has handed down to us a twofold confession concerning the Saviour, both pointing out what is according to the flesh and proclaiming him God. And again the Apostle, in the letter to Timothy: ‘There is one God and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all.’”

[P. 241.] The holy Ambrose says this: “God the Word did not take his beginning from the Virgin, but, being coeternal with his own Father, he deigned in his great goodness to unite to himself the firstfruits of our nature; not blended, but [?] appearing one and the same in each of the two substances, as it is written: ‘Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.’ For Christ Jesus is destroyed according to my substance, which he took, and the same one raises up his own temple once destroyed according to his divine substance, by which he is also the creator of all things.”

And in the Gospel according to Matthew the Lord says to the one who was betraying him: “Are you betraying the Son of Man with a kiss?” Peter, martyr and archbishop of Alexandria, explaining this (Luke 22:48),

says the following, and things like it: “All the signs he did, and the mighty works, show him to be God made man. Both, then, are shown together: that he was God by nature, and became man by nature.”

[P. 242.] We must pay attention to this: when the Apostle said “who,” he indicated the hypostasis of the Word as existing in the form of God, that is, in the substance of the Father. And he did not say that he took one already existing in the form of a servant, so as not to show the man as pre-existing, according to the madness of Nestorius; but he said that he took the form of a servant, that is, the substance of a man, showing that the flesh had its existence in the hypostasis of the Word, so that, being one and the same in one hypostasis, he might be made known in each form, that is, in each nature, the divine and the human. For it is clear that God the Word, begotten of the Father before all ages, is not of the same hypostasis as the Father, but of the same substance, in that he is God; while he has his own hypostasis, in that he is the Word. And the same, born according to the flesh in the last days of the holy and glorious Virgin and Theotokos Mary, is not of the same hypostasis as his Mother, but of the same substance. How then do the Acephali [?] a union of hypostases, while not admitting the union according to hypostasis? Or do they not know that Nestorius too was condemned for just such an error, introducing two hypostases into the dispensation? But since this is so, the Acephali would rather put up with uttering doctrines more loathsome than those of Nestorius and of every heresy than agree with the truth. So much, then, from us against them.

The holy Ambrose too, explaining this same saying of the Apostle in his discourse Against Apollinarius, writes as follows: “Most beautifully does the Apostle use the repetition of the same words when he says of our Lord Jesus Christ: ‘who, being in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.’ What is the form of God, if not that impress of divine perfection in the fullness of the Godhead? Being, then, in the perfection of the Godhead, he emptied himself and took the perfection of a complete human nature; and just as he lacked nothing as God, so he lacked nothing in the fitting-out of the man, so that he might be perfect in each nature.”

[P. 244.] We consider, then, that what we have set out from the divine Scripture and from the holy Fathers is sufficient to demonstrate that there is one hypostasis, or one person, of our Lord Jesus Christ, but that he is made known in two natures, that is, in Godhead and manhood, even though we have brought forward only a few passages out of many, so as not to burden what we are writing with their sheer number. But since the truth is sometimes made plain even by its enemies, just as the demons confessed Christ to be the Son of God even against their will, we shall show that Severus himself, the successor of Apollinarius

and the one who swelled the error of the Acephali, confesses that all the holy Fathers spoke of two natures in Christ without reproach. Thus he says the following in the discourse which he calls, forsooth, an Exposition of Faith: “To speak of two natures…” etc. (which we have already cited elsewhere). Then, persisting in the same line, he says in what follows that the expressions of the Fathers who used the term without reproach cannot be brought forward, even if they were spoken before this time by Cyril himself. If, then, Severus himself confesses that all the holy Fathers, and indeed the holy Cyril too, used the term without reproach, who then had such authority as to reject the teaching of the holy Fathers? Or how can Severus call them Fathers whose doctrines he says have been rejected? But he plainly shows himself up: unable to escape the truth, he confessed that this expression had been used by the holy Fathers, yet, wishing to plead the cause of his own disease, he says that the teachings of the holy Fathers were rejected because of the blasphemies of Nestorius, which is worth a laugh. By this he attempted to set aside the holy Fathers, and did not shrink from slandering the holy Cyril as contradicting both what he himself had said earlier and the holy Fathers.

However, since he says that the holy Fathers used this expression without reproach up to the time of Nestorius, we shall show that the holy Cyril, using the expression “two natures” of the Saviour’s dispensation, condemned Nestorius, and that again, after the condemnation of Nestorius, the same holy Cyril used the same teaching. For Severus seems to have understood neither the holy Fathers nor the reason for which Nestorius was condemned. The holy Fathers, while confessing two united natures, of the Godhead of Christ and of his manhood, forbade speaking of two hypostases or two sons in him. For Nestorius confessed that nature, hypostasis and person are the same thing, and for this reason denied the union of the two natures according to hypostasis, speaking of the two natures as separate and as each having its own hypostasis, and so fabricating two sons and two Christs; and for this blasphemy of his he was condemned by the holy Fathers. Indeed the holy Cyril, exposing his Jewish madness at the synod of Ephesus, brought forward the holy Fathers forbidding us to speak of two Sons, but proclaiming two natures and one Son.

[P. 251.] From all that has been said, then, it has been demonstrated that the holy Cyril, both before the condemnation of Nestorius, and at the condemnation itself, and after his condemnation, never ceased always to proclaim the confession of the two natures in the one Christ. But Severus, the enemy of the truth, understanding none of this, calls the Fathers by the name of Fathers, forsooth, yet denies the doctrines rightly handed down by them to the Church, not knowing that Nestorius was condemned for his own impiety, but that the teaching of the Fathers was not done away with on his account. For if, according to the madness of Severus, the expressions which by the holy

…of the Fathers, rightly spoken but wrongly taken up by heretics, must be rejected, then he will also set aside the divine Scripture itself, since all heretics think they can use it to support their own disease. Plainly, by his nonsense, both the divine Scriptures and the traditions of the Fathers will be thrown out. We say this against the heretics who set aside the teaching of the Fathers. The holy Church of God, however, turns away from these same empty words of the heretics and guards the tradition of the Lord and of the holy apostles and Fathers. It proclaims one and the same only-begotten God the Word, the Lord Jesus Christ, made known in both essences: that of God the Father and that of the Virgin Mother. Those who do not confess this deny either the birth of the only-begotten Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, from God the Father, or his birth from the holy, glorious Theotokos and Ever-Virgin Mary. For on their view, if Christ does not have someone's essence, he has also ceased to be that one's Son. But suppose that, compelled by the divine Scripture and the teaching of the Fathers, they confess with us that Christ is truly the Son of God the Father, and that the same Christ is truly the Son of the Virgin Mother. Then they must also confess that he has two essences, just as the two births belong to one and the same. The Fathers teach that the nature of Christ's Godhead has not been changed into the nature of his flesh, nor the nature of his flesh into that of the Godhead. Nor has the difference of the natures been abolished by the union: each has remained what it is by nature. The proclamation about him is twofold, and he is made known in both essences, that is, in Godhead and in manhood. If this is so, how do they not see their own error, these people who fabricate a single nature of Christ? They blasphemously abolish the realities themselves and grant Christ only the bare names of Godhead and manhood. Disregarding all right teaching, they fix their minds on one thing alone: the idea that nature, that is, essence and form, means the same as hypostasis and person.

This was shown in enough detail in the treatise we have already written to Zoilus, the most blessed archbishop and patriarch of Alexandria. There we established that nature and form mean the same thing and are used in a common sense, while person and hypostasis are said of particular individuals. Even so, we will show the same point here by other testimonies of the holy Fathers. — [P. 535] We have said these things, then, to show that essence, nature and form mean the same thing. The heretics, in their error, say that essence and hypostasis are the same, but the theology of the holy Trinity also teaches us that they are not. When we say "God," we signify the one essence of the holy Trinity. But when we say "Father

and Son and Holy Spirit," we are pointing to the three hypostases, or the three persons, made known in the one nature of the Godhead. The divine voice teaches us this when it says, "Let us make man in our image and likeness." The words "let us make" do not signify one person, as the madness of Sabellius would have it. They are spoken in the plural, and so they indicate the holy Trinity. The words "in our image" indicate the one essence of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. God did not say "in our images," in case we supposed, with the madness of Arius, that the essences of the Trinity are different. He said "in the image," to show that the holy Trinity is one essence and consubstantial. And by saying "man" with "in our image," he signified the rational nature of humanity, by which we are the image of God. He did not say "Let us make this man," which would suggest a person; he said "Let us make man," to point to the rational nature of humanity. When he wished to present the hypostases, he named the male and the female Adam and Eve, and these are persons or hypostases. [P. 256.] Who would not marvel at how unreasonable the heretics are? They speak of a union, and at times they confess the difference of the natures in Christ, yet they deny the number that the difference of the united realities brings with it. In this too they plainly suffer from the madness of Apollinaris. Apollinaris himself says this in the syllogisms he wrote: "Intermediates arise when different properties come together into one. So in a mule there is the property of the donkey and of the horse; in the colour grey there is the property of white and of black; and in the air the property of winter and of summer produces spring. But no intermediate has both extremes in full; it has them partly mixed. Now Christ is an intermediate between God and men. Therefore he is neither wholly man nor wholly God, but a mixture of God and man." Again, in his treatise entitled "That Christ Is God Incarnate," which he wrote as a dialogue of questions and answers, he is asked: "What then? Is Christ not both God and man? Or do you call Christ God while denying that he is also man?" And he replies: "Not in two essences, but in one." We have quoted these passages to show that the Acephali follow the wicked doctrines of Apollinaris. They do not confess that Christ exists and is made known in two essences, but in one. Yet our holy Fathers, speaking of the ineffable union of the Godhead and the manhood of Christ, did not hand down one nature. They taught us to confess the number of the united natures. [P. 257.] The heretics, then, are shown up: by denying the number of the realities that came together, they abolish the union itself. They call Christ God and man only to deceive simpler people. If they truly called Christ perfect God and perfect man, they would plainly also confess that the two essences are preserved in him;

but since they do not confess the number of the united realities, they are shown to be saying that nothing in Christ is perfect. The teacher of their error, Apollinaris, writes exactly this in his treatise On the Divine Incarnation: "For if perfect God had been joined to perfect man, they would be two. But what is imperfect, when it is compounded with what is perfect, is not regarded as a pair." [P. 259] From what has been said, then, it is clear that wherever a union of different realities is understood, the number of the united things is always recognized as well. But the enemies of the truth always devise the worse course in their impiety. They not only err about the economy of the One of the holy Trinity; they even blaspheme the consubstantial Trinity itself. Severus went so far as to say that the Thrice-Holy hymn refers to the Son alone, and that the Father and the Holy Spirit have no share in that doxology. This is nothing other than to follow the madness of Arius, separating the Son from the essence of the Father and the Holy Spirit and making him of another essence. Or if not that, it is to follow the blasphemy of Nestorius: they do not confess that Christ is God and one of the holy Trinity, but in their folly send up such a hymn to some fourth person. They think they are honouring the Son, but without knowing it they dishonour him, because they separate him from being worshipped together with the Father and the Holy Spirit. In saying this they have not even managed to be consistent with themselves. For when the hymn has been sung a third time, we at once add: "Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit." But why speak of their being inconsistent with themselves? They have no respect even for the Seraphim, who offer the doxology to the holy Trinity through the Thrice-Holy cry, as our holy Fathers have also handed down on this point. [P. [?]] The Fathers set these things out to refute the blasphemy of the heretics, and so handed down the right confession of the Church. They taught us to confess one Godhead, one power and one essence of the holy Trinity, and to offer the same glory and worship to the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. They also taught us to confess the one person of the holy and consubstantial Trinity, our Lord Jesus Christ, as true God and true man. He is consubstantial with the Father in his Godhead, and the same is consubstantial with us in his manhood. He is not consubstantial with the Father by the same essence by which he is consubstantial with us, nor with us by the essence by which he is consubstantial with the Father. For it is impossible for one essence, or nature, to be consubstantial with God and with men. Rather, of the two natures made known in one hypostasis, one shares in common with the Father and the other with us. We want you to know clearly the confession that we keep in following the catholic and apostolic Church. So we have set it out briefly in chapters, and we make it plain to you, and through you to those who have chosen the monastic life in Alexandria and the country around it.
1. If anyone does not confess that the holy Trinity has one essence, that is, one nature and Godhead, in three hypostases, or persons, worshipped in Father, Son and Holy Spirit, let him be anathema.

2. If anyone says that God the Word or the Holy Spirit is a creature, or is of another essence than that of the Father, let him be anathema. 3. If anyone says that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are the same, supposing one person with many names and one hypostasis called by three titles, we class such a person with the Jews and anathematize him. 4. If anyone does not confess that the one person of the only-begotten Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, has two births, let him be anathema. One birth is before the ages from the Father, according to the Godhead. The other is the birth of the same in the last days from the holy Virgin and Theotokos Mary, according to the manhood. He must also be confessed as one of the holy Trinity, that is, one hypostasis of the three hypostases. 5. If anyone does not confess the holy, glorious, ever-virgin Mary as Theotokos, let him be anathema. 6. Let such a person be anathematized by all Christians: anyone who brings in two Sons, one from God the Father and another from the Mother; or who says that Jesus was moved to act as a mere man, and that the glory of the Only-begotten was attached to him as to someone other than himself, as Paul of Samosata and Nestorius blaspheme; and who does not confess one and the same Son, the only-begotten God the Word, the Lord Jesus Christ. 7. If anyone says that he passed through the Virgin as through a pipe, and was not formed within her both divinely and humanly at once (divinely because without a man, humanly because by the law of pregnancy), likewise [?]

8. If anyone divides between two persons, or hypostases, the sayings in the Gospel writings, whether the saints said them about Christ or he said them about himself, let him be anathema. 9. If anyone does not confess that the Godhead and the manhood of Christ have one hypostasis, that is, one person, let him be anathema. 10. If anyone says that the Only-begotten had two natures before the union but one after it, and so invents a single nature of his Godhead and his flesh, let him be anathema. 11. If anyone does not confess the following, let him be anathema: that the two natures, of Godhead and of manhood, came together into one hypostasis and made up one Christ; that he is made known in both natures, unconfused and undivided, which is why we confess the same as perfect [?] in manhood; and that the miracles and the sufferings belong to one and the same.
These are the things we have been taught by the divine Scripture. These are the doctrines of the catholic Church. These are the traditions of the Fathers, both of those

who have shone out in the holy Church of God through the ages, and of those at the four holy councils: the three hundred and eighteen at Nicaea, the hundred and fifty at Constantinople, the two hundred assembled at the first council of Ephesus, and the six hundred and thirty at Chalcedon. These Fathers are the law of the Church. With the help of the Holy Spirit they drove out of the Church the heretics who sprang up from time to time, together with their abominable doctrines. But the enemies of true religion cling to the tares the devil sowed and will not follow the good seed. They are always making excuses, and since they have no argument at all, they take refuge in saying that their teaching was handed down from their fathers and that they cannot abandon it. The followers of Nestorius claim as fathers Paul, Photinus, Marcellus and those who thought as they did. The Acephali claim Eutyches, Dioscorus, Timothy Aelurus and those who thought as they did, and these have been shown to follow the madness of Apollinaris, Mani and Valentinus. How, then, will people who say such things lead Jews and Greeks to Christianity, when Jews and Greeks put forward the same kind of plea? They say that their impiety is not only handed down from their fathers but is much older than that of these heretics. We therefore urge your God-belovedness to solemnly charge everyone who fears the Lord and awaits the judgment of God not to be carried away by various and strange teachings. Instead, once they are taught the right and blameless faith, they should hurry to the holy catholic and apostolic Church of God, where the priests of God proclaim the apostolic teaching with one voice throughout the whole world.

From the dogmatic letter of the most pious Emperor Justinian to Zoilus, the most holy patriarch of Alexandria. Christ, then, is one. The difference of the natures has not been abolished by the ineffable union: he is understood as the Word and seen as man. The union did not produce confusion, nor does the difference of the essences in him allow any cutting or division.

For when we see the miracles of Christ, we proclaim his Godhead; when we see his sufferings, we do not deny his manhood. We do not take the miracles apart from the flesh, nor the sufferings apart from the Godhead. And it is a paradox that he himself was the one who suffered and also did not suffer. He suffered because his own body suffered. Yet in that very body he did not suffer, for the Word, being God by nature, was impassible. He, the incorporeal, was in the passible body, and the body had within it the impassible Word, who did away with the weaknesses of the body. For each form does what is proper to it in communion with the other: the Word performs what belongs to the Word, and the body carries out what belongs to the body. Cyril among the saints teaches this in the thirty-second chapter of the Thesaurus, where he interprets the Epistle to the Romans: "Surely we will not grant that God and a created thing have one natural operation. Otherwise we would raise what was made to the divine essence, or bring down what is unique to the divine nature to the level that suits begotten things." The same holy Father teaches us the same thing in his writings to Theodosius: "We say that the Word from God was united, whole, to the whole of our humanity. He would not have counted the better part of us, the soul, as worthless by granting the purposes of his coming to the flesh alone. The mystery of the economy was rightly carried out through both. He used his own flesh as an instrument for the works of the flesh and for its natural weaknesses, so far as these are free from blame. And he used his own soul for human and blameless passions. For he is said to have been hungry, to have endured the weariness of long journeys, alarm and fear, grief and agony, and death on the cross. No one compelled him; of his own accord he laid down his own soul for us, so that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living. He paid his own flesh as a truly fitting ransom for the flesh of all, and made his own soul a ransom in exchange for the soul of all. And he came back to life, because as God he has life by nature. It is not right to say that the flesh united to the Word could ever be overpowered by corruption, or that the divine soul was held fast by the gates of Hades themselves. For he was not abandoned to Hades, as the inspired Peter also said. Nor can we say that the nature that death can never seize or capture, that is, the Godhead of the Only-begotten, was brought up from the depths of the earth. The event would not have been thought a wonder if the Word from God had remained in Hades, since by the operation and nature of his Godhead he fills all things and is present to all, in a way that is wondrous and beyond reason." Then, further on in his discourse, he says again: "To have died is a human passion, but to have come back to life is a divine operation. He shows that through both he is known to be like us and at the same time above us, as God." Do you see how this venerable Father

hands down the operations of the two natures in the one hypostasis, that is, the one person, of Christ our God? And a little later: "Then, having become man for our sake, he became visible and tangible. He was shown through divine and human operations to exist in Godhead and in manhood, and so he has given us to know that he consists of those things in which he was made known." In the same way the holy Fathers confess both kinds of sayings, those that come from the Godhead and those that come from the manhood. Through each of them they hand down that the economy of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ is without confusion and without division.

Chrysobull of the Emperor Justinian of blessed memory, which he granted to the abbot of Mount Sinai. The ruler grants fitting honour to those of his subjects who are loyal and skilled in the service of emperors and rulers. These are men who have been entrusted with commanding armies, governing cities, leading peoples, or doing other such things that seem useful to the power of the Roman realm. If that is so, how much more do men deserve to see their proposals carried through when they are venerable in life and character and draw near to God? They seek nothing that concerns outward things. They seek better things, which bring benefit to the soul itself, or rather which secure both kinds of benefit for them, since the hand from above sets emperors on high. How, then, could it not be the duty of rulers to lend a willing ear, to grant, and to carry out whatever such men ask? And suppose that what is asked has reason on its side as well, so that the thing deserves to be done not only because these men ask it but already on its own merits. Then sovereigns are all the more to be praised for granting their requests, and they should give whatever such men wish. In this way they gratify not only the petitioners but also, as is fitting, justice itself. My Majesty can now see this being fulfilled as it grants to those on Mount Sinai the exalted honour of the hypertimoi. It does so, first, because of the petition made to me by the

most sacred metropolitan of Ptolemais, who is himself hypertimos. I judged it wholly wrong not to give a willing hearing to him, since he asked for reasonable things, and leaving them undone would have done some harm to justice. Second, I do so because in any case I regard such a mountain as venerable and rightly entitled to enjoy every honour. I consider, too, that my Majesty is itself honoured by the honour shown to it, since God knows how to glorify those who glorify him. For this mountain rises above all others in our lands. It is a divine mountain and [?], thickly wooded and shaded by the labours of the saints, and covered with the foliage of every kind of virtue. If anyone wishes to call it a holy place and the house of the God of Jacob, the name fits it well and comes very close to the truth. Indeed, anyone who looks more clearly will see that this divine house is full of great glory. Yet in these last times there will also be this share of glory, granted to it by my Majesty. So one may see the glory it had of old advancing to something greater, as the prophet says. This, then, is what the present decree of my Majesty intends. My Majesty honours whoever presides on Sinai at any given time with the dignity of the hypertimoi. It decrees that he be counted third among those who hold this honour, and that he share their honour in every respect: in processions, in seating, in standing places and in assemblies. He is also to wear vestments like those of the archbishops who have received this honour from earlier times until now. All the other privileges that belong to them shall belong to him too, reduced in no respect. It was for this purpose that the present decree of my Majesty was issued. In the month of Panemus in the Greek reckoning, that is, July, in the fourteenth indiction.
